domain.tag: the machine · files and paths · a terminal · the network · accounts · typing
domain.why: This domain assumes nothing — not that you've used a terminal, not that you know what a 'file' really is versus a shortcut to one. That's deliberate: everything after this silently assumes you can open a command line, find a file, and not lose your work. You need a real laptop or desktop for this and for the C and shell work right after it, but the explanations themselves are written to be readable on a phone, so you can read them on the bus and try them out later on a borrowed machine.

sections.note: Exit: name what is inside the box, and say what the OS does that the programs do not.

concepts.t: What a computer is made of

L0.body:
+------------------------------------+
 | CPU   runs the instructions        |
 | RAM   working memory; forgets      |
 | disk  storage (SSD); remembers     |
 | GPU   draws pixels, does matrices  |
 +------------------------------------+
   screen, keyboard, mouse, network:
   data in, data out
 a 3 GHz core: 3 000 000 000 ticks/s
 a laptop CPU: 4 to 16 such cores
 power off: RAM blank, disk intact
L0.cloze: Inside the box: the {{c1::CPU}} runs the instructions, about {{c4::3}} billion steps a second on each of 4 to 16 cores; {{c2::RAM}} is the working memory and forgets at power off; the {{c3::disk}} (an SSD) is storage and remembers; the {{c5::GPU}} draws pixels and does matrix arithmetic. Screen, keyboard, mouse and network only move data in and out.

concepts.L1: A computer is four parts in a box plus things plugged into it. The CPU executes instructions, billions per second per core. RAM holds what is in use right now. The disk (an SSD) keeps files through power off. The GPU draws the screen and does matrix arithmetic. Screen, keyboard, mouse and network compute nothing.
concepts.L2: The miss is treating the CPU as 'the brain that knows things'. It knows nothing: it does whatever the next instruction says, three billion times a second, and every fact, picture and program is bytes in RAM or on the disk. So a faster CPU does not fix 'disk full', and more disk does not fix 'out of memory'.
concepts.L3: A CPU core is a loop: read the next instruction from RAM, do it (add two numbers, compare, copy a byte, jump elsewhere), repeat. A 3 GHz core runs that loop about three billion times a second and a laptop has 4 to 16 cores each running their own. RAM is an array of numbered bytes the CPU reads and writes directly. The disk is not: the CPU cannot execute from it, so a program is copied from disk into RAM before it runs, which is what 'loading' is and why a slow disk shows as a slow start rather than a slow run. The GPU is a second processor with hundreds or thousands of very simple cores; it draws the screen and, since about 2012, does the matrix arithmetic of machine learning. Foundations' 'Fetch, decode, execute' and 'Memory as one addressed array of bytes' are this paragraph with the mechanism filled in, and 16 GPU Kernels & Compilers is the GPU half.

L4.prompt_tpl: You plug a faster external keyboard and a sharper monitor into a laptop. Neither makes any program run faster. Why not?
L4.answer: Screen and keyboard only move data in and out; the computing is done by the CPU
L4.explanation: A computer's in/out devices carry data across the boundary of the box; not one of them adds, compares or copies a byte on its own. A sharper screen changes what you see and a better keyboard changes how it feels to type, and neither changes how long a program takes. The parts that decide that are the CPU, the GPU, the RAM and the disk.
options: Screen and keyboard only move data in and out; the computing is done by the CPU
The laptop's ports are the bottleneck, so better devices behind them change nothing
Windows must be told about a new device before any program can get the speed

L4.prompt_tpl: A CPU core runs at {g} GHz, which is {g} billion ticks per second. How many ticks is that in one microsecond (one millionth of a second)?
L4.answer: A billion ticks per second divided by a million microseconds per second: g times 1000. g=2 -> 2000; g=3 -> 3000; g=3.5 -> 3500.
L4.explanation: A gigahertz is a billion ticks a second and a microsecond is a millionth of a second, so one microsecond holds a billion divided by a million, a thousand ticks for every GHz. At 3 GHz that is 3000 ticks. Keep the number: in the time a key press takes to register, a core has already done tens of millions of steps.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which description of the CPU is right?
L4.answer: It follows one simple instruction after another, and keeps only the few numbers it is working on
L4.explanation: The CPU is an instruction-following machine. It keeps a few dozen numbers in registers while it works on them, plus a cache of recently used bytes, and nothing else: all files, pictures and programs are bytes in RAM or on the disk. 'The part that knows things' is the mental model to unlearn.
options: It follows one simple instruction after another, and keeps only the few numbers it is working on
It stores your files and photos and hands them to programs when they ask for them
It holds the computer's knowledge, the way a brain holds what a person has learned

L4.prompt_tpl: A machine-learning program spends almost all its time multiplying large tables of numbers. Which part of the machine does that work fastest?
L4.answer: The GPU
L4.explanation: The CPU has a handful of strong cores and does one thing at a time very fast; the GPU has hundreds or thousands of weak cores that all do the same arithmetic on different numbers at once, which is the exact shape of a matrix multiply. RAM holds the numbers and computes nothing at all. This is why machine learning runs on GPUs, and it is where 16 GPU Kernels & Compilers begins.
options: The GPU
The CPU
The RAM

L4.prompt_tpl: A laptop has 8 cores, each running at 3 GHz. A learner concludes that their single program therefore runs at 24 GHz. Say what is wrong, and what 8 cores actually buys.
L4.answer: Nothing runs at 24 GHz. Each core is a separate loop stepping at 3 GHz, and one program's instructions have to be done in order, so a program written as a single sequence runs on one core at 3 GHz however many cores sit idle beside it. Eight cores buy eight things happening at once: eight programs, or one program deliberately split into eight pieces that do not have to wait for each other. Speed per step and number of steps at once are different quantities and do not add.
L4.explanation: Clock speed and core count multiply only when the work can be cut into independent pieces, and most everyday work cannot. That is why a laptop with twice the cores does not open a document twice as fast, and it is the beginner half of everything Whetstone later says about parallelism.

L4.prompt_tpl: A laptop takes twenty seconds to open a large program, then runs it smoothly. Which component is the bottleneck during those twenty seconds, and why does the slowness stop once the program is open?
L4.answer: The disk. The CPU cannot run code from the disk, so the program's files are copied from disk into RAM first; that copy is the twenty seconds. Once the code and data are in RAM the CPU works from RAM, which is roughly a thousand times faster to reach, so the disk drops out of the loop.
L4.explanation: Loading is a disk-to-RAM copy. A slow disk (or a spinning hard drive instead of an SSD) shows up as slow starts, not slow running; a slow CPU or too little RAM shows up as slow running. Diagnosing which is which is the first thing this concept buys you.

L4.prompt_tpl: With forty browser tabs open the machine says it is out of memory. The SSD is only half full. Would replacing the 256 GB SSD with a 1 TB SSD fix it?
L4.answer: No: 'memory' here is RAM, and the SSD is storage
L4.explanation: The message is about RAM, the working memory that holds every open tab. A bigger SSD stores more files; it does not hold more open programs. The OS does spill parts of RAM out to the disk when it runs short, which is why the machine crawls before it complains, but the disk is roughly a thousand times slower, so that is a delay and not a substitute. The fix is fewer tabs or more RAM.
options: No: 'memory' here is RAM, and the SSD is storage
Yes: more space means more memory
Yes, but only if the SSD is faster

L4.prompt_tpl: A training job on a machine with 64 GB of RAM and a graphics card carrying 24 GB of its own memory stops with 'CUDA out of memory'. Which of the two memories ran out, and why does the machine's 64 GB not help?
L4.answer: The 24 GB on the graphics card. A GPU has its own memory beside its own cores and can compute only on numbers that are in it, so the model's weights and the batch it is working on have to fit there. The 64 GB belongs to the CPU, on the far side of a slow connection, and the GPU cannot execute out of it, exactly as the CPU cannot execute out of the disk. The fix is a smaller batch, a smaller model, or a card with more memory, never more system RAM.
L4.explanation: Transfer of the same rule one level out: a processor computes only from the memory attached to it, and everything else must be copied in first. That copy is what 16 GPU Kernels & Compilers spends its first weeks on, and it is why 'out of memory' on a GPU is a different sentence from 'out of memory' on a laptop.

L4.prompt_tpl: Foundations' 'Fetch, decode, execute' describes the CPU's loop. Explain why a program sitting on the disk must be copied into RAM before it can run, rather than being executed where it is.
L4.answer: The loop reads its next instruction from RAM by address, does it, and repeats, billions of times a second. The disk is not wired to the CPU that way: it is reached as whole blocks, through the OS, rather than as numbered bytes, and it is far too slow to feed a loop running at that rate. So the OS copies the program's instructions from the disk into RAM, points the CPU at the first one, and only then does the loop run. That copy is what 'loading' means; the next concept puts numbers on the speed gap.
L4.explanation: The CPU executes only from RAM. Every later fact about memory (the heap, virtual memory, caches) refines this one: where the bytes are decides whether the CPU can touch them and how fast.

concepts.t: Storage versus memory: what survives a power cut

L0.body:
RAM (memory)        DISK (storage)
 8 to 16 GB          256 GB to 2 TB
 forgets at power    keeps files
 off                 for years
 reach: ~100 ns      ~100 us (SSD)
                     ~10 ms  (HDD)
 typing in an open   Save copies
 document = RAM      it to disk
 power cut before    power cut after
 Save: edits gone    Save: safe
 sold: 1 GB  = 1 000 000 000 bytes
 shown: 1 GiB = 1 073 741 824 bytes
L0.cloze: RAM is the working memory: it {{c1::forgets}} when the power goes, and a laptop has 8 to 16 GB of it. The disk is storage: it {{c2::keeps}} files for years, hundreds of GB. Typing in an open document changes {{c3::RAM}}; Save copies the document to {{c4::disk}}. A power cut before Save loses the edits since the last Save.

concepts.L1: Memory (RAM) is where running programs and their data live: fast, small (8 to 16 GB), blank the moment power stops. Storage (the disk) holds files: large (hundreds of GB), a thousand times slower to reach if an SSD and far worse if it spins, intact through power off. 'Save' is the copy from the first to the second.
concepts.L2: The miss is one undifferentiated 'memory' that is both 'where my files are' and 'why it is slow'. From it follow 'I lost my work' (the edits were only in RAM), 'the disk is full, so add RAM', and reading '16 GB' as pitifully small storage. There are two quantities: how much you can hold open at once, and how much you can keep.
concepts.L3: RAM forgets because each bit is a charge on a capacitor that leaks away in tens of milliseconds; the chip walks the whole array every 64 milliseconds rewriting each cell, and with no power there is nothing to refresh. An SSD cell traps its charge behind an insulator and holds it for years while the drive is healthy. The price is speed: reaching RAM takes about 100 nanoseconds, an SSD about 100 microseconds, a spinning disk about 10 milliseconds, so the CPU works only from RAM and everything on disk is copied in first. An open document is a copy in RAM; editing changes the copy; Save writes it back. The GB gap: makers sell GB of $10^{9}$ bytes, Windows reports GiB of $2^{30}$ bytes and labels them GB, so a '500 GB' drive shows 465.7 GB. Foundations' 'Virtual memory' is the OS giving each program its own private map of addresses, which is also how it spills RAM to disk when it runs out.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have typed for an hour in a document you saved twenty minutes ago. The power fails. What survives?
L4.answer: The version saved twenty minutes ago; the edits since then are gone
L4.explanation: The saved version is bytes on the disk and survives. The last twenty minutes of edits existed only as the copy in RAM, which went blank with the power, so there is no partial rescue: being open is what made them vulnerable, not what protected them. An editor with autosave recovers a few minutes only because autosave already wrote them to disk, which is Save on a timer.
options: The version saved twenty minutes ago; the edits since then are gone
That version plus the last few minutes, because the document was still open
Everything you typed, because the computer remembers what was on the screen

L4.prompt_tpl: A drive is sold as {g} GB, where the maker counts 1 GB as 1 000 000 000 bytes. Windows counts in units of 1 073 741 824 bytes (2^30) but still writes GB. What size does Windows show, in GB, to 3 decimal places?
L4.explanation: Divide the byte count by 1 073 741 824. A '500 GB' drive shows 465.661 GB in Windows. No space is missing: the maker counts in powers of ten, Windows in powers of two. macOS and Ubuntu's file manager count in powers of ten too and show 500.

L4.prompt_tpl: A laptop has 16 GB of RAM and {f} GB free on the disk. Each photo is {m} MB (1 GB = 1000 MB). How many whole photos can you keep?
L4.answer: floor(1000 f / m), where f is the free disk space. f=10, m=3 -> 3333; f=10, m=4 -> 2500; f=10, m=6 -> 1666.
L4.explanation: Photos are kept on the disk, so the 16 GB of RAM is no part of this sum; reaching for it is the mistake the item is looking for. Convert to one unit, divide, drop the fraction: 10 GB free is 10 000 MB, and 10 000 / 3 = 3333.3, so 3333 photos. This sum uses the maker's 1 GB = 1000 MB, unlike the Windows item above, which counts in powers of two.

L4.prompt_tpl: A laptop is listed as: 3.2 GHz, 16 GB, 512 GB. Which of the three numbers limits how many programs you can have open at once?
L4.answer: The 16 GB figure
L4.explanation: The middle figure is RAM: what can be open now. The 512 GB is the SSD, storage: what can be kept, which is why it is the largest number on the sheet. The 3.2 GHz says how fast instructions run and holds nothing at all. Read a spec sheet as three separate questions: how fast, how much open, how much kept.
options: The 16 GB figure
The 512 GB figure
The 3.2 GHz figure

L4.prompt_tpl: A learner's laptop keeps saying 'disk almost full'. They buy and fit 16 GB of RAM. What happens to the message, and what should they have done?
L4.answer: Nothing improves, and on Windows it gets slightly worse: the hibernation file and the page file are both sized from the amount of RAM, so more RAM consumes a few more GB of the disk. The message is about storage and RAM is memory, so the disk is at least as full as before. They needed to delete or move files, or fit a larger SSD. The RAM upgrade would only have helped a different complaint: programs slowing down, or 'out of memory' with many things open.
L4.explanation: Two quantities, two fixes. 'Disk full' is about what is kept; 'out of memory' is about what is open. Matching the message to the component is the whole skill, and mismatching it is the most common wasted purchase.

L4.prompt_tpl: A friend says 'my SSD is fast, so it barely matters whether data is in RAM or on the disk'. RAM takes about {r} nanoseconds to reach and an SSD about {s} microseconds (1 microsecond = 1000 nanoseconds). Work out how many times slower the SSD is, and enter that number.
L4.answer: Put both in nanoseconds and divide: 1000 s / r. r=100, s=100 -> 1000; r=100, s=50 -> 500; r=80, s=100 -> 1250.
L4.explanation: Put both in nanoseconds: 100 microseconds is 100 000 ns, and 100 000 / 100 = 1000. Three orders of magnitude is not 'barely matters'; it is the difference between an instant and a wait, and it is exactly why loading exists and why the CPU never works from the disk directly. A spinning hard drive at about 10 ms is another hundred times slower again.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does RAM lose everything the moment the power stops?
L4.answer: Each bit is a charge on a tiny capacitor that leaks away and must be constantly rewritten
L4.explanation: RAM is millions of tiny buckets of charge. Left alone each one drains in a fraction of a second, so the chip walks the whole array every 64 milliseconds and writes each cell back to what it was. Pull the power and there is nothing left to do the rewriting, so the charge drains and the bits are gone. Nothing decided to erase them, and nothing is left behind to recover: this is hardware, not a policy of the OS.
options: Each bit is a charge on a tiny capacitor that leaks away and must be constantly rewritten
The operating system deliberately clears it for security as the machine shuts down
The data is still there, but the list of names that pointed at it has been lost

L4.prompt_tpl: A learner keeps a browser with thirty tabs, a video call and a document open, and stores four years of photos. Which number on the spec sheet should they spend money on, and which complaint would tell them they got it wrong?
L4.answer: The RAM figure. Thirty tabs, a call and a document are all open at once, and holding what is open is what RAM does; four years of photos are kept rather than open, and an external drive or a cloud account fixes that far more cheaply than a bigger SSD. If they spent the money on the SSD instead, the complaint that tells them so is the machine crawling, or saying 'out of memory', with everything open. If they bought RAM and in fact needed storage, the complaint is 'disk almost full'.
L4.explanation: The sizing question turned round: count what has to be open at once, count what has to be kept, and buy against whichever is nearer its limit. The two complaints are the feedback, and each of them names its own component, which is exactly why this distinction is worth money.

L4.prompt_tpl: A phone lists 8 GB RAM and 128 GB storage. You switch away from a game to answer a message; when you switch back, the game restarts from its title screen. Which of the two numbers ran out, and was anything on the 128 GB lost?
L4.answer: RAM ran out. The phone needed memory for the messaging app, so it closed the game and freed the game's RAM; when you returned, the game had to start again from its files. Nothing on the 128 GB storage was lost: the game's files, your saved progress and your photos are all still there. Only the game's unsaved in-memory state went.
L4.explanation: Transfer of the rule: RAM is what is open, storage is what is kept, and 'closing to make room' is the OS reclaiming RAM. The same thing happens on a laptop with too many tabs, except the laptop usually spills to disk and crawls instead of closing things.

L4.prompt_tpl: Foundations' 'Virtual memory' describes the OS pretending RAM is larger than it is. A laptop with 8 GB RAM and forty tabs open slows to a crawl and the disk light flickers constantly. Using only RAM-versus-disk, explain what the OS is doing and why it is slow rather than failing.
L4.answer: The tabs need more than 8 GB, so the OS is copying the least recently used parts of RAM out to a file on the disk (swap) and copying them back when a tab needs them. Every such copy costs disk time, about a thousand times slower than RAM, and with forty tabs the copying never stops, so the machine crawls. It does not fail because the disk is large enough to hold the overflow; it is slow because the disk is the wrong speed.
L4.explanation: Swap is the storage-versus-memory distinction turned into a mechanism: the OS uses the big slow thing as an overflow for the small fast thing. Foundations names the machinery (pages, page faults); this concept is the reason it is needed.

concepts.t: What an operating system actually does

L0.body:
you -> programs -> OS -> hardware
        browser     |
        editor      |  shares the CPU
        terminal    |  hands out RAM
                    |  keeps the files
                    |  drives devices
                    |  knows who you are
 Windows 11 | macOS | Ubuntu (Linux)
 Android and iOS are OSes too
 a program never touches hardware;
 it asks the OS, and the OS decides
L0.cloze: Programs never touch the hardware; they {{c1::ask the OS}}. The OS gives each running program turns on the {{c2::CPU}}, a private slice of {{c3::RAM}}, files by name, the devices, and it knows which {{c4::user}} you are. Windows, macOS, Ubuntu (Linux), Android and iOS are operating systems.

concepts.L1: The OS is the software that is always running and owns the hardware. It gives each running program turns on the CPU, a private slice of RAM, files by name, and access to screen, keyboard, disk and network, and it keeps users apart. Windows, macOS, Ubuntu (Linux), Android and iOS are OSes; Chrome and Word are not.
concepts.L2: The miss is 'the OS is the desktop and the icons'. The desktop is one ordinary program the OS starts; the OS is underneath and runs just the same on a server with no screen. Second miss: a program that stops responding 'crashed the computer'. It did not; the OS is fine, and killing it from the system's task manager proves it.
concepts.L3: The mechanism is two modes. Programs run in user mode, where instructions that touch hardware are forbidden; when a program wants a file or the network it makes a system call, the CPU switches to kernel mode, OS code does the work and hands back a result. A timer interrupts the CPU many times a second and gives the OS the chance to pause one program and resume another: that is how two hundred programs share eight cores, and why a stuck program cannot hold the machine hostage. Each program sees its own private addresses, so it cannot read another's RAM or the OS's. Ubuntu is the Linux kernel plus the standard commands, a desktop and a package system; Android is that same kernel under a different surface; macOS and iOS share a kernel. Foundations' 'What a process is' is this with the name attached, and 'Processes and job control' is the same machinery seen from the terminal.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of these is an operating system?
L4.answer: Ubuntu
L4.explanation: Ubuntu is a Linux-based OS: it owns the hardware and gives the other two their turns on it. The desktop and its icons are one ordinary program that the OS starts, which is why a server with no desktop still has an OS; Chrome is a browser. The test: which one hands out the CPU and the RAM to the rest? Take Ubuntu away and nothing else has anything to run on.
options: Ubuntu
The Windows desktop and its icons
Google Chrome

L4.prompt_tpl: A photo editor is told to save a picture to the disk. What does the program actually do?
L4.answer: It asks the OS, which does the writing
L4.explanation: Programs run in user mode, where the instructions that touch hardware are forbidden. To save a file the editor makes a system call: it asks the OS by name, the CPU switches to kernel mode, OS code writes the bytes and hands back a result. That is why one program cannot overwrite another's files by accident, why 'permission denied' is possible at all, and why the same editor works on a disk it has never heard of.
options: It asks the OS, which does the writing
It writes the bytes to the disk itself, using the disk's own controller
It hands the bytes to the desktop, which passes them on to the disk

L4.prompt_tpl: The OS gives each of {n} programs that all want the CPU a turn of {t} milliseconds on a single core, in strict rotation. How many milliseconds pass from the start of one program's turn to the start of its next turn?
L4.answer: The number of programs times the length of one turn: one full rotation is n turns of t ms. n=4, t=4 -> 16; n=4, t=10 -> 40; n=10, t=4 -> 40.
L4.explanation: One full rotation is n turns of t ms each: 10 programs at 4 ms is a rotation every 40 ms, short enough that every program looks continuously alive. Only programs that actually want the CPU take a turn, which is why a real laptop runs hundreds of programs and stays smooth: almost all of them are asleep waiting for a key or a packet, and are skipped.

L4.prompt_tpl: A program enters an endless loop and never asks the OS for anything at all. What stops it from freezing the whole machine?
L4.answer: A timer interrupts the CPU and hands control back to the OS
L4.explanation: The OS does not depend on programs behaving. A hardware timer interrupts the CPU hundreds of times a second whatever the running program is doing; on each interrupt the OS gets control and can pause that program and resume another. That is why the mouse still moves and the task manager still opens while one program spins forever. Early home operating systems did rely on programs handing the CPU back voluntarily, and one bad program froze everything.
options: A timer interrupts the CPU and hands control back to the OS
The program must give the CPU back once its work is done
The OS notices and asks the user whether to end the program

L4.prompt_tpl: A program stops responding to clicks and its window goes grey. What has happened?
L4.answer: That program is stuck; the OS is still running and can end it
L4.explanation: The OS is unaffected: it is still giving other programs their turns, which is why the mouse moves and Task Manager opens. The stuck program has simply stopped answering. End it from Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc), Activity Monitor on macOS, or the system monitor on Ubuntu, and the machine is as it was.
options: That program is stuck; the OS is still running and can end it
The operating system has crashed and the machine must be restarted
The CPU has stopped working

L4.prompt_tpl: Suppose any program could write directly to the disk and the screen without asking the OS. Name two things that would break for you as a user.
L4.answer: Isolation and safety. A buggy or hostile program could overwrite any file, including other programs and the OS itself, since nothing checks what it writes; and two programs writing to the same disk blocks or screen region at once would corrupt each other's work. There would also be no user separation: nothing could stop one person's program reading another's files.
L4.explanation: The OS being the only thing that touches hardware is what makes a crash local to one program and makes 'this file belongs to that user' enforceable. Everything in Foundations' 'File permissions' rests on programs having to ask.

L4.prompt_tpl: Program A crashes while program B is editing a document that has not been saved. Can A have corrupted B's document in memory? Say why or why not.
L4.answer: No. The OS gives each running program its own private set of addresses, and A can only name addresses in its own set, so there is no address A can write that lands in B's memory. B's unsaved document sits in B's private RAM and is untouched by A's crash. What A could damage is a file on the disk that both are allowed to write, because the disk is shared: the OS hands out files by name and permission, not by address.
L4.explanation: Isolation is why a crash is local to one program instead of taking the machine with it. Foundations' 'Virtual memory' is the machinery underneath: a per-program map from the addresses a program uses to the actual RAM behind them, so two programs can both use address 1000 and never meet.

L4.prompt_tpl: A server in a data centre has no screen, no keyboard and no desktop; you reach it only over the network. Does it have an operating system, and which of the OS's jobs are still being done?
L4.answer: Yes. All of them except driving a screen and keyboard: it shares its CPUs between the programs it runs, hands out RAM, keeps the files, drives the disk and network card, and keeps users apart. The desktop was never the OS; it was one program the OS could start, and here it simply is not started.
L4.explanation: Transfer: strip away everything visible and the OS's jobs remain, which shows what the OS actually is. Every Whetstone server you later talk to, and this app's own host, is exactly such a machine.

L4.prompt_tpl: Foundations' 'What a process is' names the thing the OS creates when it runs a program. You open the same editor twice without closing it. How many copies of the program exist on disk, how many processes exist, and what does the OS give each process that it does not share with the other?
L4.answer: One file on disk, two processes. Each process gets its own private RAM (its own copy of the code and its own open documents), its own turns on the CPU, and its own list of open files. Closing or crashing one does not touch the other, because they share nothing the OS did not deliberately let them share.
L4.explanation: The program is the file; the process is the running instance the OS built from it, and there can be many. This is the distinction 'A program is a file the machine can run' develops and that Task Manager shows directly.

concepts.t: A program is a file the machine can run

L0.body:
$ file /usr/bin/ls
 /usr/bin/ls: ELF 64-bit LSB pie
   executable, x86-64, ...
 hello.py holds: print("hello")
 $ file hello.py
 hello.py: ASCII text
 $ python3 hello.py
 hello
 program: python3    data: hello.py
 Windows: notepad.exe   (.exe runs)
 macOS:   Safari.app    (a folder)
 Linux:   /usr/bin/ls   (no suffix)
 running program = process
 see them: Task Manager, Activity
 Monitor, or top in a terminal
L0.cloze: A program is a file whose bytes are instructions the CPU can run; the file command calls it an {{c1::executable}}. In the command python3 hello.py the program is {{c2::python3}} and hello.py is {{c3::text it reads}}. Windows marks runnable files with {{c4::.exe}}; a running program is a {{c5::process}}.

concepts.L1: A program is a file whose bytes are CPU instructions, or a script that an interpreter reads and carries out. Windows marks runnable files .exe, macOS wraps double-clickable apps in a .app folder, Linux adds nothing. To run one the OS copies it into RAM and starts a process; the same file can be running twice at once.
concepts.L2: The miss: reading 'python3 hello.py' as running hello.py. The program is python3; hello.py is text it reads. So 'install Python' and 'write a Python file' are two acts: a .py file with no python3 does nothing. Second miss: what you click is the program. The icon is a signpost to a file elsewhere; deleting it uninstalls nothing.
concepts.L3: The file command reads the first bytes: 7F 45 4C 46 ('ELF') on Linux, 'MZ' on Windows, and the loader uses that header, not the name, to find the first instruction; Windows' desktop still decides what a double-click does from the extension. The loader copies the code into RAM, sets up a stack and jumps to the entry point; from then on it is a process with its own memory and its own turns on the CPU. A file that starts with plain text has no such header, so you name the interpreter yourself: python3 hello.py. Linux allows a shortcut, a first line of #! and a path, itself a two-byte header the kernel acts on. That is why a source file is a document and an interpreter is a program, and why Foundations' 'A C program, compiled and run' turns text into an ELF file that needs no interpreter. Where the OS finds python3 from the bare name is Foundations' 'Environment variables and PATH'.

L4.prompt_tpl: In the command 'python3 hello.py', which is the program being run?
L4.answer: python3
L4.explanation: python3 is the executable file the OS loads and runs. hello.py is an argument: a text file that python3 opens and reads, exactly as Word opens a document. Nothing in hello.py runs by itself; without python3 installed it is just text.
options: python3
hello.py
python3 hello.py, as one program

L4.prompt_tpl: You run file on two files you have not seen before. It reports 'report.docx: Microsoft Word 2007+' and 'runme: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64'. Which of the two can the OS run without handing it to another program? Answer with the filename.
L4.answer: runme
L4.explanation: The file command reads the first bytes, not the name. 'ELF ... executable' is the header a Linux program carries, so runme is a file the OS can load and run on its own. report.docx is a document: data that a word processor opens, and with no word processor installed the OS can do nothing with it at all. The name and the icon are decoration; the header decides.

L4.prompt_tpl: On Windows, which filename extension marks a file the OS will run when you double-click it? Answer with the extension, including the dot.
L4.answer: .exe
L4.explanation: Windows decides what a double-click does by extension: .exe (and a few relatives such as .com and .scr) are run as programs; .txt, .pdf and .py are opened in the program registered for them. An .msi is not one of them: it is data that msiexec.exe reads, the same shape as python3 hello.py. macOS uses .app folders and Linux uses no suffix at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: You open the same PDF reader twice without closing it. Which is true?
L4.answer: One program file on the disk, two processes
L4.explanation: The file on disk is the program; each running instance, with its own RAM and its own turns on the CPU, is a process, and one file can be the source of many. Opening it twice copies nothing on the disk. Task Manager and Activity Monitor list processes, not files, which is why the same name can appear several times there.
options: One program file on the disk, two processes
Two program files on the disk, two processes
One program file on the disk, one process

L4.prompt_tpl: You copy hello.py to a laptop that has never had Python installed and double-click it. What happens, and why?
L4.answer: Either a text editor opens showing the source, or the OS asks what program to open it with. Nothing runs. hello.py is text; the program that would carry out its instructions is python3, and that file is not on the machine. Installing Python is what supplies it.
L4.explanation: The consequence of 'the script is data'. Every 'my code does nothing on my friend's machine' report from a beginner is this: the document travelled, the interpreter did not.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a Windows laptop that does have Python installed, you double-click hello.py. A black window appears for half a second and vanishes, and nothing else happens. Did the program run, and what became of its output?
L4.answer: Yes, it ran. The double-click started python, which opened a console window, read hello.py, printed hello into that window and finished. The moment the program finished the process ended, and Windows closed the window that belonged to it, taking the output with it. To read the output, start the program from a terminal that was already open and stays open afterwards, or add a last line that waits for a key press.
L4.explanation: A process lives exactly as long as the program has something to do; nothing keeps it alive afterwards, and the window belonged to the process rather than to the file. This is the most common first report from a beginner on Windows, and it is a fact about process lifetime, not a bug in the program.

L4.prompt_tpl: Safari.app is a folder. It contains Contents/Info.plist, Contents/MacOS/Safari, Contents/Resources/Safari.icns and Contents/Resources/en.lproj. Give the path, inside Safari.app, of the file whose bytes the OS actually runs.
L4.answer: Contents/MacOS/Safari
L4.explanation: The rule 'the program is the file of instructions' finds the program even inside unfamiliar packaging. Info.plist is a description file, Safari.icns is the icon, en.lproj holds the English text; only Contents/MacOS/Safari is executable. The .app folder is a wrapper shown as one icon so the pieces cannot be separated by accident. The same test works on Windows, where an installed application is a folder in Program Files holding one .exe and many data files.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are in a folder that contains only hello.py. You type 'python3 hello.py' and it runs, although there is no file named python3 in that folder. Where is the python3 file, and how did the OS find it from the bare name?
L4.answer: python3 is an ordinary executable file somewhere else on the disk, /usr/bin/python3 on Ubuntu. When you type a bare name the OS does not search the whole disk: it walks a short fixed list of folders that it keeps for exactly this purpose, in order, and runs the first file of that name it finds. The folder you are standing in is not normally on that list, which is why a program you have just written yourself does not run by its bare name either.
L4.explanation: The last piece of 'a program is a file': it is a file that has to be found. That list is Foundations' 'Environment variables and PATH', and 'command not found' means only that no folder on the list held a file of that name, never that the program is broken.

L4.prompt_tpl: Foundations' 'A C program, compiled and run' starts with hello.c and produces a.out with gcc. For each of hello.c, gcc and a.out, say whether it is a program or data, and what the file command would report.
L4.answer: hello.c is data: text, and file reports 'C source, ASCII text'. gcc is a program (an executable, ELF on Linux) that reads hello.c. a.out is a program: the ELF executable gcc produced, and file reports it as 'ELF 64-bit LSB ... executable'. Compiling is a program turning a text document into a new executable file.
L4.explanation: Interpreting and compiling are the two ways text becomes behaviour: python3 reads the text every time; gcc reads it once and writes a file the OS can run without help. a.out is 'assembler output', the name of the original Unix executable format from Ritchie and Thompson's toolchain; ELF replaced it on Linux and only the filename survives.

concepts.t: Installing and removing software, and where software comes from

L0.body:
Ubuntu / WSL (bash):
 ($ is the prompt; you type after it)
 $ sudo apt update
 $ sudo apt install tree
 $ sudo apt remove tree
 macOS: App Store, or Homebrew
 (brew itself: from brew.sh):
 % brew install tree
 % brew uninstall tree
 Windows: Microsoft Store, or
 (PowerShell)
 > winget install Microsoft.VisualStudioCode
 remove: Settings > Apps
 sources, in order of trust:
 1 repository (apt, Store): signed
 2 the maker's own website: read the URL
 3 a stranger's link or forward: no
L0.cloze: Software comes from three places, in order of trust: a {{c1::repository}} (apt, the App Store, the Microsoft Store), where packages are signed and checked; the maker's {{c2::own website}}, where you must read the address; and a {{c3::stranger's link}}, which is how machines get owned. On Ubuntu the install command is {{c4::sudo apt install}} followed by the package name.

concepts.L1: Installing puts a program's files where the OS can find them and registers it; removing reverses that. Three sources: a package repository (apt, the App Store, the Microsoft Store), where software is signed and checked; the maker's own website; or a link from a stranger. Use them in that order; refuse the third.
concepts.L2: The miss: 'free download' from a search result or a forwarded link feels like installing from the Store. It is not. The first search result is often an advert or a lookalike, and a 'free PDF converter' that also installs a password stealer is how home machines get owned. Installing hands a stranger's program all your powers.
concepts.L3: A repository publishes a list of its packages, signed by the distributor with a key that shipped with Ubuntu, and that list carries a checksum for every package file. 'apt update' fetches the list and verifies the signature; 'apt install' checks the file it downloads against the checksum, so a package altered on a mirror fails on arrival. The .deb files are not signed one by one; the signed list is what pins them. A vendor download has only the vendor's word plus a warning (SmartScreen, Gatekeeper) that can be clicked past: installing Homebrew by running a script from brew.sh is exactly that trade. sudo is the OS asking a human to confirm a change to the whole machine, and a program you run has every power your account has, which is why 'just run this installer' is the attack. 00b's 'A URL, part by part' is how to read a vendor's address; 20 Security's supply chain is the adult version.

L4.prompt_tpl: On Ubuntu, which command installs the program tree?
L4.answer: sudo apt install tree
L4.explanation: apt is Ubuntu's package manager and install is the sub-command; sudo runs it with permission to change the machine for every user, which is why it asks for your password. Without sudo, apt cannot even open its own lock file and stops with 'Permission denied'. And install is a real command, but a different one, the coreutils file-copying tool, so 'install tree' answers 'install: missing destination file operand after tree'.
options: sudo apt install tree
apt install tree
install tree

L4.prompt_tpl: You want a media player on Ubuntu. Which source should you try first?
L4.answer: The Ubuntu repository, with apt or the Software app
L4.explanation: All three would get you a media player; the question is who vouches for it. The repository's copy is pinned by a list Ubuntu signed, and apt checks it before installing, which is worth more than a newer version number. The maker's own site is second: the vendor vouches, and you have to read the address to know you are on it. A search result vouches for nothing and is often an advert or a lookalike.
options: The Ubuntu repository, with apt or the Software app
videolan.org, the maker's own site, because the repository's build is a version behind
The first search result for 'free media player download'

L4.prompt_tpl: What does 'sudo apt update' do?
L4.answer: Refreshes the list of available packages and their checksums
L4.explanation: 'apt update' downloads the signed catalogue: which packages exist, at which version, with which checksum. It changes nothing you already have installed. Updating the installed programs themselves is 'sudo apt upgrade'; moving to the next Ubuntu release is 'sudo do-release-upgrade'. Running update first is what lets install verify the file it then downloads.
options: Refreshes the list of available packages and their checksums
Installs the newest version of every program already on the machine
Upgrades Ubuntu to the next release

L4.prompt_tpl: Using apt (not apt-get), give the complete command that removes the installed package tree without touching its configuration files. Type the command only, not the prompt symbol at the start of the line.
L4.answer: sudo apt remove tree
L4.explanation: Removal is the mirror of installation: the same tool, the remove sub-command, the same sudo because it changes the machine for everyone. 'sudo apt purge tree' would delete the configuration files too, and 'sudo apt-get remove tree' is the older interface for the same thing. apt records which files it installed, so the removal is clean. On macOS a Homebrew package goes with 'brew uninstall tree'; a Store or disk-image app is dragged from Applications to the Bin.

L4.prompt_tpl: apt reports: 'After this operation, {d} MB of additional disk space will be used.' Your disk has {f} GB free (1 GB = 1000 MB). How many GB will be free after the install?
L4.explanation: Convert MB to GB and subtract: 12 - 0.35 = 11.65 GB. Installing writes the program's files to the disk (storage), not to RAM; that line is apt telling you the storage cost before you agree. Reading it is the habit that prevents 'disk full' surprises.

L4.prompt_tpl: apt asks for your password before installing, but the browser downloads a file with no password at all. Why the difference, and what does typing the password actually grant?
L4.answer: A download only writes a file into your own Downloads folder, which your account may always do. On Ubuntu, apt installs system-wide, so sudo asks for the password to confirm that a human authorised a change to the machine for every user. Some installers write only into space your account already owns, such as Homebrew's own folder or a per-user Windows installer, and ask for nothing. So the prompt tells you the scope of the change, not that the software is safe: a program run as you, with no password at all, can still read, encrypt or send away every file you own.
L4.explanation: The password prompt is the OS drawing the line between 'your files' and 'the machine'. Knowing that the line is about scope, not safety, is what makes 'click Yes on the warning' recognisable as the dangerous step in a scam's instructions.

L4.prompt_tpl: You want tree gone, so instead of running 'sudo apt remove tree' you delete the file /usr/bin/tree by hand. What is now wrong?
L4.answer: apt's records still say the package is installed, so the package manager and the disk now disagree. Anything that depends on tree still looks satisfied, 'apt list --installed' still lists it, and the next time the package is upgraded apt puts the file straight back. Removing a package means telling the tool that installed it, so that its record of the machine stays true; deleting files by hand leaves a record that lies.
L4.explanation: Installing is not just copying files, and so removing is not just deleting them. The package manager keeps a list of what it put where, and that list is what makes clean removal and safe upgrades possible; step around it and the list is wrong from then on.

L4.prompt_tpl: A site called vlc-player-free-download.com offers 'VLC media player, free download'. The VLC project's real site is videolan.org. What do you do?
L4.answer: Ignore that site; install vlc from the repository or from videolan.org
L4.explanation: The address is the tell: it is not videolan.org, so whatever it serves is a stranger's program, however familiar the name in the heading. Scanning it afterwards is too late, since a fresh installer is rarely recognised. On Ubuntu 'sudo apt install vlc' gets the package the signed list pins; on any OS the maker's own domain is the second choice.
options: Ignore that site; install vlc from the repository or from videolan.org
Download it from that site: VLC is free software anyway
Download it from that site, then scan the file with antivirus before running it

L4.prompt_tpl: A forum answer to an error you searched for says: download fix.exe from the link below, right-click it, choose Run as administrator, and click Yes when Windows warns you. Classify this by the three-source rule and say what each of the three instructions is doing.
L4.answer: Source three: a stranger's link. 'Download fix.exe' fetches a program with no signature and no review; 'Run as administrator' gives it the whole machine rather than your account's files; 'click Yes when Windows warns you' is telling you to override SmartScreen, the one check that would have stopped it. The correct action is to close the page and search the actual maker's documentation or the repository for the fix.
L4.explanation: Transfer: an unfamiliar instruction sequence reduced to source, power granted, and warning bypassed. Every real malware delivery contains those three steps in some costume, and the rule identifies them before the costume matters.

L4.prompt_tpl: Foundations' 'Running Python: interpreter, scripts, environments' has you run 'pip install requests', which fetches the package from PyPI. Which of the three sources is PyPI, and what does it lack compared with apt's repository?
L4.answer: PyPI is a repository, source one, but an open one: anyone can publish a package under any unclaimed name, and nobody reviews it before it is served. apt's index is signed by Ubuntu and every package in it was uploaded by a named maintainer who packaged it; on PyPI nobody stands between the author and you. So pip carries the trust question inside the first source: a package named 'requets' can be a stranger's program wearing a repository's clothes, and the defence is the same as for websites, read the name exactly.
L4.explanation: The three-source rule is not about tools but about who vouches. apt: a distributor and a named maintainer vouch. PyPI: nobody does. That gap is where 20 Security's supply-chain material begins.

concepts.t: What a file is

L0.body:
file manager:
   Name        Size     Modified
   report.txt  1.2 KB   10 Sep
 what the OS keeps for a file:
   a name, a size, dates, an owner,
   and the bytes themselves
 the bytes of report.txt, in decimal:
   72 101 108 108 111  =  Hello
 the OS does not know what they mean
 the program that opens the file does
 open as text:  Hello
 open as hex:   48 65 6C 6C 6F
 the bytes never changed
 1 KiB = 1024 bytes  1 MiB = 1024 KiB
L0.cloze: A file is a {{c1::name}} attached to a sequence of {{c2::bytes}} on the disk; beside them the OS records a size, dates, an owner and a few flags such as permissions. The OS does not know what the bytes {{c3::mean}}; the program that opens the file decides that. 1 KiB is {{c4::1024}} bytes.

concepts.L1: A file is a named sequence of bytes kept on the disk, plus a little bookkeeping beside it: size in bytes, timestamps, owner. The OS moves the bytes in and out by name and never interprets them. Whether they are a letter, a photo or a program is decided by the program that reads them, not by the disk.
concepts.L2: The miss, for anyone who learned computing on a phone: that a file lives inside the app that made it, so the photo is 'in Photos' and the essay is 'in Word'. On a computer a file is an object on the disk that belongs to no program; any program can open it, and uninstalling Word deletes no essays.
concepts.L3: Unix (Thompson and Ritchie, 1970s) settled the definition every later system copied: the OS imposes no structure on a file, it is an array of bytes with a length, read and written by offset. Meaning is supplied by whoever reads it, which is why one file can be opened by an image viewer and a text editor and each shows something different from the same bytes. The bookkeeping (name, size, dates, owner) is stored separately from the bytes, so renaming touches no content and the size is an exact byte count; a file of 0 bytes is a real file with a name and no content. Sizes: the OS counts bytes; file managers round to KB, and Windows's KB is 1024 bytes while macOS's is 1000. Foundations' 'Memory as one addressed array of bytes' is the same picture for RAM, and 'stdin, stdout, stderr and redirection' rests on this concept: because a file is only bytes, any program's output can become one.

L4.prompt_tpl: Besides the bytes themselves, what does the operating system keep for every file?
L4.answer: A name, a size, dates and an owner
L4.explanation: That, plus a few flags such as permissions, is the whole record: bookkeeping beside the bytes. The OS keeps no note of what the bytes mean, no copy inside any program, and no 'type' beyond whatever the name suggests. Everything else you see, the icon, the preview, the word count, is a program reading the bytes and reporting.
options: A name, a size, dates and an owner
A name, a size, and the program that owns the bytes
A name, a size, and a description of what the bytes mean

L4.prompt_tpl: A plain text file holds {w} words of {k} ASCII letters each, separated by single spaces, and ends with one newline character. Each character is one byte. How many bytes is the file?
L4.explanation: Count every byte: the letters (w times k), the spaces between words (w minus 1), and the final newline (1). With 10 words of 4 letters: 40 + 9 + 1 = 50 bytes. The file manager's size column is exactly this count; a text file has no hidden overhead.

L4.prompt_tpl: A file is {b} bytes. Windows counts 1024 bytes per KB. What is the file's size in KB, to 3 decimal places?
L4.explanation: Windows's KB is a KiB, 1024 bytes, so 10 000 bytes is 9.765625 KB, entered as 9.766; Explorer's own list view shows no decimals and rounds it up to 10 KB. macOS counts 1000 bytes per KB, so the same file is 10 KB there. Neither is wrong; they are counting in different units with the same label.

L4.prompt_tpl: You rename report.txt to notes.txt in the file manager. How many of the file's bytes change?
L4.answer: None: the name is bookkeeping kept beside the bytes
L4.explanation: The name is not inside the file. It is an entry the OS keeps pointing at the bytes, and renaming rewrites the entry only. That is why a rename is instant on a 4 GB video and why no program that reads the file can tell it was renamed.
options: None: the name is bookkeeping kept beside the bytes
The first 4 bytes: the OS stores the name at the front of the file
All of them: the OS copies the bytes into a new file under the new name

L4.prompt_tpl: A drive is sold as {g} GB, where the maker's GB is 1 000 000 000 bytes. Windows counts 1024 x 1024 x 1024 bytes per GB instead. How many of Windows's GB does the drive hold, to 3 decimal places?
L4.explanation: Two units wear the label GB. The maker divides the byte count by 1 000 000 000; Windows divides it by 1 073 741 824, which is about 7 percent larger, so a 500 GB drive is reported as 465.661 GB. No bytes are missing and nothing is faulty: one count, two divisors. At the MB scale the same gap is about 5 percent.

L4.prompt_tpl: A learner says 'my essay is in Word'. Word is about to be uninstalled. Where is the essay, and what two things must be true for it to open tomorrow?
L4.answer: The essay is a file on the disk, most likely essay.docx in the Documents folder; Word is a separate program that could read it. Uninstalling Word removes the program and moves no files. Two things must be true tomorrow: you must be able to find the file, which means knowing its folder rather than which app it appeared in; and some installed program must understand .docx bytes, such as LibreOffice or Google Docs. Neither has anything to do with Word still being there.
L4.explanation: Files and programs are separate objects on the disk. A phone hides this by showing files only inside apps; a computer shows them side by side in the file manager, and the essay outlives any single program.

L4.prompt_tpl: One file, opened in an image viewer, shows a photograph; opened in a text editor, it shows pages of rubbish. Which program is showing what the file 'really' is?
L4.answer: Neither. The file is a sequence of bytes and nothing more. The image viewer reads the bytes as pixel data and draws them; the text editor reads the same bytes as characters and prints whatever they happen to map to. The photograph is the useful interpretation, but it is an interpretation the viewer supplies, not a property the disk stores.
L4.explanation: The OS stores bytes and bookkeeping; meaning is added by the reader. Holding that line explains every 'the file is corrupted' message that is really 'the wrong program opened it'.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a phone, a WhatsApp voice note appears to live 'inside WhatsApp'. Using this concept, say where its bytes are, and what would have to be true for an ordinary music player to play it.
L4.answer: Its bytes are in a file in the phone's storage, named something like PTT-20260910-WA0003.opus, in a folder WhatsApp created. On Android that folder is under Android/media/com.whatsapp/WhatsApp/Media/WhatsApp Voice Notes and a file manager can browse it; on an iPhone it sits in the app's private container and only Share or Export lets another program see it. For a music player to play it, the player must reach the folder and be able to decode Opus audio. Nothing about the file is WhatsApp-specific except its name and where it was put.
L4.explanation: Transfer: the rule 'a file is bytes on the disk, owned by no program' holds on a phone, where the OS merely hides the folders. Share or Export is the phone letting another program see the same bytes.

L4.prompt_tpl: Foundations' 'stdin, stdout, stderr and redirection' lets any program's screen output be written to a file instead. Using only 'a file is a named sequence of bytes', explain why this works for every program without the program being told.
L4.answer: A program writing to the screen is producing a sequence of bytes and handing them to the OS. The screen and a file are both destinations for bytes, so the OS can point the program's output at a file instead: the program keeps handing over bytes, and the OS appends them to the file. Because a file has no required structure, any stream of bytes is a valid file, so no program needs to know or care where its output is going.
L4.explanation: The generality of 'bytes with a name' is what makes redirection possible at all. A system where files had types the OS enforced could not do this; Unix chose not to have one for exactly this reason.

L4.prompt_tpl: A camera app saving a photo, you pressing Save in an editor, and a browser finishing a download all end the same way. With what?
L4.answer: A name and a sequence of bytes handed to the OS to keep
L4.explanation: Every file is written by a program. Save is the editor asking the OS to keep these bytes under this name; the camera app asks for the same thing, and the browser asks for it with no person watching. That is why files exist that no person typed, and why a file belongs to no program: whoever wrote it is finished with it once the OS has the bytes.
options: A name and a sequence of bytes handed to the OS to keep
A copy of the work kept inside the app that produced it
A note of what the bytes mean, written down by the OS

concepts.t: The filename, the extension, and the lie an extension can tell

L0.body:
invoice.pdf      ext: .pdf
 hello.py         ext: .py
 archive.tar.gz   last ext: .gz
 .bashrc          hidden, no ext
 the OS picks the program by ext:
   .pdf -> viewer  .exe -> RUN IT
 Windows default: hide extensions
 of known types is ON, so
   invoice.pdf.exe  shows as
   invoice.pdf      (a program!)
 an extension is a claim, not a fact:
 copy photo.png to the name photo.txt
 later, in a terminal, the file
   program reads the bytes and says:
   PNG image data, 800 x 600
 turn hiding OFF on day one
L0.cloze: The extension is the part of the name after the last {{c1::dot}}; the OS uses it to pick the {{c2::program}} that opens the file on a double-click. It is a {{c3::claim}}, not a fact: renaming photo.png to photo.txt changes no bytes, and file still reports PNG image data. Windows hides known extensions by default, so {{c4::invoice.pdf.exe}} shows as invoice.pdf.

concepts.L1: The extension is the tail of the filename after the last dot, unless that dot is the first character: a leading dot marks a hidden file on Unix and is no extension. The OS uses the extension to choose the program a double-click opens, and Windows uses it to decide whether a file is run at all. It is name, not bytes.
concepts.L2: The miss: that the extension is the file's type. It is a label anyone can write, and the OS believes it. invoice.pdf.exe is a program whose name claims 'PDF'; with Windows's default of hiding known extensions it shows as invoice.pdf with a PDF icon, and a double-click runs it. Change that setting on day one.
concepts.L3: The name is stored beside the bytes, so anyone can write any extension; the bytes are unchanged and the file command still reports the truth from the first bytes (a PNG begins 89 50 4E 47). The OS keys double-click behaviour on the name alone: Windows runs a dozen or so extensions directly, among them .exe, .scr, .com, .bat, .vbs and .js, and opens the rest in a registered program, so the extension decides what gets executed. Hiding known extensions strips the last one from view, so a.pdf.exe shows as a.pdf, with a PDF icon the .exe carries. Linux does not judge runnable by extension (a permission bit does); macOS needs that bit too, but Finder launches .app bundles by name, so Gatekeeper, not the extension rule, guards Photo.jpg.app. Foundations' 'File permissions' is that bit; 20 Security's 'The security mindset' starts from the habit planted here: a label is an unverified claim.

L4.prompt_tpl: What is the extension of the file report.final.v2.docx? Answer with the extension, including the dot.
L4.answer: .docx
L4.explanation: The extension is what follows the LAST dot, so it is .docx; final and v2 are ordinary parts of the name that happen to have dots before them. The same rule reads archive.tar.gz as .gz, with .tar a second, older label saying what is inside the compressed file. The OS looks only at the last one when choosing a program.

L4.prompt_tpl: What does the operating system use a filename's extension for?
L4.answer: To choose which program opens the file on a double-click
L4.explanation: The extension is a lookup key: .pdf maps to the PDF viewer, .py to the editor (or on Windows to the Python launcher). It is not checked against the bytes and it does not change them; the OS trusts the name. That trust is the security problem in this concept.
options: To choose which program opens the file on a double-click
To record what the bytes inside the file actually are
To keep the file's bytes in the right format

L4.prompt_tpl: cp makes a copy of a file under a new name; file is a program that reports what a file's bytes are. On Ubuntu you run 'cp song.mp3 song.txt' and then 'file song.txt'. What does file report?
L4.answer: song.txt: Audio file with ID3 version 2.4.0
L4.explanation: file reads the first bytes, not the name: an MP3 usually starts with an ID3 tag and file names it, whatever the extension claims. cp copied the bytes exactly, so nothing about the audio changed. The .txt is a label the OS will believe on a double-click, so a text editor opens and shows rubbish; the bytes are still a song.
options: song.txt: Audio file with ID3 version 2.4.0
song.txt: ASCII text, with no line terminators
song.txt: data (name and contents disagree)

L4.prompt_tpl: A Windows machine with default settings shows a downloaded file as 'invoice.pdf' with a PDF icon. Its real name is invoice.pdf.exe. What is it?
L4.answer: A program
L4.explanation: The real extension is .exe and Windows hid it: 'Hide extensions for known file types' is on by default, so the last extension, .exe, is stripped from the display and 'invoice.pdf' remains. The icon is a picture the program carries. Double-clicking runs it with all your account's powers. Show extensions, and read the whole name before opening anything downloaded.
options: A program
A PDF with an unusual name
A PDF exported by some program

L4.prompt_tpl: On a Linux or macOS system, what does a filename beginning with a dot, such as .bashrc, signify? Answer with one word.
L4.answer: hidden
L4.explanation: A leading dot marks a hidden file: ls and the file manager skip it by default. It is not an extension, which is why .bashrc has none: the rule about the last dot does not apply to a dot that starts the name. Configuration files live this way in your home folder, out of the way but not protected.

L4.prompt_tpl: You rename notes.txt to notes.py. What changed, and what did not?
L4.answer: Changed: the name, and therefore what a double-click does. On macOS or Ubuntu that is usually an editor with Python colouring; on Windows with Python installed, .py belongs to the Python launcher, so the double-click now RUNS the file in a console window that closes when it finishes. The icon changes too. Not changed: a single byte of the file. If the text was a Python program it runs with python3 notes.py; if it was a shopping list, python3 reports a syntax error, because the bytes never became Python.
L4.explanation: The rename changed the claim and the OS's response to the claim. Whether the claim is true depends only on the bytes, which the rename did not touch.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does Windows's default of hiding known extensions turn invoice.pdf.exe from a suspicious name into a dangerous one?
L4.answer: With extensions shown, the name ends in .exe and a careful reader sees a program. With them hidden, Windows removes the last extension it recognises and displays invoice.pdf, and the .exe can carry a PDF icon, so the only visible clue is gone. The user sees what looks like a document and does what one does with documents: double-click. Windows then runs the program because the real extension is .exe.
L4.explanation: The setting removes exactly the evidence needed to apply this concept's rule. The fix is one checkbox (View, Show, File name extensions) and it should be the first change on a new machine. One family stays hidden regardless: shortcut files (.lnk) never show their extension, so also distrust a document whose icon carries a small arrow.

L4.prompt_tpl: song.mp3 will not play, and file reports 'PNG image data'. Which is wrong, the name or the bytes?
L4.answer: The name
L4.explanation: The bytes are a valid picture wearing an audio extension. file reports what the bytes are, and it found a well-formed PNG. The bytes are fine; the label is wrong. Rename it song.png and an image viewer opens it. Reading a 'corrupt file' complaint as 'the name and the bytes disagree' is the first diagnostic move.
options: The name
The bytes
Neither: file is guessing from an extension it does not know

L4.prompt_tpl: An email attachment shows in Windows as 'Photo_from_Priya.jpg' with a picture icon. With extensions shown, its name is Photo_from_Priya.jpg.scr. Classify it and say what happens if it is double-clicked.
L4.answer: It is a program. .scr is the Windows screensaver extension, which Windows runs exactly like .exe; the .jpg is decoration and the icon is a picture the program carries. Double-clicking runs it with your account's powers: it can read and encrypt every file you can, and install anything your account is allowed to install. The right move is to delete it and, if Priya is real, ask her by another channel whether she sent it.
L4.explanation: Transfer: the rule 'the last extension is the one Windows acts on' applied to an extension you had not met. Knowing .scr is one of the runnable ones is a fact; treating any unfamiliar last extension on a downloaded file as suspect is the habit.

L4.prompt_tpl: Foundations' 'Running Python: interpreter, scripts, environments' runs programs with python3. You have a valid Python program saved as script.txt. Does 'python3 script.txt' run it, and what does the answer show about who reads extensions?
L4.answer: Yes, it runs. python3 reads the bytes of whatever file it is given and does not look at the name; the extension is a convention for humans, editors and the OS's double-click, not for the interpreter. So the .py suffix earns syntax colouring, a double-click behaviour, and the ability to be found by Python's import machinery, which looks for a module's name followed by .py. What it does not earn is any say in whether python3 will read the file it is handed. The lesson generalises: programs read bytes, the OS's launcher reads names.
L4.explanation: Connecting the two halves of this concept: the extension matters to the OS's launcher and to people, and matters not at all to a program that is handed the file directly.

L4.prompt_tpl: You double-click data.csv and a spreadsheet opens it. You wanted a text editor. What is wrong?
L4.answer: Nothing is wrong with the file: this machine's default program for .csv is the spreadsheet
L4.explanation: The extension-to-program map is a table on your machine, not a property of the file, and you can change it: right-click, Open with, and choose the editor, or set it as the default for .csv. Renaming the file to .txt would also work but would lie about the contents, and every other program that expects .csv would stop finding it.
options: Nothing is wrong with the file: this machine's default program for .csv is the spreadsheet
The extension is wrong: a file of text should be renamed to .txt
The file is wrong: it must be saved again as plain text

concepts.t: Text files and binary files

L0.body:
$ file hello.py
 hello.py: ASCII text
 $ file notes.txt
 notes.txt: ASCII text
 $ file photo.png
 photo.png: PNG image data, 800 x 600,
   8-bit/color RGBA, non-interlaced
 text: the bytes spell characters
   .txt .py .c .html .css .json .csv
   .md .sh  - any editor opens them
 binary: bytes are pixels, samples,
   instructions - one program each
   .png .jpg .mp3 .pdf .docx .exe .zip
 .docx is NOT text (it is a zip)
 source code is text. Always.
L0.cloze: A text file is one whose bytes all {{c1::decode to characters}}: .py, .c, .html and .json are text exactly as .txt is, and any editor opens them. A binary file's bytes are pixels, sound samples or instructions: .png, .mp3, .exe, and also {{c2::.docx}}, which is a zip. The file command reports hello.py as {{c3::ASCII text}}. Source code is always {{c4::text}}.

concepts.L1: A text file is one whose bytes all decode to characters: letters, digits, punctuation, newlines. A .py, .c, .html or .csv file is text exactly as a .txt is; any text editor opens any of them. A binary file's bytes mean pixels, sound samples or CPU instructions, and only a program that knows the format can show it.
concepts.L2: The miss: 'Word makes text files', so hello.py written in Word is fine. A .docx is a zip archive of XML and pictures, and even Save As Plain Text keeps the curly quotes and non-breaking spaces AutoCorrect put in as you typed, which Python rejects. The reverse miss: that .py needs special software. Notepad opens it; it is text.
concepts.L3: Nothing in a file says 'I am text'. The file command guesses from the bytes: if every byte is printable or whitespace it reports text; otherwise it names a format from the first bytes. A PNG begins 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A: the first byte is non-ASCII, so no ASCII file is mistaken for a PNG and a transfer that clears the eighth bit is caught at byte one; the CR LF and LF that follow catch any tool that rewrites line endings. Text is the format every tool agrees on: editors, compilers, diff, grep and git all work on lines of characters; that is why source code is text. A binary format packs numbers directly: smaller, faster, legible to one program. Line endings differ: Linux and macOS end a line with one byte (LF), Windows with two (CR LF), so a Windows text file is larger and shows ^M on Linux. Foundations' 'A C program, compiled and run' is text in (hello.c) and binary out (a.out).

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of these files is text?
L4.answer: index.html
L4.explanation: HTML is characters: tags and words, readable and editable in any text editor, which is why View Source works in a browser. photo.jpg is compressed pixel data and music.mp3 is compressed audio; a text editor shows both as rubbish. The extension is a hint; the test is whether every byte is a character.
options: index.html
photo.jpg
music.mp3

L4.prompt_tpl: On Ubuntu you run 'file hello.py' on a one-line program, print('hi'), saved with nano. What does it report?
L4.answer: hello.py: ASCII text
L4.explanation: A Python program is text: every byte is a character. file finds nothing but printable characters and newlines and says so. On a longer program it may say 'Python script, ASCII text' instead, because it recognises def, import and a #! line; and a copy saved by Notepad on Windows reports 'ASCII text, with CRLF line terminators'. A compiled program is reported as ELF. Same answer as for notes.txt, which is the point.
options: hello.py: ASCII text
hello.py: Python binary, x86-64
hello.py: cannot determine type

L4.prompt_tpl: A .docx file from Word: text or binary?
L4.answer: Binary: it is a zip archive containing XML and images
L4.explanation: Rename report.docx to report.zip and any archive tool opens it: inside are word/document.xml, word/styles.xml and any pictures under word/media. Word shows you text, but the file's bytes are a compressed archive, and a text editor opening it shows 'PK' followed by rubbish. Text is about the bytes, not about what the program displays.
options: Binary: it is a zip archive containing XML and images
Text: it contains the words you typed
Text if it has no pictures, binary if it does

L4.prompt_tpl: Which program can open and edit every text file, whatever its extension?
L4.answer: Any text editor, such as Notepad, nano or VS Code
L4.explanation: Text is the one format every editor understands, because there is nothing to understand: bytes map to characters. A browser will display a .txt or .py file handed to it, but it cannot save your changes back. And no file needs the program its extension names in order to be read: .py is not a locked format, it is text.
options: Any text editor, such as Notepad, nano or VS Code
A web browser, which displays any text file it is given
Only the program the file is for: python3 for .py, a browser for .html

L4.prompt_tpl: A text file has {l} lines of {c} characters each. Saved on Ubuntu every line ends with one newline byte; saved on Windows every line ends with two bytes (CR LF). How many bytes larger is the Windows copy?
L4.explanation: Ubuntu: l (c + 1) bytes; Windows: l (c + 2) bytes; the difference is one byte per line, l. For 250 lines that is 250 bytes. This is the whole reason a file copied from Windows shows ^M at each line end on Linux and why editors offer 'LF or CRLF' in the status bar.

L4.prompt_tpl: You open photo.png in a text editor, see pages of rubbish, press one key by accident, and save. What has happened to the photo?
L4.answer: It is very likely destroyed. The editor decoded the bytes as characters, some of which were not valid characters at all; on save it wrote back its own idea of the text, replacing invalid bytes and possibly the line endings, and inserted your keystroke. The PNG's structure (header, chunk lengths, checksums) no longer matches, so image viewers refuse it. Undo in the editor does not help once the file is saved.
L4.explanation: Text editors are safe on text and destructive on binary because they re-encode what they show. Opening the wrong kind of file is harmless; saving it is not.

L4.prompt_tpl: A learner types a Python program in Word, chooses Save As, names it hello.py, and python3 reports a syntax error on the first line. Name two different things Word may have done to the bytes.
L4.answer: First, Word may have saved a .docx (binary zip) with the name hello.py.docx or with hello.py holding zip bytes; python3 then reads 'PK' and rubbish. Second, even saving as plain text, Word's autocorrect replaces straight quotes with curly ones and can insert non-breaking spaces; both are characters Python does not accept, and they look identical to the right ones on screen.
L4.explanation: A word processor is a program for producing documents, and it changes what you type. Code needs a code editor, which writes exactly the characters typed and nothing else; that is the next section's 'A code editor is not a word processor'.

L4.prompt_tpl: A colleague sends the same table twice: sales.csv and sales.xlsx. Which is text, which is binary, and which one could a plain text editor fix if one number were wrong?
L4.answer: sales.csv is text: rows of values separated by commas, one line per row, so any editor can open it and change the number. sales.xlsx is binary: a zip archive of XML, like .docx, so an editor shows 'PK' and rubbish and only a spreadsheet program can edit it safely. The CSV is also the one git can diff line by line and any language can read with ten lines of code.
L4.explanation: Transfer: two unfamiliar extensions classified by asking what the bytes are, and the practical consequence drawn. Text formats are the ones tools compose over; that is why data exchange defaults to CSV and JSON.

L4.prompt_tpl: A program writes a positive integer of {d} decimal digits to a file as text followed by one newline. A second program writes the same integer as a fixed 4-byte binary integer (Foundations' 'Fixed-width integers wrap' describes that type). How many more bytes does the text file use? A negative answer means fewer.
L4.explanation: Text costs one byte per digit plus the newline; the binary form costs 4 bytes regardless of value. Two digits: 3 bytes of text against 4 of binary, so text is smaller by one; nine digits: 10 against 4. Binary wins for big numbers and loses legibility. Both files hold the same number; only the encoding of the bytes differs.

L4.prompt_tpl: You want an archive tool to open report.docx as the zip archive it really is, without changing a byte. Give the new filename.
L4.answer: report.zip
L4.explanation: Renaming report.docx to report.zip changes the claim the name makes and no bytes at all, and the archive tool, which judges by the bytes it finds, opens it. This is the safest way to see for yourself that a .docx is binary: a zip full of XML. Rename it back to .docx afterwards and Word is none the wiser.
