concepts.t: Folders, and the tree

L0.body:
/                  the root (POSIX)
 +-- home/
 |   +-- asha/      home folder
 |       +-- proj/
 |       |   +-- main.py
 |       +-- Downloads/
 +-- usr/
     +-- bin/
         +-- python3
 a folder = a file listing names
 one name per entry, per folder
 home folders:
   Ubuntu   /home/asha
   macOS    /Users/asha
   Windows  C:\Users\Asha
 Windows: one tree per drive letter
L0.cloze: Every file sits in a folder and every folder in another, up to the {{c1::root}}, written / on Ubuntu and macOS and {{c2::C:\}} on Windows. A folder is itself a file that lists {{c3::names}}, so one folder cannot hold two entries with the same name, but two folders can. Your home folder on Ubuntu is {{c4::/home/asha}}; on macOS /Users/asha; on Windows C:\Users\Asha.

concepts.L1: Files are grouped into folders (directories), and folders into folders. Ubuntu and macOS form one tree rooted at /; Windows keeps one tree per drive, rooted at C:\, D:\. A folder is a file whose bytes list names and where each points, so a file is named by the chain of folders down to it, joined by / (\ on Windows).
concepts.L2: The miss: that a folder contains its files the way a box contains things, so a file is 'in' Downloads physically. A folder is a list of names; the bytes are elsewhere on the disk, and a name means something only inside its list: report.txt can exist in a hundred folders at once, never twice in one.
concepts.L3: Thompson's design: a directory is an ordinary file whose content is a table of (name, pointer) pairs, and a pointer may lead to another directory. Follow pointers from the root and you reach every file; the tree is this chain of tables. So a name means something only inside its folder; listing a folder reads one small file, so it is instant however large the files are; and moving a file within one partition edits two tables and no bytes. Ubuntu and macOS mount every disk inside the one tree (/media, /Volumes); Windows gives each drive its own root, C:\, D:\. Case: Ubuntu treats Report.txt and report.txt as different names, Windows and default macOS as the same. Foundations' 'Paths and the filesystem tree' names the parts of this tree; 05's 'The VFS: inodes, dentries and the dcache' opens the directory file and shows the inode behind each name.

L4.prompt_tpl: On Ubuntu, what is the name of the top of the filesystem tree?
L4.answer: / (a single slash), the root
L4.explanation: Everything on an Ubuntu or macOS machine hangs below one root, written as a lone slash. C:\ is Windows's root for the C drive (Windows has one tree per drive letter), and /home is one folder inside the root, holding the home folders of the machine's users.
options: / (a single slash), the root
/home

L4.prompt_tpl: On Ubuntu, what is the home folder of a user whose login name is asha? Answer with the full path, without a trailing slash.
L4.answer: /home/asha
L4.explanation: Ubuntu keeps every user's home folder under /home, named after the login. macOS uses /Users/asha and Windows C:\Users\Asha. It is the folder the terminal starts in and the one Downloads, Documents and Desktop live under.

L4.prompt_tpl: Can two files both named report.txt exist on one computer?
L4.answer: Yes, in different folders; never in the same folder
L4.explanation: A folder is a list of names, and a list cannot hold the same name twice. Two folders are two lists, so /home/asha/work/report.txt and /home/asha/old/report.txt coexist. 'Which report.txt?' is answered by the folder, which is what the next concept's paths are for.
options: Yes, in different folders; never in the same folder
No: every filename on the machine must be unique
Yes, even in the same folder, if their sizes differ

L4.prompt_tpl: On Windows, what is the home folder of a user whose login name is Asha? Answer with the full path, without a trailing slash.
L4.answer: C:\Users\Asha
L4.explanation: Windows keeps each user's folder under C:\Users, named after the login, so Asha's is C:\Users\Asha and Documents, Downloads and Desktop sit inside it. Ubuntu spells the same idea /home/asha and macOS /Users/asha. On a WSL machine you have two homes, one on each side, which is why a downloaded file can be hard to find from the terminal.

L4.prompt_tpl: What is a folder, in terms of what the disk stores?
L4.answer: A file whose content is a list of names, each pointing to a file or another folder
L4.explanation: That is the Unix definition and every modern system uses some form of it. The folder's bytes are the list; the files' bytes are elsewhere. This is why listing a folder is instant, and why on Ubuntu and macOS renaming a file edits the folder rather than the file's own bytes. (NTFS also keeps a copy of the name in the file's own record, so Windows updates both.)
options: A file whose content is a list of names, each pointing to a file or another folder
A region of the disk where the folder's files are physically kept together
A label the file manager attaches to a group of files

L4.prompt_tpl: In one folder on Ubuntu you create Report.txt and then report.txt. What happens?
L4.answer: Both exist: Ubuntu treats names differing only in case as different
L4.explanation: Linux filenames are case-sensitive: the two names are different strings and the folder's list holds both. On Windows, and on macOS with its default settings, they are the same name and the second creation would overwrite or be refused. Code that runs on both must get the case exactly right.
options: Both exist: Ubuntu treats names differing only in case as different
The second overwrites the first: case does not matter in filenames
Ubuntu refuses the second name as a duplicate

L4.prompt_tpl: Moving a folder that holds 20 000 photos to another folder on the same partition of the same disk finishes instantly, but copying it takes minutes. Using 'a folder is a list of names', explain both.
L4.answer: The move edits two lists: the folder's name is removed from the old parent's list and added to the new parent's list. The photos' bytes, and the moved folder's own list, are untouched, so the work does not depend on what is inside. The copy must create a new entry and a new set of bytes for every one of the 20 000 photos, so it reads and writes every byte.
L4.explanation: The tree is pointers, and moving within one partition is pointer surgery. Copying, and moving to a different partition or disk, are byte transfers: a laptop with C: and D: on one physical drive still copies between them. Knowing which you are asking for predicts whether an operation takes a second or an hour.

L4.prompt_tpl: In WSL, the Windows C drive appears inside Ubuntu's tree at /mnt/c. What is the Ubuntu path of the Windows file C:\Users\Asha\Downloads\data.csv? Answer with the path.
L4.answer: /mnt/c/Users/Asha/Downloads/data.csv
L4.explanation: WSL grafts each Windows drive into the single Linux tree: C:\ becomes /mnt/c, backslashes become slashes, and the rest of the path is kept as written. Ubuntu's own files are not reachable as C:\ paths at all: they live inside one virtual-disk file, and from Windows they appear at \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu\home\asha. Two trees, each visible from the other, but a file is fast only on its own side.

L4.prompt_tpl: Foundations' 'Paths and the filesystem tree' assumes one tree with one root. A USB stick is plugged into an Ubuntu laptop and into a Windows laptop. Where does it appear in each, and which OS keeps the single-root model?
L4.answer: Ubuntu keeps it: the stick's own tree is attached (mounted) at a folder inside the one tree, typically /media/asha/STICKNAME, so the single root holds and the stick's files are reached by an ordinary path. Windows gives the stick a new drive letter, E:\ say, so it has as many roots as drives and a path must begin by naming the drive: a forest rather than a tree. Neither is wrong, and Windows can also mount a volume into a folder; a letter per drive is its default, not a law.
L4.explanation: Transfer: an unfamiliar device placed into the tree model. Every later 'where is my file' question on a new machine is answered by first finding where its storage was attached.

concepts.t: The path: absolute and relative

L0.body:
absolute: starts at the root
   /home/asha/proj/main.py
   C:\Users\Asha\proj\main.py
 relative: starts where you are
   from /home/asha:
     proj/main.py
   from /home/asha/proj/bin:
     ../data/out.csv
     -> /home/asha/proj/data/out.csv
 .  = this folder   .. = one level up
 ~  = your home:  ~/proj = /home/asha/proj
 separator: / on POSIX, \ on Windows
 URLs and WSL always use /
L0.cloze: A path is the list of folder names from a starting point to a file. An {{c1::absolute}} path starts at the root, so it begins with / (or C:\), and names one file wherever you are; a {{c2::relative}} path starts at the current folder. {{c3::..}} means one level up and . means this folder; ~ is your home, so ~/proj on Ubuntu is {{c4::/home/asha/proj}}.

concepts.L1: A path names a file by the chain of folders leading to it. Absolute: from the root, beginning with / (or a drive letter on Windows), the same file wherever it is read. Relative: from the current folder, no leading slash. .. steps up one level, . means here, ~ is your home. POSIX separates with /, Windows with \.
concepts.L2: The miss: that 'main.py' or 'proj/main.py' names one file. It names one file per current folder: run from /home/asha it means /home/asha/proj/main.py, run from /tmp it means /tmp/proj/main.py, which does not exist. 'No such file' when the file is right there is almost always a relative path resolved from the wrong place.
concepts.L3: Resolution is mechanical: an absolute path is walked from the root, each name looked up in the previous folder's list; a relative path is joined to the current folder first, then walked the same way. A .. drops the component before it, so from /home/asha/proj/bin the path ../data/out.csv becomes /home/asha/proj/data/out.csv; .. at the root stays at the root. ~ is not understood by the filesystem; the shell replaces it with your home path before anything else sees it, so ~ inside a Python string is just a tilde. MS-DOS chose \ in 1983 because / was already its option marker; Windows inherited it. Foundations' 'Paths and the filesystem tree' adds pwd, cd, the working directory each program carries, and what .. does after a symlink; 'Running Python: interpreter, scripts, environments' is where python3 file.py against python3 -m module makes the current folder decide which imports work.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of these is an absolute path?
L4.answer: /home/asha/proj/main.py
L4.explanation: Absolute means it starts at the root, and on Ubuntu or macOS that is a leading slash. proj/main.py starts from wherever you are; ../main.py starts one level above wherever you are. Only the first names the same file from every folder on the machine.
options: /home/asha/proj/main.py
proj/main.py
../main.py

L4.prompt_tpl: On Ubuntu, ~/proj/main.py typed at a prompt by user asha stands for which absolute path? Answer with the path.
L4.answer: /home/asha/proj/main.py
L4.explanation: ~ is replaced by the home folder, /home/asha on Ubuntu, before the path is used. On macOS the same ~ would give /Users/asha/proj/main.py. The replacement is done by the shell, so inside a Python string or a configuration file ~ is just a tilde unless the program expands it itself (in Python, os.path.expanduser).

L4.prompt_tpl: A program's current folder is /home/asha/Documents and it opens notes/todo.txt. Give the absolute path of the file it opens.
L4.answer: /home/asha/Documents/notes/todo.txt
L4.explanation: A relative path with no .. in it is simply joined to the current folder: /home/asha/Documents, then notes, then todo.txt. Nothing is searched for and nothing is guessed. Started from /tmp instead, the same two words would mean /tmp/notes/todo.txt, which is a different file or none at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: What does .. mean in a path such as ../data/out.csv?
L4.answer: The folder one level above the current one
L4.explanation: .. is the parent folder, a real entry every folder carries. From /home/asha/proj/bin, ../data means /home/asha/proj/data. A lone . is the current folder itself, which is what ./run.sh uses. Neither has anything to do with hidden files, although a leading dot in a name does.
options: The folder one level above the current one
The root of the tree
A hidden folder named ..

L4.prompt_tpl: On Windows a path is written C:\Users\Asha\proj. What is the separator on Ubuntu and macOS?
L4.answer: A forward slash: /Users/asha/proj
L4.explanation: POSIX systems separate folder names with /, and the same path style is used by URLs, WSL and every programming language. Windows uses \ because / was taken as its option marker, but it accepts / in most places. A colon separated folders only on the pre-2001 classic Mac OS, which is why macOS still refuses ':' in filenames; on Windows C: marks the drive.
options: A forward slash: /Users/asha/proj
A backslash, the same as Windows
A colon: Users:asha:proj

L4.prompt_tpl: A program is started with its current folder set to /home/asha and told to open proj/main.py: it works. It is started again with its current folder /home/asha/Downloads and given exactly the same text, and reports 'No such file or directory'. What happened?
L4.answer: proj/main.py is a relative path, resolved from the current folder. The first time that folder was /home/asha, giving /home/asha/proj/main.py, which exists. The second time it was /home/asha/Downloads, so the same text means /home/asha/Downloads/proj/main.py, which does not exist. The file did not move; the starting point did. Give the absolute path, or ~/proj/main.py, or start the program from the right folder.
L4.explanation: The same relative path is a different file from every folder. 'No such file' for a file you can see is the signature of this, and the cure is to check which folder the program was started in before believing the path; the command that prints it, pwd, comes in the next section.

L4.prompt_tpl: A program is told to write its output to out.csv. Where will the file appear?
L4.answer: In whatever folder was current when the program was started
L4.explanation: out.csv is a relative path, so it is joined to the current folder of the process. Start the program from Downloads and the file appears in Downloads, not beside the program and not in your home. This is why beginners 'lose' output files: they are exactly where the current folder was.
options: In whatever folder was current when the program was started
In the same folder as the program's own file
In your home folder

L4.prompt_tpl: A program's current folder is /home/asha/notes/2026/sep and it writes to ../../../proj/./data/out.csv. Give the absolute path of the file it writes.
L4.answer: /home/asha/proj/data/out.csv
L4.explanation: Join first: /home/asha/notes/2026/sep/../../../proj/./data/out.csv. Then resolve left to right. Each .. drops the component before it, so the three of them remove sep, 2026 and notes and leave /home/asha. A lone . means this folder and drops out. What remains is walked down: proj, data, out.csv. Join, then resolve, always in that order.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your current folder is /home/asha/proj/src and you need the file /home/asha/data/raw.csv. Give the shortest relative path.
L4.answer: ../../data/raw.csv
L4.explanation: Walk up until the two paths share a folder: src to proj is one .., proj to asha is a second; /home/asha is common to both. Then walk down: data, then raw.csv. Two ups and two downs. Writing the absolute path is also correct but was not asked; the relative form is what a project uses so that it works from any home folder.

L4.prompt_tpl: The current folder is {d} folders below the root. The target file is inside a folder {t} folders below the root, and the two branches share only their first {s} folders. The root itself is not counted. How many components does the shortest relative path have, counting each .. and each folder name and the filename itself?
L4.answer: (d - s) ups + (t - s) folder names + 1 filename = d + t - 2 s + 1. d=4, t=3, s=1 -> 6; d=4, t=3, s=2 -> 4; d=4, t=5, s=1 -> 8.
L4.explanation: Climb from the current folder to the shared ancestor, which takes d - s steps of .. ; descend into the target's branch, which is t - s folder names; add the filename. From depth 4 to a file whose folder is at depth 3, sharing 1 folder: 3 ups, 2 downs, 1 name, 6 components. The example ../../data/raw.csv is d=4, t=3, s=2: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4.

concepts.t: Copy, move, rename, delete, and where deleted actually goes

L0.body:
$ cp notes.txt backup.txt   copy
 $ mv notes.txt old.txt      rename
 $ mv notes.txt archive/     move
 $ rm notes.txt              delete
   rm: gone. No bin. No undo.
 mv onto a name that exists:
   replaces it, no question asked
 file manager: Delete (Windows, Ubuntu)
   or Cmd+Delete (macOS):
   Windows -> Recycle Bin
   macOS   -> Trash (~/.Trash)
   Ubuntu  -> Trash
     (~/.local/share/Trash/files)
 space is freed when the bin is
 emptied, not before
 Windows Shift+Delete skips the bin
 Ctrl+Z (mac: Cmd+Z) in the file
 manager: undo
L0.cloze: In the terminal cp copies, mv both {{c1::renames and moves}}, and rm deletes {{c2::without}} a bin or an undo. The file manager's Delete key (Cmd+Delete on macOS) moves the file to the {{c3::Recycle Bin}} on Windows or the Trash on macOS and Ubuntu, from which it can be restored; the disk space is freed only when the bin is {{c4::emptied}}.

concepts.L1: Four operations on a file's entry in the tree. Copy makes a second file with the same bytes. Move and rename are one operation, mv: the entry changes, the bytes stay. Delete removes the entry. In a file manager, Delete moves the entry into a hidden Trash folder and can be undone; in the terminal, rm is final.
concepts.L2: The miss runs both ways. 'Deleted means gone': in the file manager it means moved to the Trash, still occupying space until emptied. 'rm is like Delete': it is not; rm has no bin and no undo, and the terminal will not ask. Second miss: that a rename is a different act from a move. Both are mv, changing where the name sits.
concepts.L3: A folder is a list of names, so rename and move are one edit: remove the name from one list, add it to another, bytes untouched, instant at any size. Copy allocates new space and duplicates every byte; the exception is macOS's APFS, where a copy within one volume shares the bytes until one side is edited. Delete removes the name and marks the space free; the bytes stay until overwritten, which is why recovery tools sometimes work and 'deleted' is not 'destroyed'. The Trash is not a disk mechanism: the file manager moves the file into a hidden folder (~/.local/share/Trash/files on Ubuntu, ~/.Trash on macOS) and records where it came from. rm bypasses it, so nothing is recorded. Moving between two volumes (a USB stick, or a second partition) is copy then delete. Foundations' 'File permissions' gives the bits behind a rule this implies: deleting needs write on the folder, not on the file.

L4.prompt_tpl: In a terminal, give the single command that renames a.txt to b.txt in the current folder. Write both names bare, with no ./ and no folder.
L4.answer: mv a.txt b.txt
L4.explanation: mv moves a name: given two filenames it renames, given a folder as the second argument it moves the file into it. There is no separate rename command because rename and move are the same edit to the folder's list. cp would leave a.txt in place as well. (mv ./a.txt b.txt works just as well in a real shell; this item asks for the bare form.)

L4.prompt_tpl: You run 'rm essay.txt' in a terminal. Where is essay.txt now?
L4.answer: Nowhere reachable: rm does not use the Trash and has no undo
L4.explanation: rm removes the name from the folder's list and frees the space; it never goes near the Trash, which is a file manager feature. The bytes may linger on the disk until overwritten, so recovery software can sometimes help, but nothing in the OS remembers the file. The terminal did not ask, and will not.
options: Nowhere reachable: rm does not use the Trash and has no undo
In the Trash, until it is emptied
In the Trash, but only for thirty days

L4.prompt_tpl: The current folder holds notes.txt and an empty folder archive. You run 'mv notes.txt archive/' and then 'ls'. What does ls print?
L4.answer: archive
L4.explanation: mv with a folder as its second argument moves the file into that folder: notes.txt is now archive/notes.txt. ls lists the current folder, which now holds only archive. The bytes did not move on the disk; one name left one list and joined another.
options: archive
archive  notes.txt
notes.txt

L4.prompt_tpl: In the Windows file manager you select a file on the laptop's own drive and press Delete. Where does it go?
L4.answer: The Recycle Bin, from which it can be restored
L4.explanation: Delete in Explorer is a move into the Recycle Bin, a hidden folder, with a note of the original location so Restore can put it back. Shift+Delete skips the bin, a file on a USB stick or a network drive is deleted outright, and a file larger than the bin's limit brings up a permanent-delete prompt. macOS (Cmd+Delete; Delete alone does nothing in Finder) and Ubuntu call theirs the Trash and behave the same way.
options: The Recycle Bin, from which it can be restored
It is erased from the disk at once
The Downloads folder

L4.prompt_tpl: A disk has {f} GB free. You move a {m} GB video from Downloads to Videos, both in your home folder on that disk. How many GB are free afterwards?
L4.explanation: A move within one filesystem edits two folder lists and copies no bytes, so the space used does not change: 20 GB free before, 20 after. Only a copy, or a move to a different volume (which is a copy followed by a delete), needs room for a second set of bytes.

L4.prompt_tpl: On Ubuntu, a disk has {f} GB free. In the file manager you delete a {m} GB video with the Delete key, do not empty the Trash, then copy a {c} GB file from a USB stick onto the disk. How many GB are free now?
L4.answer: f - c: the deleted file still occupies its space in the Trash. f=20, m=4, c=1.5 -> 18.5; f=20, m=4, c=6 -> 14; f=20, m=8, c=1.5 -> 18.5.
L4.explanation: Delete moved the video into the Trash, a folder on the same disk, so its bytes are still there and its space is not free. The copy brings c GB in from the stick. 20 - 6 = 14 GB. Emptying the Trash would return the m GB. 'Disk full' right after deleting things is exactly this. On Windows a video too big for the Recycle Bin would instead be deleted outright, freeing its space at once.

L4.prompt_tpl: You press Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac) in the file manager immediately after deleting a file, and it comes back. You press Ctrl+Z in a terminal immediately after rm, and it does not. Why the difference?
L4.answer: The file manager's delete was a move into the Trash, which it recorded, so undo is another move back. The terminal's rm removed the name from the folder and freed the space; nothing was recorded, and Ctrl+Z in a terminal is not undo at all (at an empty prompt it does nothing; with a program running it pauses that program, which is a different thing again). There is nothing to reverse because the operation was designed not to be reversible.
L4.explanation: Undo exists only where a program kept a record. The file manager keeps one; rm keeps none. Treat rm as final, and prefer the file manager, or a tool such as trash-cli, when the file matters.

L4.prompt_tpl: Moving a 4 GB file from Downloads to a USB stick takes minutes, but moving it from Downloads to Videos takes no time. Why?
L4.answer: Within one disk a move edits folder lists; to another disk it must copy every byte, then delete
L4.explanation: The USB stick is a different disk with its own tree; there is no list on the stick pointing at bytes on the laptop, so the bytes must be copied across and the original then deleted. Within the laptop's disk, the move is two list edits. Same word 'move', two mechanisms.
options: Within one disk a move edits folder lists; to another disk it must copy every byte, then delete
The USB stick is slower to rename files on
The file manager checks the file for viruses before moving it off the machine

L4.prompt_tpl: In WSL you run 'rm /mnt/c/Users/Asha/Desktop/draft.docx'. Does the file appear in the Windows Recycle Bin?
L4.answer: No. The Recycle Bin is a feature of Windows Explorer, which moves files into a hidden folder when you press Delete; rm is a different program that removes the name from the folder outright. WSL reaches the Windows disk through /mnt/c but uses Linux commands, so Explorer is never involved. draft.docx is gone, exactly as if rm had been run on a Linux file.
L4.explanation: Transfer: the rule 'the bin is the file manager's habit, not the disk's' applied to a two-OS machine. Whichever tool edits the folder list decides whether anything is recorded.

L4.prompt_tpl: Yesterday you committed report.md with git (Foundations' 'git: commits and the staging area'). Today you rm report.md. A friend says it is gone for good, as anything rm removes is. Using what you know about what rm removes and what recovery always needs, is she right, and what would you check?
L4.answer: She is right about rm and wrong about the file. rm removed one name from one folder and freed the space; it never asks whether a copy exists elsewhere, and recovery always depends on some other program having kept one. git kept one: every committed file is stored as an object inside the project's .git folder, so git checkout or git restore writes the bytes back. What I would check is whether the file was ever committed. A file git never saw has no second copy, and then she is right.
L4.explanation: Recovery always needs a copy somewhere: the Trash, a backup, or a version control system. rm removes one name; whether other copies exist is a question about what else was recording.

L4.prompt_tpl: The current folder holds notes.txt and nothing else. You run 'cp notes.txt backup.txt' and then 'ls'. What does ls print?
L4.answer: backup.txt  notes.txt
L4.explanation: cp copies: the original keeps its name and a second file appears under the new name with the same bytes, so the folder's list now holds two entries and ls prints both, in alphabetical order. mv would have left one name. Two names, two sets of bytes: a copy costs disk space, a rename costs none.
options: backup.txt  notes.txt
backup.txt
notes.txt

L4.prompt_tpl: The current folder holds notes.txt and old.txt, both with work in them. You run 'mv notes.txt old.txt'. What happened to the previous contents of old.txt?
L4.answer: Replaced silently: they are gone, and in no Trash
L4.explanation: A folder's list cannot hold the name old.txt twice, so mv points that name at notes.txt's bytes; whatever old.txt pointed at has lost its last name and its space is marked free. No question, no bin, no undo, and cp onto an existing name behaves the same way. A file manager would have asked; the terminal assumes you meant it, so read the destination name before pressing Enter.
options: Replaced silently: they are gone, and in no Trash
Nothing: mv refuses to write over a name that exists
Moved to the Trash, from which they can be restored

The prompt, the command, the argument, and the Enter key

concepts.t: Text is bytes: UTF-8 in one concept

L0.body:
char   code point   UTF-8 bytes   n
 A      U+0041       41           1
 é      U+00E9       C3 A9        2
 ₹      U+20B9       E2 82 B9     3
 न      U+0928       E0 A4 A8     3
 smiley U+1F600      F0 9F 98 80  4
 ASCII = code points 0 to 127:
   1 byte, same in every encoding
 नमस्ते  6 characters, 18 bytes
 wrong decoder:  café -> cafÃ©
   (mojibake: UTF-8 read as Latin-1)
 EF BB BF at file start: a BOM
   (U+FEFF), added by some Windows
   programs. Invisible, not content.
 MySQL: utf8mb4, not utf8 (3 bytes max)
 a character is not a byte
L0.cloze: A character is not a byte. Unicode gives every character a number (a code point) and UTF-8 stores it in {{c1::1}} byte for the 128 ASCII characters, 2 for é, {{c2::3}} for ₹ and every Devanagari letter, and 4 for the emoji above U+FFFF; नमस्ते is 6 characters and {{c3::18}} bytes. Decoding UTF-8 bytes as Latin-1 turns café into {{c4::cafÃ©}}, which is mojibake. MySQL's full UTF-8 is utf8mb4.

concepts.L1: Text in a file is bytes; an encoding is the rule turning characters into bytes. Unicode numbers every character (A is U+0041); UTF-8 writes that number in 1 to 4 bytes, ASCII's 128 taking one each. macOS, Linux, browsers and editors assume an unlabelled file is UTF-8; some Windows programs guess a code page.
concepts.L2: The miss: one character, one byte. True of ASCII, false for Hindi and emoji. A Devanagari name of 6 letters is 18 bytes; a 'string of length 10' may be 10 characters or 10 bytes, and languages disagree on which: Python's len counts characters, C's counts bytes. Second miss: a file 'is' text; it is bytes plus a decoder.
concepts.L3: UTF-8 is a variable-length code. A code point below 128 is one byte with top bit 0, so an ASCII file is already valid UTF-8. Larger code points use 2, 3 or 4 bytes: the first byte's leading bits say how many follow and every continuation byte begins 10, so a reader can resynchronise anywhere. Devanagari (U+0900 to U+097F) and the rupee sign are in the 3-byte range; most emoji (U+1F300 and up) sit above U+FFFF and take 4. Mojibake is the wrong decoder: é is C3 A9, and a reader assuming Latin-1 shows each byte as its own character, so café becomes cafÃ©. Boxes mean a missing font, question marks a lossy conversion. MySQL's 'utf8' stops at 3 bytes, so an emoji fails to store; use utf8mb4. Foundations' 'Strings and formatting' warns that len() counts code points, not bytes; 13 LLMs' 'Byte-level fallback and tokenizer-free models' is where these 3-byte letters cost several tokens each.

L4.prompt_tpl: A string holds {a} ASCII characters, {d} Devanagari letters and {e} emoji from the U+1F300 range. How many bytes is it in UTF-8?
L4.explanation: Each ASCII character is one byte, each Devanagari letter three, each emoji in that range four; add them. 10 ASCII, 6 Devanagari, 2 emoji: 10 + 18 + 8 = 36 bytes for 18 characters. Character count and byte count are different numbers, and a file's size is the second one.

L4.prompt_tpl: How many bytes does UTF-8 use for each of the 128 ASCII characters (A to Z, digits, punctuation)?
L4.answer: One, and the same byte values as ASCII
L4.explanation: UTF-8 was designed so that ASCII text is unchanged: code points 0 to 127 are one byte each, identical to ASCII. That is why a plain English file is the same bytes in both and why old tools never noticed the switch. Everything beyond ASCII takes 2 to 4 bytes.
options: One, and the same byte values as ASCII
Two, with a zero byte in front
Four, like every other character

L4.prompt_tpl: A Hindi word is written with {n} Devanagari characters (letters and vowel marks). How many bytes does the word take in UTF-8?
L4.explanation: Every Devanagari code point is in the 3-byte range of UTF-8, so a 6-character word such as namaste in Devanagari is 18 bytes. A text editor's character count says 6; the file manager's size says 18; both are right about different things.

L4.prompt_tpl: A price that should read ₹499 appears on a web page as â‚¹499. What has happened?
L4.answer: UTF-8 bytes were decoded with the wrong encoding (Windows-1252)
L4.explanation: ₹ is three bytes in UTF-8, E2 82 B9. A reader assuming one byte per character shows each of the three as its own Windows-1252 character, so one sign becomes three odd ones. The bytes are intact; the decoder was wrong. One character becoming two or three is the signature of mojibake, and the fix is to declare or select UTF-8, not to retype the text.
options: UTF-8 bytes were decoded with the wrong encoding (Windows-1252)
The bytes were corrupted when the page was saved
The font on the page has no glyph for the rupee sign

L4.prompt_tpl: A text editor says a file is 200 characters; the file manager says 260 bytes. Is the file damaged?
L4.answer: No. The file is 60 bytes over its character count, and every non-ASCII character costs 1 to 3 bytes more than the 1 byte a character 'looks like': sixty accented letters at 2 bytes each, or thirty Devanagari letters at 3, or twenty emoji at 4, or any mix adding to 60. The editor counts characters after decoding; the file manager counts the bytes on disk. They differ whenever any character is non-ASCII, and agree only for pure ASCII.
L4.explanation: Two counts, two questions. A discrepancy is not corruption; it is the encoding doing its job. Real damage looks like a decoder error on an invalid byte sequence, or replacement characters in the text; a size that exceeds the character count is the normal case for any language but English.

L4.prompt_tpl: A MySQL table was created with the 'utf8' charset. Storing a customer's name succeeds; storing their review, which contains an emoji, fails with 'Incorrect string value'. Why, and what is the fix?
L4.answer: MySQL's 'utf8' is really utf8mb3: at most 3 bytes per character, which is everything up to U+FFFF (the Basic Multilingual Plane) and nothing above it - no emoji, and no script that lives higher, such as Adlam or the rarer CJK ideographs. The name fit; the emoji did not. The fix is the utf8mb4 charset, which is real UTF-8. Whetstone's own schema uses utf8mb4 for this reason.
L4.explanation: A named limit on bytes per character is a limit on which characters exist. The historical label 'utf8' lies by omission; the byte count per character is the fact that decides.

L4.prompt_tpl: A file's bytes begin EF BB BF. What are they?
L4.answer: A UTF-8 byte-order mark that some Windows programs prepend
L4.explanation: EF BB BF is U+FEFF in UTF-8, a zero-width marker some Windows programs prepend to say 'this is UTF-8'. It is invisible in an editor and breaks programs that expect the file to start with real content (a Python script whose first line is a shebang, a CSV header). Seeing those three bytes in a hex view explains many 'my first line is ignored' bugs.
options: A UTF-8 byte-order mark that some Windows programs prepend
The PNG file signature, so the file is an image
The UTF-16 encoding of the first letter, so the file is not UTF-8

L4.prompt_tpl: A Tamil name is displayed as a row of empty boxes in one program and as question marks after export from another. Classify each symptom: wrong decoder, missing font, or lossy conversion.
L4.answer: Boxes are a missing font: the bytes decoded to the right Tamil code points, but the program has no glyphs to draw them, so it draws placeholder boxes. Question marks after export are a lossy conversion: the exporting program wrote the text in an encoding (such as ASCII or Latin-1) that has no code for Tamil letters and substituted ? for each. Neither is mojibake, which would show a wrong but readable string of Latin-looking characters.
L4.explanation: Transfer: three failures that all look like 'the text is broken' are told apart by what survived. Bytes fine, glyphs missing: font. Bytes replaced by ?: conversion. Bytes fine, decoded wrongly: mojibake.

L4.prompt_tpl: In Python (Foundations' 'Strings and formatting'), a string s holds {a} ASCII characters and {n} Devanagari characters and nothing else. What is len(s.encode('utf-8')) - len(s)?
L4.answer: 2 n: each Devanagari character costs 3 bytes but counts as 1 character. a=5, n=3 -> 6; a=5, n=7 -> 14; a=12, n=3 -> 6.
L4.explanation: len on a str counts characters: a + n. encode turns the string into bytes: a bytes for the ASCII characters, 3 n for the Devanagari ones. The difference is 2 n, and the ASCII count cancels entirely, which is why an English file shows no gap at all. C's strlen would report the byte count, because C strings are byte arrays (Foundations' 'Strings are NUL-terminated char arrays').

L4.prompt_tpl: A byte in the middle of a UTF-8 file is 10100100 in binary. A lead byte's leading one-bits say how many bytes the character has, and every continuation byte begins 10. What can you say about this byte?
L4.answer: It is a continuation byte: its character started at an earlier byte
L4.explanation: A byte beginning 10 never starts a character: lead bytes are 0xxxxxxx (1 byte), 110xxxxx (2), 1110xxxx (3) or 11110xxx (4). So this is the second, third or fourth byte of a character that began earlier. That is what lets a reader dropped into the middle of a file scan forward to the next lead byte and resynchronise, and why a search for an ASCII character can never match part of a longer one.
options: It is a continuation byte: its character started at an earlier byte
It starts a 2-byte character, because it begins with a one bit
It is an ASCII character, because 10100100 is a single byte

concepts.t: Which operating system you will work in, and how to get a POSIX shell on it

L0.body:
one target: a POSIX shell (bash or zsh)
 Windows 10 (build 19041+) or 11:
   PowerShell, Run as administrator:
   wsl --install
   restart; open Ubuntu from Start;
   choose a Linux username + password
   (typing the password shows nothing)
 macOS: Applications > Utilities >
   Terminal, or Spotlight: Terminal
   shell: zsh
 Linux (Ubuntu): Ctrl+Alt+T
   shell: bash
 check:  echo $SHELL
   Ubuntu prints /bin/bash
   macOS  prints /bin/zsh
L0.cloze: One target on every machine: a POSIX shell. Windows 10 (build 19041 or later) or 11: open PowerShell as administrator, run {{c1::wsl --install}}, restart, open {{c2::Ubuntu}} from Start and choose a Linux username and password. macOS: {{c3::Terminal}} (Applications, Utilities), shell zsh. Ubuntu: {{c4::Ctrl+Alt+T}}, shell bash. Check with echo $SHELL: Ubuntu prints {{c5::/bin/bash}} and macOS prints {{c6::/bin/zsh}}.

concepts.L1: Every command in this curriculum is typed into a POSIX shell: bash on Ubuntu, zsh on macOS. Windows does not ship one, so on Windows you install WSL2, which runs a real Ubuntu inside Windows; one command in an administrator PowerShell does it. macOS and Linux already have the shell; you only need to find the terminal.
concepts.L2: The miss is 'Windows has a command line, so I will use that'. PowerShell and cmd are command lines, but not the shell that Foundations and the OS and command-line domains teach: pipes, grep, permissions, processes and signals are all POSIX. Learning cmd first means unlearning it two domains later. Pay the WSL cost once, now.
concepts.L3: Why one shell: the toolchain that starts in Foundations ('The shell: command, arguments, flags' onwards) is written against POSIX behaviour, and C, Python and git are most predictable there. WSL2 is Microsoft's own answer: it runs a real Linux kernel in a lightweight virtual machine, so the Ubuntu you get is the one a Linux laptop runs, with two consequences to know at once. The Linux username and password you choose belong to Ubuntu only, not to your Windows login; and there are two sets of files: Windows' disk appears inside Ubuntu at /mnt/c, and Ubuntu's files appear in Windows Explorer under \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu. Keep project files on the Ubuntu side. On macOS the shell is zsh, whose prompt ends in `%` instead of `$`; every command in this domain works the same in both. If wsl --install prints usage text instead of installing, the Windows build predates 19041: update Windows first.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have a Windows 11 laptop. Which route gives you the shell this curriculum uses?
L4.answer: Install WSL2 and use the Ubuntu it installs
L4.explanation: The target is a POSIX shell, and Windows does not ship one. WSL2 installs a real Ubuntu inside Windows with one command; PowerShell and Command Prompt are command lines, but every later domain assumes bash, not them. Choosing them now means discarding what you learn.
options: Install WSL2 and use the Ubuntu it installs
Use PowerShell, since it is already a command line
Use Command Prompt, since it is the oldest and simplest

L4.prompt_tpl: You open PowerShell as administrator on Windows 11 and want WSL with its default Linux distribution. What exact command do you type? Answer with the command only.
L4.answer: wsl --install
L4.explanation: One command: wsl --install. It enables the needed Windows features, installs the WSL2 kernel, and installs Ubuntu as the default distribution. Afterwards you restart, open Ubuntu from the Start menu, and choose a Linux username and password. It must be run in an administrator PowerShell, not an ordinary one.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a fresh Ubuntu, in WSL or on a Linux laptop, you type `echo $SHELL` and press Enter. What is printed?
L4.answer: /bin/bash
L4.explanation: Ubuntu's default shell is bash, and the program lives at /bin/bash. The variable SHELL names your login shell; echo prints it. On macOS the same command prints /bin/zsh. This is the one-line check that you have reached a POSIX shell and which one it is.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a Mac, where is the Terminal application?
L4.answer: Applications, then Utilities; or type Terminal into Spotlight
L4.explanation: Terminal.app ships with macOS inside Applications > Utilities, and Spotlight (Cmd+Space, then type Terminal) finds it faster. Nothing needs installing: macOS already has zsh, a POSIX shell. WSL is a Windows-only step.
options: Applications, then Utilities; or type Terminal into Spotlight
It must be downloaded from the App Store first
Inside System Settings, under Developer

L4.prompt_tpl: After wsl --install and a restart, Ubuntu asks you to create a username and password. How do these relate to your Windows login?
L4.answer: They are separate: they belong to Ubuntu only, and nothing appears on screen while you type the password
L4.explanation: The Linux account lives inside the Ubuntu installation and has no connection to the Windows account. The password prompt shows nothing at all while you type, not even dots; this is normal for Linux, and beginners often assume the keyboard has stopped working. Type it and press Enter.
options: They are separate: they belong to Ubuntu only, and nothing appears on screen while you type the password
They must match your Windows username and password exactly
Ubuntu copies them from Windows, so it should not ask; something has gone wrong

L4.prompt_tpl: PowerShell is a capable command line and it is already on every Windows machine. Give the specific reason this curriculum still insists on WSL and bash.
L4.answer: Because everything that follows is written for a POSIX shell: Foundations teaches pipes, stdin and stdout, grep and find, file permissions, processes and signals, and the C and Python toolchains, all in bash on Linux. PowerShell has different commands, different syntax and a different model of text and files, so time spent learning it would have to be unlearned two domains later. WSL2 gives a real Ubuntu on the same laptop, so the Windows learner and the Linux learner run identical commands from here on.
L4.explanation: The choice is about the next two years, not the next week. One shell means one set of commands in every later concept, and it means the learner's laptop matches the servers they will eventually work on, which run Linux.

L4.prompt_tpl: A friend's laptop from 2018 runs Windows 10 and has never been updated. In an administrator PowerShell, wsl --install prints a page of usage text and installs nothing. Diagnose it and say what to do first.
L4.answer: wsl --install exists only on Windows 10 version 2004 (build 19041) and later, or Windows 11. An old, never-updated Windows 10 predates it, so the wsl command does not recognise --install and just prints its usage. Update Windows first (Settings, Windows Update), check the build with winver, then run wsl --install again. Microsoft's manual installation page covers the older builds if updating is impossible.
L4.explanation: Transfer: the same symptom, usage text instead of an install, has one likely cause on an old machine. Reading the page of text as 'the command is not understood' rather than 'the machine is broken' is the skill; checking the build number against the documented minimum is the fix.

L4.prompt_tpl: After installing WSL, a learner has a bash prompt inside a window titled Ubuntu, on a machine whose desktop is Windows. How many operating systems are running, which one owns the hardware, and where do the Windows files appear from inside the Ubuntu window?
L4.answer: Two: Windows owns the hardware, and Ubuntu runs inside it in a lightweight virtual machine that WSL2 manages. From inside Ubuntu the Windows disk is mounted at /mnt/c, so the Windows desktop of a user named Asha is /mnt/c/Users/Asha/Desktop. Going the other way, Ubuntu's files show up in Windows Explorer under \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu. Two file trees, one laptop; keep code on the Ubuntu side.
L4.explanation: This is the concept from 'What an operating system actually does' applied to an unfamiliar instance: an OS inside an OS. Knowing there are two file trees prevents the most common WSL confusion, a file saved on one side that cannot be found on the other.

concepts.t: The terminal: what that window actually is

L0.body:
+------------------------------------+
 | Terminal                           |
 | asha@laptop:~$ ls                  |
 | Desktop  Documents  notes.txt      |
 | asha@laptop:~$                     |
 +------------------------------------+
 terminal: the window. Draws text,
   sends your keystrokes on.
 shell: the program inside it that
   reads a line and runs it.
 same machine, same files the file
   manager shows. Not a second PC.
 close the window: what was running
   in it stops; files on disk stay.
L0.cloze: The {{c1::terminal}} is the window: it draws text and sends your keystrokes on. The {{c2::shell}} is the program inside it that reads a line and runs it. It shows {{c3::the same files}} the file manager shows, on the same machine. Closing the window stops what was running in it; files on disk stay.

concepts.L1: A terminal is an ordinary program whose window shows text and passes your keystrokes to another program, the shell. The shell reads what you type, runs it, and hands the output back to the window. Both run on your machine and see the same files as the file manager. It is not a separate computer or a special mode.
concepts.L2: Two fears to kill. First, that the terminal is dangerous: it is exactly as powerful as the file manager, it just does not ask 'are you sure'. Second, that it is somewhere else: a different computer, or a hidden part of this one. The Documents that ls lists is the Documents folder you double-click. Same disk, two views.
concepts.L3: The terminal was once a physical device, a keyboard and screen wired to a shared computer, and the shell was the program on that computer that talked to it. The device is gone; the window emulates it, which is why such programs are called terminal emulators. The division of labour survived: the window handles characters and drawing, the shell handles meaning. That is why the prompt on macOS ends in `%` and on Ubuntu in `$`: different shell program (zsh, bash), same kind of window. It is also why VS Code can show a terminal in its bottom panel: one more window running the same shell. Closing a window sends a hang-up to the shell and everything it started, so a program running there stops; Foundations' 'Processes and job control' shows the machinery. The text you see is not the file system but the shell's report on it, and 'Where am I? The current directory' says which part it reports on.

L4.prompt_tpl: You type ls and press Enter. Which program reads that line and decides to run ls?
L4.answer: The shell, the program running inside the terminal window
L4.explanation: The terminal window only draws characters and passes keystrokes on. The shell (bash or zsh) receives the line, splits it into words, finds the program called ls and runs it, then hands the output back to the window to draw. Window and shell are two programs with two jobs.
options: The shell, the program running inside the terminal window
The terminal window itself
The operating system's desktop

L4.prompt_tpl: In a terminal, ls prints Desktop, Documents and Downloads. Where are these?
L4.answer: On this machine's disk: the same folders the file manager shows in your home folder
L4.explanation: The terminal is a view of the same disk. Open the file manager and the same three folders are there; make a folder in one and it appears in the other. There is no separate terminal computer and no hidden terminal storage.
options: On this machine's disk: the same folders the file manager shows in your home folder
Inside the terminal program, separate from the desktop's files
On a remote computer the terminal is connected to

L4.prompt_tpl: The prompt reads `asha@laptop:~$` and you type the line whoami and press Enter. What single word is printed?
L4.answer: asha
L4.explanation: whoami prints the username of whoever the shell is running as, which is the account you logged in with: asha, the same name the prompt shows before the @. It is the quickest proof that the terminal is you, on this machine, not some other user or some other computer.

L4.prompt_tpl: You type echo hello there and press Enter. What line is printed?
L4.answer: hello there
L4.explanation: echo prints its arguments back, separated by single spaces, followed by a newline. The shell split the line into the command echo and two words; echo printed them. This is the smallest complete round trip: keystrokes to the shell, output back to the window.

L4.prompt_tpl: A terminal window is {c} columns wide and {r} rows tall. How many characters can it show at once?
L4.explanation: The terminal is a grid of character cells, not a page: 80 by 24 is 1920 cells, the size of the original hardware terminals and still the default for many windows. Text that scrolls off the top is kept in a scrollback buffer, but only the grid is drawn.

L4.prompt_tpl: Is typing a command in the terminal more dangerous than doing the same thing in the file manager?
L4.answer: It has the same power; the difference is that it does not ask 'are you sure' and there is no Recycle Bin
L4.explanation: The shell and the file manager both ask the OS to do things to the same files, so neither can do anything the other cannot. What differs is the safety rail: the file manager confirms and keeps a Trash; a shell command does exactly what you typed, immediately. The habit that follows is to read a line before pressing Enter.
options: It has the same power; the difference is that it does not ask 'are you sure' and there is no Recycle Bin
Yes: the terminal can reach parts of the machine the file manager cannot
No: the terminal is a sandbox and cannot change real files

L4.prompt_tpl: A program you started in the terminal is still running and you close the terminal window. What happens to the program, and what happens to a file it finished writing a minute ago?
L4.answer: The program stops: closing the window sends a hang-up to the shell and to everything the shell started, so the running program is ended. The file it finished writing a minute ago is on the disk and stays; only things that had not yet been written are lost. Closing the window is closing a program, not switching off the machine.
L4.explanation: The window is one program among many; the disk is shared by all of them. Foundations' 'Processes and job control' shows the signal that does this and how to keep a program alive past the window.

L4.prompt_tpl: In VS Code a learner sees a dark panel at the bottom of the editor showing `asha@laptop:~/proj$` and asks whether that is a real terminal or a fake one built into the editor. Answer, and say what happens if they type ls there.
L4.answer: It is a real terminal: VS Code opens a terminal panel and runs the machine's ordinary shell inside it, bash here. Typing ls lists the files of the current directory, ~/proj, exactly as a separate terminal window would, and any file it shows is the same file the editor's sidebar shows. The window changed; the shell and the files did not.
L4.explanation: Transfer: once the terminal is understood as 'a window that runs a shell', an unfamiliar window with a prompt in it is recognisable on sight, whether it is inside an editor, a browser-based lab, or a remote session.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a Mac the prompt ends in `%` and on Ubuntu it ends in `$`. A learner concludes that Macs have a different kind of terminal. Correct this using the window-versus-shell distinction.
L4.answer: The window is the same kind of thing on both, a terminal emulator that draws text and forwards keystrokes. What differs is the shell program running inside it: macOS starts zsh, whose default prompt ends in `%`, and Ubuntu starts bash, whose default prompt ends in `$`. Every command in this domain (pwd, ls, cd, echo, whoami) behaves the same in both, because those are programs the shell runs, not features of the shell.
L4.explanation: The prompt's shape is the shell's choice, not the terminal's and not the machine's. Reading the last character tells you which shell you are talking to; Foundations' 'The shell: command, arguments, flags' builds on that same separation.

concepts.t: The prompt, the command, the argument, and the Enter key

L0.body:
asha@laptop:~$ echo hello world
 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^
 prompt         cmd  arguments
 hello world           <- output
 asha@laptop:~$        <- ready again
 nothing runs until you press Enter
 the line is split into words on spaces
 first word = the program to run
 case matters: ls runs, LS does not:
   bash: LS: command not found
 clear   wipes the screen, harmless
 exit    ends the shell, closes window
L0.cloze: The {{c1::prompt}} is the shell saying it is ready. You type a line; nothing happens until you press {{c2::Enter}}. The shell splits the line on spaces: the first word is the {{c3::command}}, the rest are its {{c4::arguments}}. Output follows, then the prompt returns. Case matters: LS gives 'command not found'.

concepts.L1: The prompt is text the shell prints to say it is waiting. A line is words separated by spaces: the first names a program to run, the rest are handed to that program as arguments. Enter sends the line; until then nothing has happened. Output appears under the line, and a fresh prompt means the shell is ready again.
concepts.L2: The miss is reading a command line as a sentence the computer understands. It is not: the shell only splits on spaces and looks up the first word as a program name, as typed. So LS is not ls, a misspelling gets 'command not found' rather than a guess, and that message means a typo or a missing program, never a broken machine.
concepts.L3: The shell's loop: print a prompt, read one line, split it into words at spaces, treat the first word as the name of a program, start that program with the remaining words as its arguments, wait for it to finish, print the prompt again. Each part has a visible consequence. No prompt yet means a program is still running. Extra spaces vanish from echo's output because the shell hands echo words, not the raw line. The shell attaches no meaning to the arguments; what -l means to ls is ls's business, which is where Foundations' 'The shell: command, arguments, flags' begins. The default Ubuntu prompt `user@host:~$` and the macOS prompt `user@host ~ %` carry the same three facts: who you are, which machine, and the current directory, which the next concept reads. clear and exit are ordinary commands: clear redraws an empty screen and destroys nothing; exit ends the shell and closes the window.

L4.prompt_tpl: You type echo one two three and press Enter. What line is printed?
L4.answer: one two three
L4.explanation: The shell splits the line into the command echo and three arguments; echo prints its arguments separated by single spaces. The word echo itself is not printed: it named the program, it was not part of the message.

L4.prompt_tpl: In the line echo hello world, which word is the command?
L4.answer: echo
L4.explanation: The first word of a line is always the command, the program the shell will run; everything after it is arguments passed to that program. hello and world are what echo is told to print. The prompt before the line is not part of it at all.
options: echo
hello
The whole line, echo hello world

L4.prompt_tpl: You type a line of {n} words separated by single spaces and press Enter. The first word is the command. How many arguments does the command receive?
L4.explanation: The shell splits on spaces; one word names the program and every other word is an argument. A line of 5 words is one command with 4 arguments. Counting this way is how you read any command line before pressing Enter.

L4.prompt_tpl: On Ubuntu you type LS in capitals and press Enter. What happens?
L4.answer: An error saying the command LS was not found; nothing is listed
L4.explanation: Program names are case-sensitive on Linux and the shell looks up exactly what you typed. There is no program called LS, so nothing runs. Plain bash prints bash: LS: command not found; Ubuntu's command-not-found helper words it as Command 'LS' not found and may suggest ls; macOS zsh prints zsh: command not found: LS. Same fact each time: retype it as ls.
options: An error saying the command LS was not found; nothing is listed
The files are listed, exactly as with ls
The terminal window closes

L4.prompt_tpl: You typed pwd and nothing happened; the cursor sits at the end of the line. What is the most likely reason?
L4.answer: You have not pressed Enter; the shell has not received the line yet
L4.explanation: Typing only edits the line. The shell reads it when Enter is pressed and not before. Beginners coming from a search box expect results to appear as they type; the terminal waits.
options: You have not pressed Enter; the shell has not received the line yet
pwd is not installed on this machine
The terminal has frozen and should be closed

L4.prompt_tpl: You type echo hello with five spaces between echo and hello, then press Enter. What is printed, and why?
L4.answer: hello, with no extra spaces. The shell splits the line into words at runs of spaces, so echo receives one argument, hello, and never sees how many spaces you typed. The gaps were between words, not inside one.
L4.explanation: The command line is not sent to the program as a string; it arrives as a list of words. Everything the shell does starts from that split, which is why a filename with a space in it becomes two arguments and causes trouble later on.

L4.prompt_tpl: bash prints: bash: pwdd: command not found. What does it mean?
L4.answer: The shell could not find a program named pwdd; almost always a typo, here for pwd
L4.explanation: The shell looked for a program with exactly that name and there was none (Ubuntu's helper may word it Command 'pwdd' not found and suggest pwd). It does not autocorrect. Read the word it names, compare with what you meant, retype. The message is the shell being precise, not the machine being broken.
options: The shell could not find a program named pwdd; almost always a typo, here for pwd
The terminal is broken and needs reinstalling
You do not have permission to run commands

L4.prompt_tpl: After you press Enter, how do you tell whether the shell is ready for the next command, and what does it mean if the prompt has not come back?
L4.answer: The prompt returning is the signal: the shell prints it only when the program it started has finished. If the prompt has not reappeared, the program is still running, perhaps waiting for input or working. Typing more at that point goes to the running program, not to the shell.
L4.explanation: The prompt is not decoration; it is a status line. Reading it as 'ready' is what lets you tell a slow command from a stuck one, which is where Ctrl+C in 'Copy and paste in a terminal' becomes useful.

L4.prompt_tpl: A screenshot shows: ravi@MacBook-Air ~ % echo good morning, followed by the line good morning, followed by ravi@MacBook-Air ~ %. Identify the prompt, the command, the arguments, the output, and say what the last line tells you.
L4.answer: Prompt: ravi@MacBook-Air ~ %, printed by zsh (the % is zsh's default). Command: echo. Arguments: good and morning, two words. Output: good morning, printed by echo. The last line is the prompt again, meaning echo finished and the shell is waiting for the next line. The machine is a Mac, the user is ravi, and ~ says the current directory is ravi's home.
L4.explanation: Transfer: an unfamiliar prompt shape (macOS instead of Ubuntu) reads the same way once you know the parts. The prompt is whatever the shell prints; the structure command, arguments, output, prompt is the same in every shell.

L4.prompt_tpl: Foundations' 'The shell: command, arguments, flags' says ls -l lists files in long form. Using only this concept, say what the shell does with -l and what it does not do.
L4.answer: The shell splits ls -l into two words, runs the program ls, and passes -l to it as an argument, exactly as it would pass any word. The shell does not know that -l means 'long form'; it attaches no meaning to arguments at all. ls receives the word -l and decides what it means. Flags are a convention that programs follow, not something the shell understands.
L4.explanation: The separation matters because it predicts behaviour: the shell treats every word the same way, so what an argument means is always a question for the program's own documentation, which is what Foundations goes on to teach.

concepts.t: Where am I? The current directory

L0.body:
asha@laptop:~$ pwd
 /home/asha
 asha@laptop:~$ ls
 Desktop  Documents  Downloads
 asha@laptop:~$ cd Documents
 asha@laptop:~/Documents$ pwd
 /home/asha/Documents
 asha@laptop:~/Documents$ cd
 asha@laptop:~$
 ~ = your home: /home/asha on Ubuntu,
     /Users/asha on macOS
 every command runs from the current
 directory; each window has its own
L0.cloze: The shell always has a current directory. {{c1::pwd}} prints it, ls lists what is in it, {{c2::cd Documents}} moves into Documents, and cd with no argument returns to {{c3::home}}. ~ in the prompt means home: /home/asha on Ubuntu, {{c4::/Users/asha}} on macOS. Each terminal window has its own current directory.

concepts.L1: Every shell sits in one folder, its current directory, and every command runs from there: ls lists that folder, a file a program creates lands there. pwd prints it as a full path from the root. cd name moves into a folder inside it; cd alone goes home. The prompt shows it, with ~ standing for your home folder.
concepts.L2: The miss is thinking the terminal looks at the whole machine at once. It does not: ls shows one folder, cd Documents only works if Documents is inside the folder you are in, and 'No such file or directory' usually means you are not where you think. Second miss: two windows share a location. They do not; each shell has its own.
concepts.L3: The current directory is a property of the shell, held by the OS for every running program: when a program names a file without saying where, the OS looks in that program's current directory. That is why 'where am I' comes before any command that touches a file. cd does not move anything; it changes the shell's idea of where it is, which is why it is instant and why it is the one command here that changes the prompt. A path like /home/asha/Documents reads from the root, /, downward, one name per slash; pwd prints that full form, and the prompt abbreviates the home part to ~. Home is /home/asha on Ubuntu and WSL, /Users/asha on macOS; a Windows folder seen from WSL is /mnt/c/Users/Asha/Desktop. 'Folders, and the tree' gives the whole tree and 'The path: absolute and relative' the two ways to name a place in it; Foundations' 'Paths and the filesystem tree' takes both further.

L4.prompt_tpl: The prompt reads `asha@laptop:~$` and pwd prints /home/asha. You type cd Documents, then pwd. What does the second pwd print?
L4.answer: /home/asha/Documents
L4.explanation: cd Documents moves the shell into the Documents folder inside the current one, so the current directory is now /home/asha/Documents, and pwd prints it in full. The prompt changes to `asha@laptop:~/Documents$` to show the same fact.

L4.prompt_tpl: A macOS user named asha opens Terminal and types pwd. What is printed?
L4.answer: /Users/asha
L4.explanation: A new terminal starts in the home directory, and on macOS home directories live under /Users, so the answer is /Users/asha. On Ubuntu and in WSL the same user's home is /home/asha. The prompt shows ~ for either; pwd shows the real path.

L4.prompt_tpl: What does ~ in the prompt `asha@laptop:~$` mean?
L4.answer: The current directory is your home folder
L4.explanation: ~ is the shell's abbreviation for your home directory, /home/asha here. When you cd elsewhere the prompt shows the new place relative to it, such as ~/Documents. It is not the root of the disk (that is /) and not a placeholder for nothing.
options: The current directory is your home folder
The current directory is the root of the disk
No directory has been chosen yet

L4.prompt_tpl: pwd prints /home/asha, a path of 2 names. You go down {k} folders, one cd at a time, without ever going up or home. How many slash-separated names does pwd print now?
L4.answer: 2 + k: each cd into a subfolder appends one name. k=1 -> 3; k=2 -> 4; k=3 -> 5.
L4.explanation: Each cd name adds exactly one name to the end of the path, because the new folder is inside the old one. From /home/asha, two cds might give /home/asha/proj/data, four names. Counting names is a quick way to check you are as deep as you think.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are in /home/asha/Documents/proj. You type cd with no argument, then pwd. What is printed?
L4.answer: /home/asha
L4.explanation: cd with no argument always returns to your home directory, from anywhere. It is the reset button when you are lost: cd, then pwd, then start again from a place you know.

L4.prompt_tpl: You type cd documents and bash prints: bash: cd: documents: No such file or directory. Give the two most likely causes and how to check each.
L4.answer: Either there is no folder with exactly that name in the current directory, or the name is spelt or capitalised differently: on Linux documents and Documents are different names. Check with pwd to confirm where you are, then ls to see the folder's real name and spelling, then cd using the name exactly as ls shows it.
L4.explanation: The message means 'not here, under that name'; it says nothing about whether the folder exists elsewhere. pwd and ls are the two questions to ask before repeating a cd.

L4.prompt_tpl: In one terminal window you cd into Documents. You then open a second terminal window. Where is the second one?
L4.answer: In your home directory; each shell has its own current directory
L4.explanation: The current directory belongs to the shell, not to the machine or to you. A new window starts a new shell, and a new shell starts at home. Moving in one window changes nothing in the other. The same holds for a terminal panel inside an editor.
options: In your home directory; each shell has its own current directory
In Documents, because that is where you are
In the root of the disk

L4.prompt_tpl: You ran a command in ~/Downloads that created a file called out.txt. Later you look in Documents and it is not there. Explain what happened and where the file is.
L4.answer: The command created out.txt in the shell's current directory at the time, which was ~/Downloads, so the file is /home/asha/Downloads/out.txt (or /Users/asha/Downloads/out.txt on macOS). A program that names a file without a folder puts it where the shell is. Nothing went wrong; the file is simply where you were, not where you expected.
L4.explanation: Files land in the current directory unless told otherwise. That is the practical reason to run pwd before any command that creates something, and to keep each project's work in its own folder.

L4.prompt_tpl: On an Ubuntu machine the prompt reads `ravi@box:~/work/data$`. You type pwd. What is printed?
L4.answer: /home/ravi/work/data
L4.explanation: Read the prompt: the user is ravi, so ~ is /home/ravi, and ~/work/data expands to /home/ravi/work/data. pwd prints the full path with ~ replaced. Transfer test: a different user and folders you have never seen, read with the same rule.

L4.prompt_tpl: Inside WSL Ubuntu, a learner whose Windows username is Asha types cd /mnt/c/Users/Asha/Desktop and then pwd. What is printed?
L4.answer: /mnt/c/Users/Asha/Desktop
L4.explanation: WSL mounts the Windows C: drive at /mnt/c, so the Windows desktop is reachable at that path and cd moves there like any other folder; pwd prints it exactly. The capital A in Asha is the Windows account name and must match. This is where the two file trees of the WSL concept meet.

concepts.t: A code editor is not a word processor

L0.body:
word processor (Word, Docs, Pages):
   you type  print("hi")
   it saves  print(“hi”)   curly quotes
   spaces may become non-breaking ones
   file is .docx: layout, not your text
 code editor (VS Code):
   saves exactly the keys you pressed
   as plain text: hello.py, notes.txt
 Python on a Word-made file:
   SyntaxError: invalid character
   '“' (U+201C)
 rule: code goes in VS Code, never Word
L0.cloze: A word processor (Word, Docs, Pages) turns the quotes in print("hi") into {{c1::curly quotes}} and some spaces into {{c2::non-breaking spaces}}, and saves layout, not text, in a .docx. A code editor such as {{c3::VS Code}} saves exactly the keys you pressed as plain text. Python on a Word-made file fails with SyntaxError: invalid character '“' (U+201C).

concepts.L1: A code editor (VS Code here) stores exactly the characters you type as a plain text file, coloured but unchanged. A word processor stores a document, fonts and layout and text, in a format like .docx, and silently improves your typing: straight quotes become curly, some spaces non-breaking. Code needs the first.
concepts.L2: The miss is that the two are the same kind of thing with different features. They are not: a word processor changes what you typed, on purpose, invisibly. A curly quote looks like a quote and a non-breaking space looks like a space, and Python rejects both. The error points at a character you cannot see the difference in.
concepts.L3: Python reads source one character at a time against a small alphabet: the quote it accepts is U+0022, the plain double quote. Word's autocorrect replaces it with U+201C and U+201D, the typographic quotes, because they look better in prose, and may replace a space with U+00A0, a non-breaking space, to keep two words together. To Python these are unknown characters, and its message says so: SyntaxError: invalid character '“' (U+201C), or invalid non-printable character U+00A0. The code point is the clue, and 'Text is bytes: UTF-8 in one concept' explains what it names. VS Code substitutes nothing, saves plain UTF-8 text, and can show whitespace on request, which is how a non-breaking space is found. On macOS, TextEdit defaults to rich text with smart quotes on, so it is a word processor unless set to plain text. Foundations' 'Reading an error message' begins from this kind of message.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are about to write your first Python file, hello.py. Which program should you open?
L4.answer: VS Code
L4.explanation: VS Code is a code editor: it saves exactly what you type as plain text, which is what Python reads. Word and Google Docs are word processors; they autocorrect quotes and spaces and save a document format, and Python cannot run either. The distinction is about what is saved, not about features.
options: VS Code
Microsoft Word
Google Docs

L4.prompt_tpl: You typed print("hello") in Word, saved it as hello.py, and ran it with Python. Which message do you see?
L4.answer: SyntaxError: invalid character '“' (U+201C)
L4.explanation: Word replaced the straight quote with a left curly quote, U+201C. Python does not know that character and names it in the error, with its code point. The other two messages are real Python errors for different mistakes: a missing bracket, or a name that was never defined.
options: SyntaxError: invalid character '“' (U+201C)
SyntaxError: '(' was never closed
NameError: name 'print' is not defined

L4.prompt_tpl: What does a .docx file saved by Word contain?
L4.answer: A document: text plus fonts, layout and formatting, in Word's own format
L4.explanation: A .docx is a package describing a document, with the text buried inside formatting data. Python, the shell and every tool in this curriculum read plain text: a file that is nothing but the characters. A code editor writes that; a word processor writes a document.
options: A document: text plus fonts, layout and formatting, in Word's own format
Exactly the characters you typed and nothing else
A picture of the page

L4.prompt_tpl: A line of code has {n} characters, all plain ASCII, and ends with a newline character. How many bytes does the file take on disk?
L4.answer: n + 1: one byte per ASCII character plus one for the newline. n=11 -> 12; n=24 -> 25; n=40 -> 41.
L4.explanation: Plain text is one byte per ASCII character; the newline that ends the line is a character too. print("hi") is 11 characters, so that file is 12 bytes. Counting bytes is the first evidence that a text file is nothing but its characters.

L4.prompt_tpl: The same {n}-character line plus its newline is retyped in Word, which turns {q} of its straight quotes into curly ones. A curly quote is 3 bytes in UTF-8 instead of 1. How many bytes is the saved plain-text export now?
L4.answer: n + 1 + 2q: each replaced quote adds 2 bytes. n=11, q=2 -> 16; n=11, q=4 -> 20; n=24, q=2 -> 29.
L4.explanation: Each straight quote was 1 byte; each curly quote is 3 bytes, so every substitution adds 2. For print("hi") with both quotes replaced: 12 + 4 = 16 bytes. The file is visibly the same length in characters and silently longer in bytes, which is the whole problem: the change is real and invisible.

L4.prompt_tpl: You copied a few lines of code from a web page into your file and Python says: SyntaxError: invalid non-printable character U+00A0. What is that character, why can you not see it, and what is the fix?
L4.answer: U+00A0 is a non-breaking space, which web pages and word processors use to stop a line breaking between two words. On screen it looks exactly like an ordinary space, so the line looks fine. Python only accepts ordinary spaces (U+0020) for indentation and between words. Fix: in VS Code, delete and retype the spaces on the line the error names, or turn on rendering of whitespace so the odd character shows, then replace it.
L4.explanation: The error message tells you the exact character, by code point, and the exact line. Trusting the message over your eyes is the skill; the eyes cannot distinguish the two spaces.

L4.prompt_tpl: A learner proposes to keep writing code in Word and use Save As, plain text (.txt), to strip the formatting. Will Python then run the file?
L4.answer: No: the curly quotes and non-breaking spaces are characters in the text and survive the export
L4.explanation: Save As plain text drops fonts and layout but keeps every character, including the ones autocorrect substituted. The quotes are still U+201C and U+201D in the .txt. The substitution happened while typing, so the only reliable fix is to type code in an editor that does not substitute.
options: No: the curly quotes and non-breaking spaces are characters in the text and survive the export
Yes: plain text format has no curly quotes
Yes, as long as the file is renamed to .py

L4.prompt_tpl: A learner's script fails at line 7: SyntaxError: invalid character '’' (U+2019). Line 7 is a message containing the word it's, typed on their phone and sent to themselves, then pasted into VS Code. Diagnose it.
L4.answer: The apostrophe in it's is not the ASCII apostrophe U+0027 but a right single quotation mark, U+2019. VS Code did not change it; the phone keyboard did, since phone keyboards substitute typographic quotes automatically, and the paste carried it across. Python sees an unknown character. Retype the apostrophe in VS Code, and in general treat text that passed through a phone, a chat app or a word processor as suspect.
L4.explanation: Transfer: the same mechanism, automatic substitution somewhere upstream, in an instance the concept did not mention. The code point in the error, U+2019, is what identifies it; VS Code is innocent here, and the rule generalises from Word to every tool that improves your typing.

L4.prompt_tpl: Foundations' 'Reading an error message' teaches reading the message before guessing. Given SyntaxError: invalid character '“' (U+201C) with a caret under the first quote of line 3, list what the message already tells you and what one action it implies.
L4.answer: It tells you the kind of problem (a character Python cannot accept, not a logic error), the exact character (a left double quotation mark), its code point (U+201C), the line (3) and the position (the caret). The action: replace that character with a plain straight quote in VS Code, then check the closing quote on the same line, which will be U+201D for the same reason.
L4.explanation: Nothing needs guessing: the file was edited in something that substitutes quotes, and the message locates every fact needed to repair it. Learning to read that much from one line is the habit Foundations builds on.
