concepts.t: Copy and paste in a terminal is not the same as everywhere else

L0.body:
everywhere else:
   Ctrl+C copies, Ctrl+V pastes
 in a terminal:
   Ctrl+C = STOP the running program
            (an interrupt); not copy
   Linux:  Ctrl+Shift+C, Ctrl+Shift+V
   macOS:  Cmd+C, Cmd+V
           (Ctrl+C still interrupts)
   Windows Terminal: select text, then
           right-click copies; right-
           click again pastes
 to share an error: copy its TEXT,
 not a photo of the screen
L0.cloze: In a terminal Ctrl+C is not copy: it sends an {{c1::interrupt}} that stops the running program. Copy and paste are {{c2::Ctrl+Shift+C and Ctrl+Shift+V}} on Linux, {{c3::Cmd+C and Cmd+V}} on macOS, and select then right-click in Windows Terminal. To share an error, copy its text, not a photo.

concepts.L1: Ctrl+C was a terminal key decades before it was a copy key: it tells the running program to stop. Terminals keep it and put copy and paste elsewhere: Ctrl+Shift+C and Ctrl+Shift+V on Linux terminals, Cmd+C and Cmd+V on macOS, select and right-click in Windows Terminal. Ctrl+V in a Linux terminal does nothing useful.
concepts.L2: The miss: a beginner sees an error, selects it, presses Ctrl+C to copy, and the program dies. They conclude the terminal is hostile or they broke something. Nothing broke: Ctrl+C did its job. Second miss: pasting a command from a web page and pressing Enter without reading it; pasted text can contain a newline and run at once.
concepts.L3: Ctrl+C reaches the terminal as a keystroke, but the terminal does not pass it on as text: it turns it into an interrupt signal delivered to whatever is running in the foreground, and the default response is to stop. At an empty prompt the shell prints ^C and a fresh prompt; nothing is harmed. That path is why the key cannot also mean copy, and why every terminal adds a second binding. Cmd+C was never a terminal key, so macOS uses it freely; Linux terminals add Shift; Windows Terminal takes Ctrl+Shift+C and V and right-click. To the shell, pasting is ordinary keystrokes, which is the danger: a pasted line that ends in a newline is a line plus Enter. Paste, read, then press Enter yourself. Foundations' 'Processes and job control' names the signal, SIGINT, and its family; here it is enough that Ctrl+C means stop, and that to copy an error you select its text and use the terminal's copy key.

L4.prompt_tpl: A program is running in an Ubuntu terminal and you press Ctrl+C. What happens?
L4.answer: The program is interrupted and stops; nothing is copied
L4.explanation: Ctrl+C in a terminal sends an interrupt to the running program, and the usual response is to stop immediately. It does not touch the clipboard. If you wanted to copy, select the text and press Ctrl+Shift+C instead.
options: The program is interrupted and stops; nothing is copied
The selected text is copied, as in any other program
The terminal window closes

L4.prompt_tpl: Which keys copy selected text in a Linux terminal such as Ubuntu's?
L4.answer: Ctrl+Shift+C
L4.explanation: Linux terminals add Shift to the usual copy and paste keys, because plain Ctrl+C is taken by interrupt and plain Ctrl+V is taken by the shell. Ctrl+Shift+C copies, Ctrl+Shift+V pastes. Right-click also offers Copy and Paste in a menu.
options: Ctrl+Shift+C
Ctrl+C
Ctrl+Insert only

L4.prompt_tpl: Which keys copy and paste in Terminal on macOS?
L4.answer: Cmd+C and Cmd+V, as in every other Mac program
L4.explanation: macOS uses the Command key for copy and paste everywhere, and Command was never a terminal key, so Terminal.app keeps the usual Cmd+C and Cmd+V. Ctrl+C on a Mac terminal still interrupts the running program, exactly as on Linux.
options: Cmd+C and Cmd+V, as in every other Mac program
Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V
Cmd+Shift+C and Cmd+Shift+V only

L4.prompt_tpl: Nothing is running; the prompt is showing and the line is empty. You press Ctrl+C. What do you see?
L4.answer: ^C is printed and a fresh prompt appears; nothing else happens
L4.explanation: With no program to interrupt, the shell itself receives the interrupt, prints ^C to acknowledge it, throws away whatever was typed on the line, and prints a new prompt. It is the safe way to abandon a half-typed line you no longer want.
options: ^C is printed and a fresh prompt appears; nothing else happens
The terminal closes
The previous command runs again

L4.prompt_tpl: You saw an error, selected it with the mouse, pressed Ctrl+C to copy it, and the program vanished. What happened, and what should you do now?
L4.answer: Ctrl+C sent an interrupt to the program, which stopped; the clipboard is unchanged. Nothing is broken. Run the program again to reproduce the error, select the text, and copy it with the terminal's own key: Ctrl+Shift+C on Linux, Cmd+C on macOS, right-click in Windows Terminal. Then paste it into your message as text.
L4.explanation: The reflex from every other program is exactly wrong here, and the consequence, losing the thing you were trying to save, is what makes beginners distrust the terminal. Knowing that Ctrl+C means stop turns the incident into a non-event.

L4.prompt_tpl: You copy a command from a web page and paste it into your terminal. What should you do before pressing Enter, and why might Enter already have been pressed for you?
L4.answer: Read the pasted line in full and make sure it is the one command you expected. Pasted text is delivered as if you had typed it, so if the copied text ends with a newline, or contains one, the shell runs the command the moment it arrives, without waiting for you. Web pages can also hide text inside the copied region, so what runs may be more than what was visible. Paste into a place you can read first, or read carefully after pasting, then press Enter yourself.
L4.explanation: A terminal does what it is told at once and has no confirmation dialog. Reading before Enter is the one habit that makes pasting commands from the internet reasonably safe; the security domain revisits why.

L4.prompt_tpl: In an Ubuntu terminal you press Ctrl+V to paste and nothing sensible appears. Why, and what key does paste?
L4.answer: Plain Ctrl+V is a key the shell keeps for itself (in bash it means 'insert the next key literally'), so the terminal does not treat it as paste. Paste in a Linux terminal is Ctrl+Shift+V, or right-click and choose Paste. The clipboard still holds your text; only the key was wrong.
L4.explanation: Every ordinary program agrees on Ctrl+V; terminals cannot, because the shell had those control keys first. The pattern to remember is: add Shift on Linux, use Cmd on macOS.

L4.prompt_tpl: A program you started keeps printing lines and never gives the prompt back. Say how to stop it, then how to copy its last few lines into a message, on your own OS.
L4.answer: Ctrl+C stops it: the interrupt reaches the foreground program and it exits, and the prompt returns. Then select the lines with the mouse and copy them with the terminal's copy key: Ctrl+Shift+C on Ubuntu, Cmd+C on macOS, right-click on the selection in Windows Terminal. Paste with the matching paste key into the message. The order matters: stop first, then copy; pressing Ctrl+C with a selection would still stop the program.
L4.explanation: Transfer to an unfamiliar situation, a program that will not finish, using only the two facts of the concept: Ctrl+C means stop, and copy lives on a different key. The same two moves handle a stuck command in every later domain.

L4.prompt_tpl: Foundations' 'Processes and job control' says Ctrl+C sends the signal SIGINT. Using this concept, explain why the key is intercepted by the terminal rather than delivered to the program as a character, and what that implies for the choice of copy key.
L4.answer: The program is reading characters from the terminal, and a character cannot force a program to stop if the program is not reading. So the terminal treats Ctrl+C specially: instead of queueing it as input, it asks the OS to deliver an interrupt signal to the foreground program, which the OS does regardless of what the program is doing. Because the key is consumed for that purpose, it cannot also mean copy, which is why every terminal puts copy on another key.
L4.explanation: This is the first meeting with signals, and it explains a design that otherwise looks like an annoyance. The OS domain develops signals fully; the practical residue is that in a terminal, Ctrl+C means stop.

concepts.t: What the internet is, in one concept

L0.body:
laptop -wifi-> router -> your ISP ->
   other networks -> the server
 every machine has a numeric address:
   8.8.8.8          (an IPv4 address)
 you type a name; DNS returns the number:
   dns.google  ->  8.8.8.8
 data travels as packets, about 1500
 bytes each; a page is many, reassembled
 $ ping -c 1 dns.google
 64 bytes from dns.google (8.8.8.8):
   icmp_seq=1 ttl=117 time=28.4 ms
 the internet = networks that agreed to
 pass each other's packets (the IP rule)
 the web, email, WhatsApp: built on top
L0.cloze: The internet is many independent networks that agreed on one rule, {{c1::IP}}, for passing each other's {{c2::packets}}. Every connected machine has a numeric address such as 8.8.8.8; {{c3::DNS}} turns a name like dns.google into that number. The web, email and WhatsApp are services built on top of it, not the internet itself.

concepts.L1: The internet is a set of independently owned networks (your ISP, a university, Google) that agreed on one rule, IP, for passing packets to each other. Every connected machine has a numeric address; DNS is the lookup from a name to that number. A website is a program on one such machine, a server, answering requests.
concepts.L2: The miss: that 'the internet', 'the web', 'Google' and 'Chrome' are one thing, and that a website is somewhere vague called 'online'. A website is files and a program on a specific machine with an address, in a building somewhere. 'The cloud' is that machine too: someone else's computer, someone else's disk.
concepts.L3: Mechanism: your laptop hands the router a packet addressed to 8.8.8.8; the router passes it to the ISP; each router on the way knows only which neighbour is nearer the destination, which is why a cut cable reroutes traffic rather than stopping it. A page is split into packets of about 1500 bytes, sent separately and reassembled by your machine. First, DNS is asked what number dns.google is, because packets carry numbers, not names. Two limits follow. Bandwidth (Mbps) is bits per second through the pipe: a 250 MB file at 50 Mbps needs 8 x 250 / 50 = 40 s. Latency is one packet's time there and back, floored by light in fibre at about 200 000 km/s: a 14 000 km route cannot answer in under 140 ms, whatever the plan costs. 19 Networking owns the real material: 'IPv4 addresses and CIDR arithmetic', 'DNS: the resolution path and its caching layers', 'The speed of light in fibre is the floor'.

L4.prompt_tpl: What does DNS do?
L4.answer: Turns a name such as dns.google into the numeric address packets are sent to
L4.explanation: Packets carry numeric addresses, and people type names, so every visit begins with a DNS lookup. DNS does not carry the page, and it does not connect you to the internet; it is a directory. The ping line '64 bytes from dns.google (8.8.8.8)' shows the name and the number DNS found for it.
options: Turns a name such as dns.google into the numeric address packets are sent to
Connects your laptop to the router
Carries the page's bytes from the server to you

L4.prompt_tpl: A file is {s} MB, and 1 megabyte is 8 megabits. Your connection is {r} Mbps (megabits per second). At full speed, how many seconds does the download take?
L4.explanation: Plans are sold in bits per second and files are measured in bytes; the factor of 8 between them is the whole calculation. 250 MB at 50 Mbps: 8 x 250 / 50 = 40 s. A real download is slower, because the server, the route and other users share the pipe; full speed is a floor on the time, not a promise.

L4.prompt_tpl: A video stream uses {b} Mbps (megabits per second). You watch for {h} hours. How many megabytes of data does that use, with 1 megabyte = 8 megabits?
L4.explanation: Bits per second times seconds gives bits; divide by 8 for bytes. 3 Mbps for 2 hours: 3 x 7200 / 8 = 2700 MB, about 2.7 GB of a data plan. This is the arithmetic behind 'why did my data finish'; streaming quality settings are exactly this number.

L4.prompt_tpl: An address is written as {n} numbers, each from 0 to 255. How many distinct addresses can be written that way?
L4.explanation: Each position has 256 choices, independent of the others, so multiply: for 4 numbers, 256 x 256 x 256 x 256 = 4 294 967 296. That is the whole IPv4 address space, about 4.3 billion, fewer than the devices alive today, which is why your home has one public address shared by every device behind the router.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of these is a machine on the internet with an address?
L4.answer: The server that holds the files of the website you are reading
L4.explanation: A website is files and a program on a server, a real computer in a building, with an address like any other machine. The web is a service that runs over the internet, not a machine. Wi-Fi is the radio link from your laptop to the router; it has no address on the internet of its own.
options: The server that holds the files of the website you are reading
The web
Wi-Fi

L4.prompt_tpl: Light in fibre travels about 200 000 km/s. The cable route from your city to a server is {d} km one way. What is the smallest possible round-trip time, in milliseconds?
L4.explanation: Out and back is 2d km at 200 000 km/s: 14 000 km gives 28 000 / 200 000 = 0.14 s = 140 ms, before a single router adds its delay. Buying a faster plan raises bandwidth and does nothing to this number, which is why a game or a video call to a far server feels laggy on any connection. 19 Networking's 'The speed of light in fibre is the floor' is this calculation done properly.

L4.prompt_tpl: A page will not load. How do you tell 'my internet is down' from 'that website is down', and why does the distinction exist at all?
L4.answer: Open a different site, or run ping -c 1 dns.google. If nothing reaches any machine, the fault is on your side: the Wi-Fi, the router, or the ISP. If other sites load, your internet is fine and that one server, or the DNS answer for it, is the problem. The distinction exists because the internet is many independent networks and machines: a server can be off while every wire between you and it works.
L4.explanation: Every 'is it me or them' diagnosis in later domains is this move: test a different destination. The model, machines with addresses joined by networks that pass packets, is what makes the test meaningful.

L4.prompt_tpl: You send a WhatsApp message to a friend sitting across the room on the same Wi-Fi. Using this concept, trace where the message goes, and say whether it crosses the room directly.
L4.answer: It does not cross the room. Your phone sends packets to the router, which sends them out through the ISP to a WhatsApp server (owned by Meta, possibly in another country), which then sends packets back through the ISP and the same router to the friend's phone. WhatsApp is a service running on servers; your phones talk to those servers, not to each other. The round trip can be thousands of kilometres for a message that travelled two metres.
L4.explanation: Transfer: applying 'a service is a program on a server with an address' to a case where the geometry is misleading. The same reasoning explains why the message fails when the Wi-Fi works but the ISP's link is down.

L4.prompt_tpl: GCFGlobal has a lesson called 'Understanding the Cloud'. Using only this concept, say what 'saving a file to the cloud' physically means and what you are trusting when you do it.
L4.answer: It means the bytes are copied over the internet to a file on a disk in a server owned by a company (Google, Microsoft, Apple), in a building you will never see, and your machine keeps at most a copy. You are trusting that the company keeps the disk running, keeps backups, keeps your account reachable, and stays in business; and that your account is not lost or stolen, since the account is now the only key to those bytes. That last point is the reason the accounts concept in this section exists.
L4.explanation: Transfer: 'the cloud' reduced to the model, with its consequences read off. The word hides a machine, an address and an owner, and the owner is the point.

concepts.t: What a browser does

L0.body:
address bar:  https://monkeytype.com
  -> browser asks THAT server for a page
  -> server sends HTML, CSS, JS, images
  -> browser draws them (rendering)
 address bar:  monkeytype
  -> no dot: this is a SEARCH, not a site
  -> a search engine ranks results;
     ads and lookalikes can rank first
 browsers: Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari
 search engines: Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo
 the browser is a program on your disk;
 a website is files on someone's server
 404 Not Found = server has no such page
 Ctrl+L (Mac: Cmd+L) jumps to the bar
L0.cloze: A browser is a {{c1::program}} on your disk that sends a request to the server named in the URL, receives HTML, CSS, JavaScript and images, and {{c2::renders}} them into the page. A bare word in the address bar is a {{c3::search}}, not a site, and the results are ranked by a search engine, which is itself a website. 404 means the server has {{c4::no such page}}.

concepts.L1: A browser is a program that takes a URL, asks the named server for a page, receives files (HTML for structure, CSS for style, JavaScript for behaviour, images) and renders them. It also keeps cookies, history and downloads. A search engine is a website the browser visits; the address bar sends a bare word to it.
concepts.L2: The miss: that Google is the internet and the first result is the site. The address bar does two things: a name with a dot is fetched directly; a bare word goes to a search engine, which ranks what it likes, adverts and lookalikes included. A search for 'monkeytype' has ranked monkeytypepro.com above the real monkeytype.com.
concepts.L3: Mechanism: the browser connects to the host, sends 'GET /path' and gets a status (200 OK, 404 Not Found) and a file. The HTML names more files, each fetched by its own request, which is why text appears before pictures on a slow link. JavaScript is a program the server sends and your browser runs inside a sandbox: it can draw and talk to servers but cannot read your disk, the deliberate line between a page and a downloaded program. A cookie is a note the server asks the browser to keep and send back; it is how a site knows you tomorrow and why another browser does not. Looks prove nothing: the browser draws whatever bytes arrive, and a copy of a bank's files draws a bank; only the address identifies the server. 19 Networking's 'HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3' is this loop in detail; 20 Security's 'Session management and session fixation' is the cookie's failures.

L4.prompt_tpl: In Chrome you type monkeytype, with no dot, into the address bar and press Enter. What happens?
L4.answer: Chrome sends the word to its default search engine and shows a results page
L4.explanation: No dot means the browser cannot treat it as a host name, so it searches. The results page is a website's ranking, and the top entries can be adverts or lookalike domains, which is exactly what happened with monkeytypepro.com and monkey-type.org outranking monkeytype.com. Typing monkeytype.com fetches the real site directly.
options: Chrome sends the word to its default search engine and shows a results page
Chrome opens monkeytype.com, the closest matching site
Chrome reports an error because the address is incomplete

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of these is a browser?
L4.answer: Firefox
L4.explanation: Firefox, Chrome, Edge and Safari are browsers: programs on your disk that fetch and render pages. Google is a company whose search engine is a website, visited through a browser. Wi-Fi is the radio link between your machine and the router. Confusing the three is the commonest beginner model, and it hides who ranks what.
options: Firefox
Google
Wi-Fi

L4.prompt_tpl: You open https://monkeytype.com/no-such-page-here in a browser. The server has no page at that path. What status number does it reply with? Answer with the number.
L4.explanation: 404 Not Found is the server saying: I am here, I heard you, and I have nothing at that path. It is not 'the internet is down' (nothing would arrive at all) and not 'the site is down'. A mistyped path gives 404; a mistyped host gives a different error, because no server was reached.

L4.prompt_tpl: A page's HTML is {h} KB and it references {i} images of {k} KB each. How many KB does the browser download in total to show the page?
L4.explanation: The HTML is one file; each image it names is a separate request and a separate transfer. 20 images of 150 KB plus 60 KB of HTML is 3060 KB, about 3 MB, most of it pictures. This is why a page keeps loading after its text is readable, and why a data plan goes on images, not words.

L4.prompt_tpl: Where is a website's content when nobody is looking at it?
L4.answer: In files on the server that answers requests for it
L4.explanation: A website is files and a program on a specific machine. The browser holds a copy only while you look at it (and a cache for a while after). Nothing is 'in the cloud' except on a disk somewhere; 'online' is a place only in the sense that a server has an address.
options: In files on the server that answers requests for it
Inside the browser, which downloads the whole site at install time
Spread across the internet, held by the routers between you and it

L4.prompt_tpl: You sign in to Gmail in Chrome, close Chrome, and reopen it: still signed in. You open Firefox on the same machine: not signed in. Explain both with the cookie mechanism.
L4.answer: When you signed in, Google's server asked Chrome to keep a cookie, a note, and Chrome sends it back with every later request to google.com, so the server recognises you; Chrome saves cookies to disk, so closing and reopening keeps it. Firefox is a different program with its own cookie store and never received that note, so to Google it is a stranger. The sign-in lives in the browser's cookie, not in the machine or the network.
L4.explanation: Cookies are how a stateless request loop remembers you. The same fact explains why 'sign out' matters on a shared machine and why stealing a cookie is as good as stealing a password (20 Security's session management).

L4.prompt_tpl: A page shows your bank's logo, colours and layout exactly. What does that prove about which server you are talking to?
L4.answer: Nothing: the browser draws whatever bytes arrive, and files can be copied
L4.explanation: Rendering is faithful to the bytes, not to their origin. A copy of the bank's HTML, CSS and images draws an identical bank on any server. The only thing the browser cannot fake for a scammer is the address it fetched from, which is why the next concept is about reading it. Looks are evidence of nothing.
options: Nothing: the browser draws whatever bytes arrive, and files can be copied
That it is the bank: the browser checks the page against the bank's real design
That it is the bank, provided the page has a padlock

L4.prompt_tpl: On a slow connection a page shows its text at once, then pictures appear one by one over several seconds. Explain this from the request loop, and say what a page with 200 small images would feel like compared with one big image of the same total size.
L4.answer: The browser fetches the HTML first, renders the text immediately, then finds each image named in the HTML and requests it separately; each arrives when its own transfer finishes, so pictures fill in one at a time. 200 small images mean 200 requests, each paying its own round-trip latency, so the page dribbles in and feels slower than one big file of the same bytes, which pays the latency once and then streams. Bytes are not the only cost; requests are.
L4.explanation: Transfer: an unfamiliar symptom explained by the model. The observation that requests cost latency independently of bytes is the reason 19 Networking's HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 exist.

L4.prompt_tpl: A web page's JavaScript is a program from a stranger that your browser runs without asking. A downloaded program from the same site needs a click and a warning. Using this concept and 'Downloading a file, and where it lands', say why the two are treated so differently.
L4.answer: Page JavaScript runs inside the browser's sandbox: it can draw, compute and talk to servers, but the browser refuses it access to your files, other programs and the rest of the machine, so a hostile page can at worst be a hostile page. A downloaded program runs outside the sandbox with all your account's powers over every file. The warning marks the moment you leave the sandbox. That is why 'the site looked fine' is no defence for running its download.
L4.explanation: Connecting two concepts: the sandbox is the boundary between browsing (safe by construction, bounded harm) and running (unbounded harm). Every later security domain is about where such boundaries sit.

concepts.t: A URL, part by part

L0.body:
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world?page=2
 scheme   https     how to talk (encrypted)
 host     www.bbc.co.uk   WHICH machine
 path     /news/world     which page on it
 query    ?page=2         extra data
 read the host RIGHT to LEFT:
   uk . co . bbc . www
   the owned part is bbc.co.uk
 paypal.com.evil.ru
   owned part: evil.ru   NOT PayPal
 monkeytypepro.com, monkey-type.org
   are not monkeytype.com
 the owned part of the host is the only
 part that says who you are talking to
L0.cloze: A URL is scheme://host/path?query. The {{c1::host}} names the machine; read it {{c2::right to left}}: the owned part is the label just before the public ending (com, in, co.uk, co.in) plus that ending. In paypal.com.evil.ru the owned part is {{c3::evil.ru}}, so it is not PayPal. Everything left of the owned part, and everything after the host, is chosen by whoever owns that part.

concepts.L1: A URL has a scheme (how to talk: https is encrypted), a host (which machine), a path (which page on it) and an optional query (data after ?). Read the host right to left: the registered domain is one label before the public ending (com, in, co.in, co.uk) plus that ending, and it alone says whose machine this is.
concepts.L2: The miss: reading the host left to right and stopping at the first familiar word. paypal.com.evil.ru begins with paypal.com, and the eye stops there; the owner is evil.ru, who can create any name ending in .evil.ru without asking anyone. Looks, path, padlock and the word 'secure' all belong to that owner too.
concepts.L3: Mechanism: names are handed out right to left. The .ru registry gives evil.ru to whoever registers it; that owner then controls every name ending in .evil.ru, so secure.paypal.com.evil.ru is theirs. Public endings can be two labels (co.uk, co.in, gov.in): the registered domain is the first label left of the public ending, plus the ending. Path and query are the server's, so /paypal/login on evil.ru proves nothing. https means the connection to the named host is encrypted and the certificate matches that name; certificates are free, so lookalikes have them, and Chrome 117 (2023) dropped the padlock because few users understood it. monkeytypepro.com and monkey-type.org sit beside monkeytype.com; search ranked both above it. 19 Networking's 'DNS: the resolution path and its caching layers' is the lookup; 20 Security's 'X.509 certificate validation' is the adult padlock.

L4.prompt_tpl: In https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world?page=2 what is the path? Answer with the path exactly, including its leading slash.
L4.answer: /news/world
L4.explanation: The path starts at the first slash after the host and ends at the ? that begins the query. It names a page on the server; the server chooses what every path means, so a path can say anything. /news/world on bbc.co.uk is the BBC's world news; the same path on evil.ru is whatever evil.ru wants.

L4.prompt_tpl: What is the registered domain, the owned part, of the host in https://secure-login.paypal.com.evil.ru/signin? Answer with the domain only.
L4.answer: evil.ru
L4.explanation: Read right to left: ru is the public ending; evil is the first label before it; so evil.ru is what somebody registered, and everything to its left (paypal.com, secure-login) was invented by that owner. PayPal appears in the name and has nothing to do with the machine. The eye reads left to right; the rule reads right to left.

L4.prompt_tpl: What does the scheme https, on its own, tell you about a site?
L4.answer: That the connection to the host named in the URL is encrypted; nothing about whether that host is honest
L4.explanation: https encrypts the bytes between you and the named host and checks that the certificate matches that host name. Certificates are free and automatic, so a scam site has one too. It stops a third party reading your traffic; it does not tell you who the host is. Read the host for that.
options: That the connection to the host named in the URL is encrypted; nothing about whether that host is honest
That the site has been checked and is safe to enter a password on
That the site belongs to the company whose name appears first in the address

L4.prompt_tpl: Which URL is on the real Monkeytype site, whose domain is monkeytype.com?
L4.answer: https://monkeytype.com/settings
L4.explanation: Only the first has monkeytype.com as its owned part. monkeytypepro.com is a different registration (the ending com, then the label monkeytypepro); www.monkey-type.org is another. Both are real sites that outranked the original in search results, which is why the habit is to read the domain, not the result's title.
options: https://monkeytype.com/settings
https://monkeytypepro.com
https://www.monkey-type.org

L4.prompt_tpl: In https://www.google.com/search?q=monkeytype what is the query string? Answer with it exactly, without the question mark.
L4.answer: q=monkeytype
L4.explanation: The query begins after ? and is extra data for the server, here the search term under the key q. The server decides what to do with it; a URL can carry anything there, including tracking codes. It is not part of the host and says nothing about who you are talking to.

L4.prompt_tpl: A search for 'monkeytype' lists monkeytypepro.com first, monkey-type.org second and monkeytype.com third. Which do you open, and why can the wrong ones rank above the real one?
L4.answer: monkeytype.com: rank is decided by adverts and the search engine's guess, not by ownership
L4.explanation: A results page is a ranking a company sells and computes; nobody checks that the top entry owns the name. Lookalikes buy adverts and copy titles. The only fact the search engine cannot fake is the domain shown under each result, so read that before clicking. This ranking was observed while this section was being compiled.
options: monkeytype.com: rank is decided by adverts and the search engine's guess, not by ownership
monkeytypepro.com: the first result is the most trusted
Any of them: they are the same site under different names

L4.prompt_tpl: Who owns the host in https://accounts.google.com.security-check.info/verify, and which of the parts of this URL could Google have had any say in?
L4.answer: The owned part is security-check.info: info is the public ending and security-check is the label before it. Google had no say in any part: the owner of security-check.info invented accounts.google.com as a sub-name, chose the path /verify, and got the https certificate for free. Nothing in the URL involved Google. The real accounts page is on the domain google.com, where com is the ending and google the label before it.
L4.explanation: The consequence question: once the owned part is found, every other part is revealed as that owner's choice. The habit generalises to every domain and every lookalike.

L4.prompt_tpl: An SMS says your bank account is blocked and to verify at http://sbi.co.in.kyc-update.xyz/login. Read the URL part by part, say who owns the host, and say what you do instead.
L4.answer: Scheme http: not even encrypted. Host sbi.co.in.kyc-update.xyz: reading right to left, xyz is the ending and kyc-update the label before it, so the owner is kyc-update.xyz; sbi.co.in is a sub-name they invented. Path /login is theirs too. This is a stranger's machine dressed as the bank. Instead: do not open the link; reach the bank by typing the address you already know or through its app from the official store, and if worried, phone the number printed on your card.
L4.explanation: Transfer: an unfamiliar lookalike, in the Indian scam format (blocked account, KYC, a short deadline), decoded with the right-to-left rule. The public ending here has two labels inside the fake part, which is the trap the rule sees through.

L4.prompt_tpl: A browser keeps each site's cookies separate by host, so a page on evil.ru cannot read the cookie your bank set. Using this concept, explain why that protection only works if you reached the bank at the right host in the first place, and name the later Whetstone concept where this becomes the origin rule.
L4.answer: The browser sends a cookie only to the host that set it, matched by name, so evil.ru never receives the bank's cookie and cannot act as you. But if you typed your password into a lookalike, the lookalike simply received the password directly and sets up its own session with the real bank; no cookie rule helps, because you handed over the key. The boundary is drawn by host name, so the host name you actually reached is the whole security model. 20 Security's 'CSRF and SameSite' and 'Session management and session fixation' are where the cookie rule is developed.
L4.explanation: Connecting URL reading to the browser's security model: the browser isolates by host, so the human's job is to make sure the host is the right one. That division of labour persists through the entire security domain.

concepts.t: Downloading a file, and where it lands

L0.body:
click a link to a file: the browser
 copies its bytes into a FOLDER on disk
 default folder, for user asha:
   Windows  C:\Users\asha\Downloads
   macOS    /Users/asha/Downloads
   Ubuntu   /home/asha/Downloads
   WSL sees Windows's Downloads at
            /mnt/c/Users/asha/Downloads
 the list: Ctrl+J  (Mac: Cmd+Shift+J)
 $ ls ~/Downloads
 report.pdf  big.iso.crdownload
   .crdownload = still downloading
 downloaded = copied, not installed
 a downloaded PROGRAM is marked by the
 OS and warned about once. Read the name
L0.cloze: A download copies a file's bytes from a server into a folder on your disk, by default {{c1::Downloads}} in your home folder: /home/asha/Downloads on Ubuntu, /Users/asha/Downloads on macOS, C:\Users\asha\Downloads on Windows, which WSL sees at {{c2::/mnt/c/Users/asha/Downloads}}. Downloaded means {{c3::copied}}, not installed; a name ending in .crdownload is a download still in progress.

concepts.L1: A download copies bytes from a server into a new file on your disk, by default in the Downloads folder of your home folder. The browser's download list is a list of those files, not a place they live. The file belongs to no program and behaves like any other; the server keeps its copy, and nothing has been installed.
concepts.L2: The miss: 'I downloaded it but nothing happened', or 'it is in the browser somewhere'. Clicking Download produced a file in a folder, and that is all; installing and opening are separate acts not yet done. The reverse miss is worse: double-clicking a downloaded program runs a stranger's program, and a PDF icon is no evidence.
concepts.L3: Mechanism: the server's reply says 'this is a file, save it', and the browser writes the arriving bytes to disk under a temporary name (Chrome: name.crdownload, Firefox: name.part), renaming only when the last byte lands; an interrupted download leaves the fragment. The browser and the OS both record the source: Windows attaches a Zone.Identifier mark (the 'mark of the web') so SmartScreen warns before an unknown downloaded program runs; macOS attaches com.apple.quarantine and Gatekeeper asks before opening. The warnings fire on programs, not documents, and only once, so read the whole filename and the source domain before the click that dismisses them. This is the source rule of 'Installing and removing software, and where software comes from' applied to a file in Downloads; Foundations' 'Running Python: interpreter, scripts, environments' opens with such a download.

L4.prompt_tpl: On Ubuntu, user asha clicks a link to report.pdf in a browser with default settings. Give the absolute path of the downloaded file.
L4.answer: /home/asha/Downloads/report.pdf
L4.explanation: Home is /home/asha on Ubuntu; the browser's default folder is Downloads inside it; the file keeps the name the server gave it. Absolute paths start at /, so the answer starts there. The browser shows the name in its download list, but the file is on disk at this path and any program can open it.

L4.prompt_tpl: On macOS, user asha downloads data.csv with default browser settings. Give the absolute path of the file.
L4.answer: /Users/asha/Downloads/data.csv
L4.explanation: macOS keeps home folders under /Users, not /home; the default download folder is Downloads inside it. Same structure as Ubuntu, one different label. Finder shows Downloads in the sidebar; the terminal shows the same folder with ls ~/Downloads, because they are one folder.

L4.prompt_tpl: Windows user Asha downloads setup.msi with Chrome's default settings. She opens a WSL terminal. Give the absolute Linux path at which WSL sees that file.
L4.answer: /mnt/c/Users/Asha/Downloads/setup.msi
L4.explanation: WSL mounts the Windows C: drive at /mnt/c, so C:\Users\Asha\Downloads becomes /mnt/c/Users/Asha/Downloads, with forward slashes and the same folder names. The file was written by a Windows browser, so it is on the Windows side; WSL's own home, /home/asha, is a different place.

L4.prompt_tpl: You click Download on a PDF and the browser shows it in a bar at the bottom. Where is the PDF now?
L4.answer: In a file in your Downloads folder, which any program can open
L4.explanation: The bar is a list, not a location. The bytes were written to a file in Downloads, and the entry in the bar just points there. Closing the browser changes nothing; the file stays. The server still has its copy too: a download is a copy, so nothing was taken from the site.
options: In a file in your Downloads folder, which any program can open
Inside the browser, until you choose to save it
Still on the server, with the browser showing a view of it

L4.prompt_tpl: A download is {s} MB in total, {d} MB have arrived, and the browser reports a steady {r} MB/s. How many seconds remain?
L4.explanation: Remaining bytes divided by rate: 4700 - 300 = 4400 MB at 25 MB/s is 176 s. Note the unit: the browser reports MB/s (bytes), while the plan is sold in Mbps (bits), eight times larger a number for the same speed. Until this reaches zero the file is name.crdownload and is not usable.

L4.prompt_tpl: ls ~/Downloads shows ubuntu.iso.crdownload and nothing else. You double-click it. What is it, and what happens?
L4.answer: An unfinished Chrome download; it is incomplete bytes and no program can use it yet
L4.explanation: Chrome writes arriving bytes under name.crdownload and renames to the real name only when the last byte lands. If the browser is still downloading, wait; if the browser is closed, the download was interrupted and the file is a truncated fragment. Opening it gives an error or rubbish. Firefox uses .part the same way.
options: An unfinished Chrome download; it is incomplete bytes and no program can use it yet
A compressed copy of the ISO that needs to be extracted
A finished download with an odd name; renaming it fixes it

L4.prompt_tpl: You double-click a downloaded installer on Windows and see 'Windows protected your PC', with a small 'More info' link. What produced the warning, and what should you check before deciding?
L4.answer: The browser marked the file as downloaded from the internet (the Zone.Identifier mark), and SmartScreen, seeing an unfamiliar program with that mark, stopped it. The warning is about the source, not the icon. Check the download list for the exact domain the file came from and compare it with the maker's real domain; check the full filename with extensions shown; and ask which of the three sources it was. If it came from a search result or a forwarded link, delete it. 'More info, Run anyway' is the click every scam's instructions tell you to make.
L4.explanation: The warning is the OS applying this concept's mark and the source rule from 'Installing and removing software'. Knowing what triggered it turns a scary dialog into a checklist.

L4.prompt_tpl: A download page shows a small grey 'Download' link and, above it, a large green 'DOWNLOAD NOW' button. The green one saves Setup_Downloader.exe; the download list shows it came from a different domain than the page. Analyse what happened and what to do with the file.
L4.answer: The green button was an advertisement dressed as the page's button, a common trick on free-download sites; it fetched a program from the advertiser's own server, which the download list reveals by domain. Setup_Downloader.exe is a stranger's program by the source rule: delete it without running it, then use the small link, and check that its file comes from the domain of the site or of the maker. The download list's source column is the evidence, because the page's layout cannot be trusted and the filename is a claim.
L4.explanation: Transfer: an unfamiliar page layout resolved by two facts from this concept, that the list records the source and that a downloaded program is inert until run. The decoy button is one of the most common ways a home machine gets a stranger's program.

L4.prompt_tpl: Foundations' 'Running Python: interpreter, scripts, environments' begins by installing Python from python.org. Walk through what happens between clicking the installer link and Python being usable, naming where the file lands, what mark it carries, and which act is the risky one.
L4.answer: Clicking the link makes the browser copy python-3.x.y-amd64.exe into Downloads (C:\Users\name\Downloads on Windows); the OS marks it as from the internet, and the download list records python.org as the source. Nothing is installed yet. Double-clicking runs the installer, the risky act, because it runs with your powers; the mark makes Windows warn once. Because the source is the maker's own domain, that is the second-best source and acceptable. The installer then copies Python's files into the system and Python becomes a command. On Ubuntu the same result comes from apt with no download step of your own.
L4.explanation: Connecting download to install to run: three acts that beginners collapse into one, separated here so the risky one is visible. The same walk applies to VS Code, Git and every later tool.

The path: absolute and relative
The filename, the extension, and the lie an extension can tell
Installing and removing software, and where software comes from

concepts.t: Accounts, passwords, a password manager, and two-factor authentication

L0.body:
Whetstone signs you in with Google.
 that Google account IS your account:
 lose it and your drill history is gone
 do these once, today, at
 myaccount.google.com > Security:
  1 recovery phone AND recovery email
  2 2-Step Verification: ON
    (Google prompt, or Authenticator app)
  3 backup codes: 10 codes, 8 digits,
    each used once; print, keep at home
  4 password: 15+ characters, unique;
    four random words work:
    kite marble onion rail
  5 a password manager for every other
    site: one strong password per site
 sign in at least every 2 years:
 Google deletes inactive accounts
L0.cloze: Whetstone signs in with {{c1::Google}}, so that account is your account and losing it loses your history. Set a recovery phone and email, turn on {{c2::2-Step Verification}}, and print the {{c3::10}} single-use backup codes. Use a long unique password, 15 or more characters, and a password {{c4::manager}} so no other site shares it. Google may delete an account unused for {{c5::2}} years.

concepts.L1: An account is an identity (your email) plus proofs you own it: a password, a second factor (a code from a device you hold), and recovery options (a phone, another email, backup codes) for when one is lost. A password manager keeps a different long password per site. Whetstone's identity is your Google account.
concepts.L2: The miss: that the danger is someone guessing your password, so a clever one with symbols is the defence. Passwords are lost by reuse (a breach at one site is tried at every site) and by phishing (typed on a lookalike host). And more accounts are lost than stolen: a broken phone plus no recovery options locks you out for good.
concepts.L3: Mechanism. Breaches leak email-password pairs; attackers try every pair at every site, so one reused password is every account; a manager makes uniqueness free. Length beats symbols: 8 characters from 62 symbols give 62^8 possibilities; four random words from a 7776-word list give 7776^4, 17 times more, and are typeable. NIST SP 800-63B: length, no composition rules, no forced changes. A second factor means a stolen password alone fails: an app code or a Google prompt beats SMS, which a SIM swap can capture; SMS beats nothing. Codes typed into a lookalike are relayed live, so passkeys, which answer only the host they were made for, are phishing-proof. A lost phone is the common failure; printed backup codes and a recovery email survive it. Google deletes personal accounts unused for two years after warnings. 20 Security's 'MFA and phishing-resistant authentication' is the adult version.

L4.prompt_tpl: Whetstone signs you in with Google and has no password of its own. You lose access to that Google account. What happens to your learning history?
L4.answer: It is unreachable unless you recover the Google account; Whetstone cannot verify you any other way
L4.explanation: Whetstone stores your progress under the identity Google vouches for. No Google account, no way to prove you are you. Recovery options (phone, email, backup codes) are the way back in, and they only work if you set them before the loss. That is why this concept sits in the ramp: it is a prerequisite for using the system.
options: It is unreachable unless you recover the Google account; Whetstone cannot verify you any other way
Nothing: Whetstone keeps a separate password you can use instead
Nothing: signing in with a new Google account shows the same history

L4.prompt_tpl: A password is {L} characters long, each chosen from {N} possible symbols. How many distinct passwords are possible?
L4.explanation: Each position is an independent choice, so multiply: 62 symbols (letters both cases and digits) at 8 characters is 62^8 = 218 340 105 584 896, about 2.2 x 10^14. Adding one character multiplies by N; adding a symbol class only raises N a little. Length is the lever, which is why 15 characters is the current recommendation.

L4.prompt_tpl: A passphrase is {k} words, each picked at random from a list of 7776 words (the EFF dice list). How many distinct passphrases are possible?
L4.explanation: 7776 choices per word, k independent words: 7776^4 = 3 656 158 440 062 976, about 3.7 x 10^15, more than 8 random characters from 62 symbols, and far easier to type and remember. The words must be chosen at random (dice, or the manager's generator), not by you; a favourite phrase is in the attackers' lists.

L4.prompt_tpl: Site A is breached and your email and password there are published. Which single habit would have kept your other accounts safe?
L4.answer: A different password on every site, kept in a password manager
L4.explanation: Attackers try leaked pairs at every popular site within hours. A unique password per site means the breach at A costs you A and nothing else. Symbols in a reused password change nothing, since the attacker has the password itself. Changing passwords on a schedule does not help either; NIST dropped that advice.
options: A different password on every site, kept in a password manager
A password with symbols and digits, reused everywhere
Changing every password every 90 days

L4.prompt_tpl: What does turning on 2-Step Verification add to a Google sign-in?
L4.answer: A second proof from a device you hold, such as a prompt or a 6-digit app code, after the password
L4.explanation: The password is something you know; the second step is something you have, your phone. A stolen password alone then fails. It is not a second password, and it is not a check on the site: it does nothing against typing both into a lookalike, which is what passkeys and reading the URL are for.
options: A second proof from a device you hold, such as a prompt or a 6-digit app code, after the password
A second, longer password asked after the first
A check that the site you are signing in to is really Google

L4.prompt_tpl: P@ssw0rd! satisfies every rule a form can ask for: upper, lower, digit, symbol, 9 characters. Why does it fail anyway, and what does the current NIST guidance say instead?
L4.answer: It is 'Password' with the substitutions everyone makes, and it is in every breach list, so an attacker tries it in the first second; composition rules produce these predictable patterns rather than randomness. NIST SP 800-63B now says: length is what matters (8 minimum, 15 recommended), no composition rules, no forced periodic changes, accept long passphrases with spaces, and reject anything found in breach lists. Four random words beat any clever substitution.
L4.explanation: The why: rules that people satisfy predictably add no randomness. Strength is the number of equally likely possibilities, which length and true randomness raise and symbol rules do not.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compare 8 random characters from 62 symbols with 4 random words from a {w}-word list. How many times more possibilities does the passphrase have? Answer to 1 decimal place.
L4.explanation: 7776^4 is about 3.66 x 10^15 and 62^8 is about 2.18 x 10^14, so the passphrase has about 16.7 times as many possibilities while being four ordinary words long. Estimate first: 62^2 = 3844 and 62^2.2 is about 8800, so 7776 is about 62^2.17; then 7776^4 is about 62^8.7, and the ratio is about 62^0.7, roughly 18. Then compute exactly. Exponent estimates go wrong by factors of ten easily, so always verify them.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your phone with the Authenticator app is stolen. You have a recovery email and printed backup codes. Walk through getting back in, and say what happens to someone who set up 2-Step Verification but neither of those.
L4.answer: Sign in with the password; when asked for the second step, choose 'try another way' and enter one of the printed 8-digit backup codes, which works once. Then, in Security, remove the old phone, add the new one, and generate a fresh set of 10 codes (the old set is cancelled). The recovery email is the fallback if even that fails, and it is where Google's warnings arrive. Someone with no recovery email and no codes has a password that is no longer enough and no way to prove ownership; Google's automated recovery may refuse, and the account, and everything signed in through it, is gone.
L4.explanation: The consequence question: 2-Step Verification without recovery options turns a lost phone into a lost account. Recovery is part of the setup, not an extra.

L4.prompt_tpl: An email says: 'Your Google Account will be deleted in 24 hours under the inactive account policy. Verify now at https://accounts-google.com-verify.net/keep'. The policy is real. Using this concept and 'A URL, part by part', respond.
L4.answer: The policy is real but is about two years of no sign-in, with warnings sent over months, never a 24-hour deadline; urgency is the tell. The host's owned part is com-verify.net, not google.com; Google had no say in it. Do not click. Open a new tab, type myaccount.google.com yourself, sign in there, and check the Security page; simply signing in already counts as activity. A password typed into the lookalike would be relayed to the real Google, and an SMS or app code typed there would be relayed too, which is why only passkeys resist this.
L4.explanation: Transfer: a plausible pretext built on a true fact, defeated by two checks, the deadline against the real policy and the host against the real domain. Every phishing message contains a true fact and a wrong host.

L4.prompt_tpl: A password manager refuses to fill your bank password on paypal.com.evil.ru, though the page looks exactly like the bank. Explain why this refusal is a security feature and what it has in common with a passkey; name the 20 Security concept that develops the idea.
L4.answer: The manager stored the password against the host it was created on, and fills only when the host matches. It reads the URL by the right-to-left rule every time, tirelessly, and a lookalike fails the match, so its refusal is the machine catching what the eye misses. A passkey does the same one level deeper: the key is bound to the host name and cannot answer a different host at all, so there is nothing to relay. Both convert 'read the URL' from a habit into a mechanism. 20 Security's 'MFA and phishing-resistant authentication' is where this becomes the definition of phishing resistance.
L4.explanation: Connecting the URL concept to authentication: the strongest defences are the ones that make the host check automatic. A tool that will not fill is telling you something; do not paste around it.

prereqs: A URL, part by part

concepts.t: Touch typing, and why it is a prerequisite rather than a nicety

L0.body:
home row: left A S D F   right J K L ;
 the bumps on F and J find it blind
 each finger owns a column; thumbs: space
 eyes on the SCREEN, never on the keys
 a 'word' = 5 characters, spaces included
 2,000 words a day:
   at 25 WPM  ->  80 minutes
   at 55 WPM  ->  36.4 minutes
   gap: 43.6 minutes, every day
 accuracy first; speed follows
L0.cloze: Home row: {{c1::A S D F}} under the left hand, {{c2::J K L ;}} under the right; the raised bumps on {{c3::F and J}} find it without looking. A typing 'word' is {{c4::5}} characters, spaces included. 2,000 words a day take 80 minutes at 25 WPM and 36.4 at 55 WPM: a gap of {{c5::43.6}} minutes every day.

concepts.L1: Touch typing is typing with all ten fingers from the home row, each finger owning its keys and the eyes on the screen. Speed is words per minute, a word being 5 characters by convention. Hunt-and-peck reaches 20 to 30 WPM; a trained touch typist 55 or more, and the gap is a fixed fraction of every hour at the keyboard.
concepts.L2: The miss is that typing is a nicety because thinking is the bottleneck. The minutes are the smaller cost: when every command is effortful you stop trying things, and with eyes on the keys the screen goes unread, so every typo is found after Enter. The habit that makes programmers good, try it and see, needs a cheap keyboard.
concepts.L3: Time at the keyboard is $t = n/w$ minutes for $n$ words at $w$ words per minute, so two speeds differ by $n(1/w_{1} - 1/w_{2})$. For 2,000 words a day, 25 against 55 WPM is $2000(0.04 - 0.01818) = 43.6$ minutes, about 218 hours over 300 days; and 2,000 words is a modest day of code, commands and messages. The larger loss is not in minutes. Hunt-and-peck keeps the eyes on the keys, so the screen goes unread while typing: a typo is noticed only after Enter, and the message Foundations' 'Reading an error message' teaches you to read arrives as a surprise rather than prevented. Touch typing works because the fingers learn positions, not the eyes: the bumps on F and J anchor both hands, every key is a fixed reach from the home row, and after a few weeks the mapping runs without attention. Accuracy before speed: an error costs three keystrokes to repair, so speed built on errors plateaus.

L4.prompt_tpl: You type {n} words in a day. At {w} words per minute, how many minutes does that take? Answer to 2 decimal places.
L4.explanation: Minutes are words divided by words per minute. The division is the whole model: a fixed amount of text costs time in inverse proportion to speed, which is why doubling speed halves the time. Check the units: words divided by words per minute leaves minutes.

L4.prompt_tpl: A typing test reports that you typed {c} characters in {m} minutes with no errors. Using the convention of 5 characters per word, what was your speed in words per minute?
L4.explanation: Typing sites count a word as 5 characters, spaces included, so that 'a' and 'antidisestablishment' do not count the same. Divide characters by 5 for words, then by minutes for WPM. Every draw here comes out as a whole number, which is a useful check on the arithmetic.

L4.prompt_tpl: You type {n} words a day. How many minutes a day does a hunt-and-peck typist at {w1} WPM lose compared with a touch typist at {w2} WPM? Answer to 1 decimal place.
L4.explanation: Compute the time at each speed and subtract. At 2,000 words a day, 25 versus 55 WPM is 80 minus 36.4, or 43.6 minutes: three quarters of an hour, every day, spent on the keyboard rather than on the problem. The gap grows in proportion to the amount typed.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which keys are the home row, where the fingers rest between keystrokes?
L4.answer: A S D F under the left hand and J K L ; under the right
L4.explanation: The home row is the middle row of letters. The left fingers rest on A S D F and the right on J K L and the semicolon, thumbs on the space bar. Every other key is a short, fixed reach from there, which is what lets the fingers learn positions without the eyes.
options: A S D F under the left hand and J K L ; under the right
Q W E R under the left hand and U I O P under the right
Z X C V under the left hand and M , . / under the right

L4.prompt_tpl: The F and J keys carry a small raised bar. What is it for?
L4.answer: Finding the home row by touch, so the eyes can stay on the screen
L4.explanation: The bars are homing marks: the index fingers feel for them and the whole hand is then placed without looking. They exist precisely because touch typing keeps the eyes on the screen; after any reach away from the home row, the fingers find their way back by the bumps.
options: Finding the home row by touch, so the eyes can stay on the screen
Marking the two most frequent letters in English
Spacing the keys evenly for the manufacturer

L4.prompt_tpl: Over {d} days of study at {n} words a day, how many hours in total does typing at {w1} WPM instead of {w2} WPM cost? Answer to the nearest hour.
L4.explanation: Minutes lost per day times days, divided by 60. For 300 days at 2,000 words, the 25-versus-55 gap is 43.6 minutes a day, about 218 hours a year: roughly five full working weeks. Six weeks of fifteen-minute practice sessions is about 10 hours, so the investment repays itself within the first two months.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your speed rises from {w1} to {w2} WPM. By what percentage does the time spent typing a fixed amount of text fall? Answer as a percentage to 1 decimal place.
L4.explanation: Time is proportional to 1/speed, so the new time is w1/w2 of the old and the saving is 1 minus that. From 25 to 55 WPM the time falls by 54.5 percent, not by 120 percent: a speed that more than doubles cannot save more than half the time. Estimate first: doubling saves half, so a bit more than double saves a bit more than half.

L4.prompt_tpl: A learner types 45 WPM with three fingers while looking at the keys, faster than many beginners who touch type. Give two reasons to learn touch typing anyway.
L4.answer: First, the eyes. Looking at the keys means not looking at the screen, so a typo is seen only after Enter, and reading an error while typing the fix is impossible. Second, the ceiling: three fingers and a glance per key cap speed at roughly what they already have, while touch typing keeps improving with practice, because the fingers move to the next key while the current one is still being pressed. A third: touch typing frees attention, so the keyboard stops being something you think about.
L4.explanation: The speed number understates the difference. Hunt-and-peck is limited by the eyes and by one hand doing everything; touch typing is limited only by practice. The learner in the question would be slower for the first three weeks and faster for the rest of their life.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two typing-test results: 62 WPM at 88 percent accuracy, and 45 WPM at 99 percent accuracy. Which is the better typist for writing code, and why does the arithmetic of errors favour them?
L4.answer: The 45 WPM typist. At 88 percent accuracy 12 words in every 100 are wrong; in code one wrong character is a failed run, so each error costs far more than the word it sits in: noticing it, finding it, deleting and retyping it, and running again. Even counting only correct words, 62 times 0.88 is 54.6 against 44.6, a small lead that the repair cost wipes out many times over. Typing trainers such as keybr add a new letter only once the current ones are typed reliably, for the same reason: speed built on errors plateaus, accuracy built first keeps rising.
L4.explanation: Speed and accuracy are not two scores to be traded; accuracy is the foundation speed is built on. In prose a typo is a smudge, in code it is a stopped program, so the cost of an error is the cost of a whole edit-run cycle.

L4.prompt_tpl: Model the cost of typos in code: each typo that reaches the program costs about {s} seconds to notice, locate and fix after the run fails. You type {n} words of code a day with {e} typos per 100 words. About how many minutes a day does that cost? Answer to 1 decimal place.
L4.answer: n e s / 6000 minutes: (n / 100) typos-per-hundred blocks times e typos times s seconds, divided by 60. n=1000, e=2, s=30 -> 10; n=1000, e=2, s=60 -> 20; n=1000, e=5, s=30 -> 25.
L4.explanation: Number of typos is n/100 times e; multiply by seconds each and divide by 60 for minutes. At 2,000 words with 12 typos per 100 and a minute to fix each, that is 240 minutes: four hours, more than the whole speed gap of the previous items. The model is crude and the 30 to 60 seconds is an assumption, but the conclusion survives any reasonable figure: in code, accuracy is worth more than speed.

L4.prompt_tpl: Design the first six weeks of typing practice for a beginner with 15 minutes a day. Say what to use first, what to add later, and one thing to check about a typing website before using it.
L4.answer: Weeks 1 to 4: a structured course that places the letters one at a time and enforces accuracy, such as the Typing.com lessons or keybr, which adds a letter only when the current ones are accurate; 15 minutes every day, not an hour on Sunday, because the fingers learn by repetition spaced over days. No speed tests until every letter is placed. Weeks 5 to 6: keep the lessons and add Monkeytype for realistic text, watching accuracy stay above 97 percent. The check: read the address bar before typing anything; searches for Monkeytype rank lookalike domains above the real monkeytype.com, and a lookalike site can carry anything.
L4.explanation: Design, not recall: the plan orders accuracy before speed, distributes practice, and applies the URL-reading habit from the network section to a live case. Fifteen minutes a day is about 10 hours over six weeks, repaid within two months by the arithmetic of the tier-2 items.

The prompt, the command, the argument, and the Enter key

concepts.t: Keyboard shortcuts as a system, not as a list

L0.body:
modifier + letter = a verb
   Ctrl on Windows and Linux
   Cmd on macOS (same letter)
 Z undo    S save    F find
 A select all   X cut  C copy  V paste
 T new tab      W close tab
 Shift reverses or extends:
   Ctrl+Shift+Z redo (Ctrl+Y on Windows)
   Ctrl+Shift+T reopen the closed tab
   Shift+arrow selects
 switch program: Alt+Tab (Cmd+Tab, Mac)
 switch tab inside it: Ctrl+Tab
 terminal: Ctrl+C is stop, not copy
L0.cloze: A shortcut is a modifier plus a letter, and the letter is a verb shared by every program: {{c1::Z}} undo, {{c2::S}} save, {{c3::F}} find, A select all, X cut, C copy, V paste, T new tab, W close tab. The modifier is Ctrl on Windows and Linux and {{c4::Cmd}} on macOS. Adding Shift reverses or extends: Ctrl+Shift+Z redo, Ctrl+Shift+T reopen the closed tab, Shift+arrow selects. {{c5::Alt+Tab}} (Cmd+Tab on a Mac) switches program; Ctrl+Tab switches tab inside it.

concepts.L1: A keyboard shortcut is a modifier key held while a letter is pressed, and the letters are verbs every program is expected to honour: Z undo, S save, F find, A select all, X cut, C copy, V paste, T new tab, W close. The modifier is Ctrl on Windows and Linux, Cmd on macOS; adding Shift reverses or extends the verb.
concepts.L2: The miss is treating shortcuts as a list to memorise per program, so learning none. They are one small vocabulary the whole desktop shares: learn Ctrl+S once and it works in the editor, the browser and next year's spreadsheet. The exception is the terminal, where Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z were taken long before they meant copy and undo.
concepts.L3: The letters were chosen once and copied everywhere. The original Macintosh (1984) put undo, cut, copy and paste on Z, X, C and V, four adjacent keys under the left hand, so the right hand never leaves the mouse; Windows adopted the same letters, and a program that used its own would be unusable. A keypress arrives as a letter plus modifier flags, and each layer of the system looks at it in turn: the operating system first (Alt+Tab or Cmd+Tab to switch program, Cmd+Space to search), then the program in front (Ctrl+S, Ctrl+F, Ctrl+Tab), then the text box with the cursor (Shift+arrow selects, Ctrl+arrow jumps a word). A shortcut that 'does nothing' usually reached the wrong window. The terminal breaks the pattern: Ctrl+C is interrupt and Ctrl+Z suspends the running program, which Foundations' 'Processes and job control' explains; the previous concept gave the copy keys that replace them.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are editing hello.py in VS Code on Ubuntu and want to save it. Which keys?
L4.answer: Ctrl+S
L4.explanation: S is the save verb everywhere on the desktop, and Ctrl is the modifier on Linux and Windows. Ctrl+Shift+S is Save As in VS Code, the Shift-extended form that asks for a new name; Alt+S is nothing in particular. On a Mac the same verb is Cmd+S.
options: Ctrl+S
Ctrl+Shift+S
Alt+S

L4.prompt_tpl: On macOS, which key plays the role Ctrl plays in Windows and Linux shortcuts?
L4.answer: Cmd, the Command key
L4.explanation: The letters are the same on every system; only the modifier changes. Cmd+S saves, Cmd+Z undoes, Cmd+F finds. Option (Alt) and Fn are other modifiers with other jobs. A Mac still has a Ctrl key, and in the terminal Ctrl+C is still interrupt.
options: Cmd, the Command key
Option
Fn

L4.prompt_tpl: You deleted a paragraph by accident in your editor. Which shortcut brings it back?
L4.answer: Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on macOS)
L4.explanation: Z is undo, the most valuable verb of the set: it makes every mistake in an editor cheap. Ctrl+X is cut, which would remove more. Redo, the reverse of undo, is Ctrl+Shift+Z in most programs and Ctrl+Y in many Windows ones; both mean 'put back what undo removed'.
options: Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on macOS)
Ctrl+Y (Cmd+Y on macOS)
Ctrl+X (Cmd+X on macOS)

L4.prompt_tpl: Two programs are open on Ubuntu, a browser and VS Code, with VS Code in front. You press Alt+Tab once and release. What happens?
L4.answer: The browser comes to the front
L4.explanation: Alt+Tab is handled by the operating system, not the program: it switches to the most recently used other program, and holding Alt while pressing Tab again walks further down the list. Ctrl+Tab is the program-level cousin, switching between tabs inside the window in front. On a Mac the program switcher is Cmd+Tab.
options: The browser comes to the front
The browser's next tab is selected
VS Code opens a new tab

L4.prompt_tpl: In a web browser you closed a tab by mistake. Which shortcut reopens it?
L4.answer: Ctrl+Shift+T (Cmd+Shift+T on macOS)
L4.explanation: T is the new-tab verb, W closes one, and Shift reverses: Ctrl+Shift+T reopens the tab most recently closed. Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Safari all honour it. Knowing that Shift reverses lets you guess a shortcut you were never taught.
options: Ctrl+Shift+T (Cmd+Shift+T on macOS)
Ctrl+T (Cmd+T on macOS)
Ctrl+W (Cmd+W on macOS)

L4.prompt_tpl: You save your file {k} times a day. Reaching for the mouse, opening the File menu and clicking Save takes about {m} seconds; Ctrl+S takes about {s} second. About how many seconds a day does the shortcut save?
L4.explanation: Estimate first: 80 saves at 2 or 3 seconds each is a few minutes a day, and save is only one verb of a dozen. The seconds are the smaller gain; the larger one is that a shortcut does not break concentration, because the hands stay on the keys and the eyes on the text. The timings are assumptions; the conclusion holds for any plausible ones.

L4.prompt_tpl: You meant to save your code but pressed Ctrl+S while the browser window was in front. What happens, and what does it show about how shortcuts work?
L4.answer: The browser offers to save the web page as a file: the same verb, save, interpreted by whichever program is in front. Nothing happens to the code; your editor never saw the keypress. It shows that a shortcut is delivered to the window that has focus, so a shortcut that seems to do nothing, or something odd, usually means the wrong window was in front. Press Escape to cancel the dialog, click into the editor, press Ctrl+S again.
L4.explanation: The letter is shared; the receiver is whoever has focus. Once that is clear, the same pattern explains Alt+Tab (the operating system receives it) and Shift+arrow (the text box receives it), and the odd moments become predictable.

L4.prompt_tpl: In a text editor you hold Shift and press the right arrow key five times. What happens?
L4.answer: The five characters to the right of the cursor become selected
L4.explanation: Arrow keys move the cursor; Shift extends: the same movement with Shift held selects everything the cursor passed over. Ctrl+Shift+arrow (Option+Shift+arrow on a Mac) selects a word at a time by the same rule. Delete removes a selection, so Shift+arrows then Backspace is the keyboard's way of removing a run of text.
options: The five characters to the right of the cursor become selected
The cursor moves five characters right and nothing is selected
Five characters are deleted

L4.prompt_tpl: You open a spreadsheet program you have never used. You need to find the cell containing the word total, then undo a change you just made. Without reading any documentation, which keys do you try first, and why is that a reasonable bet?
L4.answer: Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on a Mac) for find, then Ctrl+Z for undo. It is a reasonable bet because the verbs are shared across the desktop and a program that broke them would be rejected by its users; the spreadsheet's makers know that. If a guess fails, open the menus: every entry shows its shortcut beside its name, which is how the remaining shortcuts of any program are learnt, a few at a time, when needed.
L4.explanation: Transfer: the concept was never about a spreadsheet, yet it predicts the spreadsheet's keys. The general method is guess the shared verb, then read the menu; nobody memorises a program's list.

L4.prompt_tpl: Sort these into the layer that receives them, operating system, program in front, or the text box with the cursor: Alt+Tab, Ctrl+S, Shift+Right arrow, Cmd+Space. Then say what the layering implies about a shortcut that does nothing.
L4.answer: Operating system: Alt+Tab (switch program) and Cmd+Space (Spotlight search on a Mac). Program in front: Ctrl+S. Text box with the cursor: Shift+Right arrow. The system looks at a keypress first and passes it down, so a shortcut that does nothing almost always reached the wrong layer: the intended program is not in front, or the cursor is not in the box you think it is. Check which window and which box has focus before concluding the shortcut is broken.
L4.explanation: The layering is the mechanism behind every 'my shortcut stopped working' moment. Foundations' 'Processes and job control' adds the terminal layer, where Ctrl+Z reaches the shell as suspend instead of undo.

L4.prompt_tpl: In VS Code you press Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on a Mac). What appears?
L4.answer: The Command Palette: a searchable list of every command, with its shortcut shown beside it
L4.explanation: The palette is how a shortcut you do not know is found: type a few letters of what you want to do, read the shortcut next to the match, and next time press the keys. It is the editor's equivalent of reading the menu, and the reason nobody needs a printed list of VS Code's several hundred shortcuts.
options: The Command Palette: a searchable list of every command, with its shortcut shown beside it
A print dialog
A new project window

prereqs: Touch typing, and why it is a prerequisite rather than a nicety
Copy and paste in a terminal is not the same as everywhere else
A code editor is not a word processor
