concepts.t: Screenshots, error messages, and how to report a problem so it can be solved

L0.body:
a picture of the screen:
   Windows  Win+Shift+S  (to clipboard;
            Win+PrtScn saves a file)
   macOS    Cmd+Shift+4, drag a box;
            saved on the Desktop
   Ubuntu   PrtScn, then capture;
            saved in ~/Pictures/Screenshots
 an ERROR is text: select, copy, paste
   never photograph a screen
 a report that can be answered:
   1 what I ran   (the exact command)
   2 what I expected
   3 what happened (the whole message)
   4 what I already tried
L0.cloze: Screenshot keys: {{c1::Win+Shift+S}} on Windows (to the clipboard), {{c2::Cmd+Shift+4}} on macOS (saved on the Desktop), {{c3::PrtScn}} on Ubuntu (saved in ~/Pictures/Screenshots). An error is {{c4::text}}: select it, copy it, paste it; never photograph the screen. A report that can be answered has four parts: what I ran, what I {{c5::expected}}, what happened with the whole message, and what I already {{c6::tried}}.

concepts.L1: A screenshot is a picture of the screen; each OS has a key for it and a place it lands. An error message is text and travels as text: selected, copied, pasted whole. A report that can be answered has four parts: the command run, what you expected, what happened with the whole message pasted, and what you already tried.
concepts.L2: The miss is the phone photo of the screen: blurry, uncopyable, unsearchable, cut off at the picture's edge. The helper cannot paste it into a search or compare it with their own output. The second miss is 'it doesn't work': a report with no command, no message and no expectation cannot be answered, only questioned.
concepts.L3: An error message is data a helper acts on: they search for it, run the command, and compare their output with yours. A photo destroys all three and turns a few hundred bytes of exact text into megabytes read by eye. Pictures are for what is only visual: a layout or a dialog. Paste the whole message: a Python traceback ends with the error's kind, but the lines above name the file, the line and the chain of calls, which Foundations' 'Reading an error message' reads bottom up. The four-part report is a small experiment written down: expected against actual is the observation, the command and its directory let someone reproduce it, what you tried rules out the obvious replies. Tightened into a runnable script, the same parts become what Research Practice's 'The minimal reproduction' calls the unit of currency. Before sending, read what you pasted: prompts and history can carry passwords.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your program printed a long error in the terminal. What is the best way to include it in a message asking for help?
L4.answer: Select the text, copy it with the terminal's copy key, and paste it as text
L4.explanation: Text can be searched, run and compared; a photo cannot, and a summary in your own words loses the exact wording the helper needs. Copy with the terminal's own key, Ctrl+Shift+C on Ubuntu, Cmd+C on macOS, right-click in Windows Terminal, since plain Ctrl+C stops the program instead. Paste the whole message, including the lines above the last one.
options: Select the text, copy it with the terminal's copy key, and paste it as text
Photograph the screen with your phone and send the photo
Type a short summary of what it said in your own words

L4.prompt_tpl: On macOS you press Cmd+Shift+4, drag a rectangle over part of the screen, and release. Where is the picture?
L4.answer: A .png file on the Desktop, named Screenshot followed by the date and time
L4.explanation: macOS saves screenshots to the Desktop by default, as PNG files named like Screenshot 2026-09-10 at 14.02.31.png. Cmd+Shift+3 captures the whole screen the same way; Cmd+Shift+5 opens the screenshot toolbar, which is where the save location can be changed. Holding Ctrl as well sends the capture to the clipboard instead of a file.
options: A .png file on the Desktop, named Screenshot followed by the date and time
In the clipboard only, until you paste it
In ~/Pictures/Screenshots

L4.prompt_tpl: On Windows 11 you press Win+Shift+S and drag a rectangle. Where does the capture go first?
L4.answer: To the clipboard, ready to paste, with a notification; a file is also saved only if the Snipping Tool's automatic saving is on
L4.explanation: Win+Shift+S opens the Snipping Tool's capture overlay; the snip lands on the clipboard and a notification offers to open it for editing and saving. Recent Windows 11 builds can also save every snip automatically to Pictures, Screenshots, when that option is on. Win+PrtScn is the key that always writes a file there, of the whole screen.
options: To the clipboard, ready to paste, with a notification; a file is also saved only if the Snipping Tool's automatic saving is on
Directly to a file on the Desktop, and nowhere else
To the printer

L4.prompt_tpl: On Ubuntu 22.04 or later you press PrtScn, choose an area, and click the capture button. Which folder holds the file?
L4.answer: ~/Pictures/Screenshots
L4.explanation: Since GNOME 42, which Ubuntu 22.04 ships, PrtScn opens an interactive screenshot tool and captures are saved as PNG files in Pictures, Screenshots, inside your home folder. Shift+PrtScn captures the whole screen at once, Alt+PrtScn the window in front. The tilde in ~/Pictures/Screenshots is the home directory, from the path concept.
options: ~/Pictures/Screenshots
~/Desktop
~/Downloads

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of the four parts is missing from this report? 'I ran python3 hello.py in ~/proj and got: NameError: name 'pritn' is not defined. I expected it to print hello.'
L4.answer: What you already tried
L4.explanation: The command and directory are there, the expectation is there, and the message is pasted. Missing is what was already tried, so the first reply will be 'check the spelling of print', which the reporter may have done. Here the message itself names the typo; reading it would have closed the case before the report was written.
options: What you already tried
The exact command
What happened

L4.prompt_tpl: A screenshot of a full screen is a PNG of about {kb} kilobytes (1000 bytes each). The error text it shows is {c} characters at 1 byte each. About how many times larger is the picture than the text? Answer to the nearest whole number.
L4.explanation: Hundreds to thousands of times larger, and the bytes are the least of it: the text can be searched, run and compared, and the picture can only be looked at. The sizes here are typical, not exact; a screenshot's size depends on the screen and on what is on it, which is itself a reason the photo is the wrong medium for something that is already text.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Python error fills fifteen lines and you paste only the last one: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str. What has the helper lost?
L4.answer: The location. The last line says what kind of error and its message, but the lines above it, the traceback, name the file, the line number and the sequence of calls that led there; the helper now knows what went wrong but not where, and has to ask. Paste the whole thing, from the line beginning Traceback to the end. Foundations' 'Reading an error message' teaches reading it from the bottom up; that only works if the top is there.
L4.explanation: The last line is the diagnosis and the rest is the address. A report with only the diagnosis sends the helper looking through code they have not seen for a line the message would have named.

L4.prompt_tpl: A friend sends: 'my code doesn't work, help'. Write the three questions you must ask before you can help, and say why the report should have contained them.
L4.answer: What exactly did you run, and where (the command and the directory)? What did you expect to happen? What happened instead, pasted in full as text? Possibly a fourth: what have you tried already? Each is a fact only the reporter has; without them the helper is guessing, and the exchange spends its first three rounds collecting what one message could have carried. A report with the four parts is answerable on the first reply.
L4.explanation: Every answerable report is an expected-versus-actual observation with enough context to reproduce it. That is the shape of a bug report, of a question on a forum, and later of an experiment.

L4.prompt_tpl: Rewrite this so it can be answered: 'I tried to run my program and it gave some error about a file. I tried a few things. Please help.' You know they ran python3 read.py in ~/proj and saw FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'data.csv', and that ls showed data.csv inside ~/proj/data.
L4.answer: Ran: python3 read.py in ~/proj (pwd confirms). Expected: the program reads data.csv and prints the first rows. Happened: the full pasted output ending FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'data.csv'. Tried: ls shows no data.csv in ~/proj; it is in ~/proj/data. Question: should the script open data/data.csv, or should I run it from inside data? Written this way the report contains its own answer: the program looks for the file relative to the current directory, and the file is one folder down.
L4.explanation: Transfer: the four parts applied to an unfamiliar error. Naming the working directory turned a vague file complaint into a relative-path question from this domain's path concept, and the helper can answer in one line.

L4.prompt_tpl: Research Practice's 'The minimal reproduction' calls the smallest script that shows a problem the unit of currency of experimental work. Explain how the four-part report is an early form of it, and which part of the report becomes the script.
L4.answer: A minimal reproduction is expected-versus-actual made runnable: a script that anyone can execute, with the expectation written as a check. The report already has the pieces: 'what I ran' becomes the script, 'what I expected' becomes the assertion inside it, 'what happened' is the output the script reproduces, and 'what I tried' is the record of what was stripped away without changing the result. The report is the same thing in prose; the reproduction is the same thing in code.
L4.explanation: The habit learnt here on a NameError is the habit that later files a bug against a library or reproduces a paper: state what you did precisely enough that someone else can do it, and what you expected precisely enough that a difference is visible.

L4.prompt_tpl: A stranger on a help forum asks for a screenshot of your whole terminal, 'including the top of the window'. Your prompt shows your username, and the scrollback includes a command you typed with a password in it. What do you send?
L4.answer: Only the relevant error, as pasted text, after reading it through and removing any password, token or private path
L4.explanation: Help needs the error, not the window. Text can be read and trimmed before sending; a screenshot carries everything visible, and scrollback is visible. Usernames and paths are mild, a password is not, and a request for the whole window is a reason for care rather than compliance. Asking for help is safe; sending more than the question needs is not.
options: Only the relevant error, as pasted text, after reading it through and removing any password, token or private path
The full screenshot; a picture cannot be copied, so it is safe
Nothing; asking strangers for help is unsafe

prereqs: Keyboard shortcuts as a system, not as a list
Copy and paste in a terminal is not the same as everywhere else
The path: absolute and relative
